=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robust deployment, yet standard methods often prioritize posterior fidelity over diversity. This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy with a mean paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. We conducted a controlled experiment using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics, split into Primary (43 seeds) and Confirmatory Replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the hypothesis, the entropy-maximized intervention significantly worsened accuracy relative to the deterministic baseline in both cohorts. In the Primary cohort, the contrast was -0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The Replication cohort confirmed this direction with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight noise enhances robustness in this architecture, suggesting practitioners should not prioritize this mechanism over standard regularization for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in settings where confidence in predictions is as important as accuracy, yet basic neural networks do not inherently deliver this confidence [3]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to address this challenge, treating weights as distributions rather than point estimates to quantify uncertainty [5, 12]. However, deep learning methods often remain black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, and standard variational objectives typically minimize divergence (KL minimization) rather than explicitly optimizing for diversity [12]. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives.

This gap matters because uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity may behave differently under distribution shift. Research into uncertainty propagation emphasizes evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], yet *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Furthermore, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. This study validates or refutes the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [7] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization.

We address the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. Our research question is: Does explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training? We preregistered the following hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty quantification is established as increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2]. *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [18, 7]. *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

In the context of time-series, 1D convolutional neural networks are described as standard for various operations, providing context for time-series baselines against which Transformer robustness is measured [10]. However, the specific interaction between entropy-maximized weight noise and Transformer attention mechanisms under subject-disjoint shifts remains unexplored in the cited literature.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer. To avoid external dependencies and ensure controlled distribution shift, we generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). The data included subject clusters to simulate distribution shift between training and held-out sets.

The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input projection plus learned positional embedding(128,64). The encoder contained 2 blocks, each comprising LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual. The head consisted of a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6) output.

We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). All models were trained for fixed epochs (50) with SGD. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights to ensure comparability. We evaluated on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) and applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized two distinct cohorts to ensure robustness of the findings. The Primary cohort consisted of 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The Confirmatory Replication cohort consisted of 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). We did not pool these cohorts; each was analyzed separately according to the preregistered plan.

The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' The decision rule required the mean contrast to exceed this margin with statistical significance to support the hypothesis. If the contrast was negative or failed to exceed the margin, the hypothesis would be refuted. We report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for all metrics.

=== results ===
We report results separately for the Primary and Confirmatory Replication cohorts. We do not pool the data.

**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 1 and Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero). The preregistered decision is: direction_refuted. The intervention accuracy was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while the baseline accuracy was 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. Negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082, NegCtrl2: 0.909).

**Table 1: Primary Cohort Held-Out Classification Accuracy**
| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 2 and Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero). The preregistered decision is: direction_refuted. The intervention accuracy was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while the baseline accuracy was 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. Negative controls remained stable (NegCtrl1: 0.908, NegCtrl2: 0.9088).

**Table 2: Replication Cohort Held-Out Classification Accuracy**
| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

Training dynamics (Figure 2 and Figure 4) showed consistent separation between the intervention and baseline throughout the 50 epochs, indicating the performance gap was not due to convergence issues alone but persisted across training steps.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention significantly worsened performance compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would enhance robustness in this context.

Relating these quantitative findings to the reviewed prior work, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6]. However, our results suggest that when implemented via entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise in Transformers, this promise does not hold for subject-disjoint time-series data. This aligns with warnings in *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift*, which notes that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. While *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15], our data indicates that the specific objective of entropy maximization may introduce detrimental noise rather than beneficial regularization in attention-based architectures.

Furthermore, while 1D convolutional neural networks are described as standard for various operations in time-series contexts [10], the sensitivity of Transformers to weight perturbations may differ from CNNs. The failure of the intervention suggests that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this specific domain. The consistency between the Primary and Replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this is a stable negative result rather than a statistical anomaly.

=== limitations ===
This study has specific limitations that constrain the generalizability of the findings. First, the experiment used a synthetic testbed mimicking UCI HAR statistics rather than raw real-world data collection. While this allowed for controlled subject-disjoint splits, the synthetic nature means results may not fully capture the complexity of real-world sensor noise or biological variability. Second, the architecture was limited to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration; results may differ in deeper models or different attention mechanisms. Third, the study focused on subject-disjoint shifts; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift, activity definition changes) were not tested. We avoid overgeneralizing the recommendation to practitioners beyond the scope of the experiment; the refutation applies specifically to entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise in Transformers for subject-disjoint time-series classification.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a preregistered experiment to test whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis was refuted in both Primary and Confirmatory Replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly reducing accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These results indicate that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity do not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this context. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization when deploying similar Transformer models on subject-disjoint time-series data. Future work should investigate whether alternative uncertainty objectives or architecture-specific noise injections can recover the robustness benefits theorized in prior BNN literature.

payload.content:
=== abstract ===
This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. While Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) are often proposed to enhance robustness under covariate shift [6], the specific mechanism of entropy maximization versus posterior fidelity remains underexplored in attention-based architectures. We preregistered a hypothesis that an Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than a deterministic baseline, exceeding a worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We conducted experiments across two independent cohorts (Primary and Confirmatory Replication), each comprising 43 seeds, using a Transformer encoder trained on synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened performance. In the Primary cohort, the intervention worsened the contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The Confirmatory Replication cohort yielded consistent results, with a worsening of 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These findings refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization improves subject-disjoint generalization in this context, suggesting practitioners should not prioritize this mechanism over standard regularization for such tasks.

=== introduction ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is increasingly critical for deploying models in safety-sensitive applications, yet standard networks often fail to deliver reliable confidence estimates [3]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to address this by treating weights as distributions rather than point estimates, theoretically providing better calibration and robustness [5, 12]. However, practical implementation often faces challenges regarding computational complexity and convergence stability [7, 18]. A specific open problem remains whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity via entropy maximization, rather than posterior fidelity via KL minimization, generalize effectively to modern attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

Prior work indicates that BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], yet approximate Bayesian inference can sometimes perform poorly under such shifts [13]. Furthermore, while weight noise injection has been proposed to achieve robustness [15], the specific impact of maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions in Transformers is unknown. This work addresses the gap where prior studies explore weight noise and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but none explicitly maximize entropy for subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives.

We preregistered the following hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of0.0125098 proportion. This study reports the results of a rigorous experiment testing this claim, utilizing a subject-disjoint split to simulate real-world distribution shifts often encountered in human activity recognition [8].

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this, though deep learning methods are often described as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify [12]. Neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features are model-related versus data-related [5]. Uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], and standard backpropagation often lacks calibration [17].

Regarding robustness, BNNs are frequently cited for potential improvements under covariate shift [6]. However, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6], and approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. In the context of time-series, 1D convolutional neural networks are described as standard for various operations, providing context for time-series baselines against which Transformer robustness is measured [10]. While pretrained Transformers have shown improved out-of-distribution robustness in NLP [8], their behavior with explicit weight uncertainty in time-series remains less documented.

Methods to induce uncertainty include weight noise injection training [15] and entropy regularization [14]. However, constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes exist in BNNs [7, 18]. Some work develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16], while others investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2]. Batch normalization addresses internal covariate shift [9], but its interaction with explicit weight entropy maximization is not fully established. This study positions itself against these works by isolating the entropy maximization mechanism in a controlled Transformer setting.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). The final layer involved LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6) for classification.

To avoid external dependencies while maintaining ecological validity, we generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters). This approach allowed us to strictly control the subject-disjoint split without relying on external data loading pipelines that might introduce variability. We trained models for 50 epochs using SGD.

We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic Training, Identity Control), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). For each seed, we initialized identical model weights to ensure comparability. Evaluation was performed on held-out synthetic subjects to measure subject-disjoint generalization. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline).

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment was divided into two preregistered cohorts: a Primary block and a Confirmatory Replication block. The Primary cohort utilized 43 specific seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The Confirmatory Replication cohort utilized a distinct set of 43 seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). All seeds were generated preregistration to prevent selection bias.

The preregistered decision rule required applying the hypothesis test on the Primary block first. If the decision was conclusive, the Replication block served to confirm the finding. We never pooled the cohorts. We computed held-out classification accuracy as the primary metric. Statistical analysis involved computing mean metric values with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds. We applied a paired randomisation test to assess significance of the contrast between Intervention and Baseline. The hypothesis was considered supported only if the mean contrast exceeded 0.0125098 with the 95% CI excluding zero in the positive direction.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is **direction_refuted**.

Table 1 presents the final metric values per condition for the Primary cohort. Figure 1 visualizes these final metric values with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is **direction_refuted**.

Table 2 presents the final metric values per condition for the Replication cohort. Figure 3 visualizes these final metric values with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Deterministic Baseline in both cohorts, indicating that the performance drop is specific to the Entropy Maximization objective rather than noise injection per se.

=== discussion ===
The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to the deterministic baseline (Primary: -0.04805; Replication: -0.03482). This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would generalize better than posterior-fidelity objectives in this architecture.

These results relate directly to prior work on BNN robustness. While [6] states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, our findings suggest that specific implementations matter critically; entropy maximization alone may not suffice and can be detrimental. This aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. The failure of the intervention also extends the understanding of weight noise injection [15]; while noise can aid robustness, maximizing its entropy explicitly appears to disrupt the learned representations in Transformers, unlike in simpler architectures where stochastic weight sharing has shown promise [7].

The negative controls performed comparably to the baseline, suggesting that the deterministic training regime remains highly competitive for subject-disjoint tasks in this domain, potentially outperforming complex uncertainty mechanisms when data statistics are well-matched. This challenges the notion that practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. The consistency across 86 total seeds strengthens the reliability of this negative result, providing a calibrated view against overclaiming the benefits of Bayesian modifications in attention-based models [8].

=== limitations ===
A key limitation of this study is the use of a synthetic testbed mimicking UCI HAR statistics rather than raw real-world data. While this approach avoided external dependencies and ensured strict control over subject-disjoint splits, it may not capture the full complexity of real-world sensor noise and distribution shifts. Consequently, generalization to real-world deployment scenarios should be verified with raw inertial signals in future work. We explicitly distinguish this synthetic testbed from real-world generalization; while the statistics mimic human activity recognition, the synthetic generation process may omit subtle correlations present in physical data collection.

Additionally, regarding baseline context, while 1D convolutional neural networks are described as standard for various operations in time-series [10], this study focused on Transformer architectures. The interaction between entropy-maximized noise and convolutional baselines remains untested. Finally, while the sample size of 43 seeds per cohort is robust for statistical inference, the specific hyperparameters (e.g., 50 epochs, SGD) may limit the generalizability of the negative result to other optimization regimes or architecture scales.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report provides rigorous evidence that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not improve, and significantly worsens, subject-disjoint generalization in Transformer-based time-series classification. The hypothesis was refuted in both Primary and Confirmatory Replication cohorts with high statistical significance. These findings clarify the literature on Bayesian Neural Networks and robustness, indicating that entropy maximization is not a universally beneficial mechanism for out-of-distribution accuracy in this context. Practitioners are advised to prioritize standard deterministic training or validated regularization techniques over explicit entropy maximization for similar subject-disjoint tasks.

These findings clarify the literature on Bayesian Neural Networks and robustness, indicating that entropy maximization is not a universally beneficial mechanism for out-of-distribution accuracy in this context. Practitioners are advised to prioritize standard deterministic training or validated regularization techniques over explicit entropy maximization for similar subject-disjoint tasks.

=== abstract ===
This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. While prior work suggests uncertainty-inducing mechanisms may enhance robustness, it remains unclear whether optimizing for diversity via entropy maximization generalizes to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder and evaluated it on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened accuracy compared to the deterministic baseline in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the contrast was -0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002), and in the replication cohort, -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in this setting, suggesting practitioners should not prioritize this mechanism over standard regularization for such tasks.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly critical for deployment in safety-sensitive domains, yet basic neural networks do not inherently deliver this confidence [3]. Deep learning methods are often described as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, leading researchers to adopt Bayesian statistics as a formalism to address this limitation [12]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) intrinsically increase uncertainty regarding which features are model-related versus data-related [5], and uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4]. However, standard backpropagation lacks calibration, motivating probabilistic alternatives [17].

Despite the promise of BNNs, constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes persist [7, 18]. Specifically, while BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Furthermore, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. This work addresses a specific gap: while prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

We ask: Does explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training? In the context of time-series, 1D convolutional neural networks are described as standard for various operations, providing context for time-series baselines against which Transformer robustness is measured [10]. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. This study validates or refutes the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [7] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9]. *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15].

Optimization strategies also play a critical role. *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2]. *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements and posterior modes [7, 18]. *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16]. Finally, regarding the domain context, *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations, establishing the baseline landscape for time-series modeling [10].

=== method ===
**Approach**
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer. The intervention modifies the training objective to explicitly maximize the entropy of the multiplicative weight noise distributions, contrasting with standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

**Datasets**
We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). This approach avoids external dependencies while maintaining statistical fidelity to the domain where 1D CNNs are standard [10].

**Model**
The architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input projection plus learned positional embedding(128,64). The encoder contained 2 blocks, each comprising LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual. The head consisted of a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6) output.

**Conditions**
We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic Training, Identity Control), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for fixed epochs (50) with SGD.

**Evaluation**
We evaluated on held-out synthetic subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Preregistration**
The hypothesis was preregistered before the experiment ran: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' We did not silently change the hypothesis to fit the results.

**Seeds and Cohorts**
We utilized two disjoint sets of random seeds to ensure rigorous replication.
*   **Primary Cohort:** 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, ...).
*   **Confirmatory Replication Cohort:** 43 seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, ...).

**Metrics and Decision Rule**
The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered decision rule required the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast to exceed 0.0125098. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds. Any finding not aligned with the preregistered direction is labeled as refuted.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The result failed to exceed the worthwhile margin of 0.0125098; instead, it was negative. Preregistered decision: direction_refuted.

| Condition | Seeds | Held-out Classification Accuracy |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Proposed | 43 | 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] |
| Baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] |
| Negative_Control_1 | 43 | 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] |
| Negative_Control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

*Table 1: Primary Cohort Results.*

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 2). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. Preregistered decision: direction_refuted.

| Condition | Seeds | Held-out Classification Accuracy |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |
| Baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] |
| Negative_Control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| Negative_Control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

*Table 2: Replication Cohort Results.*

**Visualizations**
Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition. In all visualizations, the Proposed condition trails the Baseline and Negative Controls.

=== discussion ===
**Interpretation of Findings**
The results consistently refute the preregistered hypothesis. Explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters worsened out-of-distribution accuracy compared to deterministic training in both primary and replication cohorts. The negative contrast (-0.04805 in Primary, -0.03482 in Replication) indicates that optimizing for diversity via entropy maximization did not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this context.

**Relation to Literature**
These findings contradict the expectation that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity would improve robustness. While *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], our results suggest that specific implementations matter; entropy maximization on weight noise parameters may introduce detrimental instability compared to standard regularization. This aligns with warnings from *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift*, which notes that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

Furthermore, while *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15], our negative controls (FixedNoise, EntropyMin) performed similarly to the Deterministic Baseline (~0.908), whereas EntropyMax performed significantly worse (~0.860-0.871). This suggests that mere noise injection is not harmful, but actively maximizing entropy of that noise is. This extends the understanding of *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks*, which identifies constraints regarding computational requirements and convergence [7], by showing that optimization objectives targeting entropy can actively degrade performance in Transformers.

Regarding optimization, *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses tuning hyperparameters for robustness [11]. Our results imply that hyperparameter tuning alone may not rescue an objective function (entropy maximization) that is fundamentally misaligned with generalization in this architecture. The context of time-series modeling, where 1D CNNs are standard [10], suggests that Transformer-specific regularization needs may differ from convolutional baselines, and entropy maximization may not be the appropriate mechanism.

**Implications**
Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in subject-disjoint time-series classification using Transformers. The core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [7] may not translate directly to multiplicative weight noise in attention layers without modification.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may vary with deeper models or different attention mechanisms. We fixed training epochs at 50; longer training schedules might interact differently with entropy regularization. Finally, while we addressed the citation context for time-series baselines [10], we did not empirically benchmark against 1D CNNs in this study, focusing instead on the Transformer internal mechanisms.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a rigorous, preregistered experiment to test whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These findings clarify that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity do not automatically generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. Future work should investigate alternative regularization strategies that align better with Transformer dynamics in time-series domains.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robust deployment, yet standard methods often fail under distribution shift. This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated it on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. The study included a primary cohort (43 seeds) and a confirmatory replication cohort (43 seeds). Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed method yielded 0.8604 accuracy versus 0.9085 for the baseline (contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The replication cohort confirmed this degradation (contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). === introduction ===
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved significant success across various domains, yet they often lack calibrated confidence in their predictions [3]. Standard neural networks operate as black boxes where quantifying uncertainty is challenging, prompting the adoption of Bayesian statistics to formalize this uncertainty [12]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) aim to address this by modeling uncertainty over weights, distinguishing between model-related features and noise [5]. However, practical implementation faces hurdles; standard backpropagation lacks calibration [17], and uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in applications [4].

While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based approaches often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Furthermore, approximate Bayesian inference, often considered robust, can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Recent work explores stochasticity to mitigate these issues, such as weight noise injection training for robustness [15]. However, a specific gap remains: whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures. This study addresses whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. Validating or refuting this mechanism is crucial for guiding practitioners on whether to prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty quantification is increasingly recognized as essential for reliable deep learning. Surveys indicate that basic neural networks do not deliver confidence estimates inherently [3]. Bayesian Neural Networks provide a formalism to address this, though they intrinsically increase uncertainty about which analysis features are model-related [5]. Techniques such as dropout-based uncertainty propagation emphasize evaluation for detecting uncertain data [4], while probabilistic backpropagation highlights disadvantages in standard learning regarding scalability and calibration [17].

Regarding robustness and optimization, Node-based BNNs state that while BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with computational complexity [6]. Warnings exist that approximate Bayesian averaging can perform poorly under covariate shift [13]. In contrast, pretrained Transformers have been systematically measured for out-of-distribution generalization in NLP [8]. Internal covariate shift during training is often addressed by normalization techniques [9]. Weight noise injection has been proposed to achieve strong robustness in diffractive neural networks [15].

In the context of baseline architectures and optimization, 1D convolutional neural networks are described as standard for various operations, establishing the baseline landscape for time-series modeling [10]. Hyperparameter tuning in robust contexts is also critical; Bayesian optimization is discussed for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Other works investigate convergence stability, such as momentum breakdown in ill-conditioned regression [1] and learning rate effects on synthetic non-linear data [2]. Structural constraints in BNNs include computational requirements and posterior mode difficulties [7], [18]. Entropy has been used to measure uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and BNNs have been developed specifically for data with limited observations [16]. This work builds on these foundations by testing entropy maximization specifically within a Transformer architecture for subject-disjoint generalization.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of the attention mechanism. The goal was to explicitly maximize the entropy of the multiplicative weight noise distributions during training. We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), consisting of raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. The data included 6 classes and subject clusters, utilizing the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows to avoid external dependencies during the experimental phase.

The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder. It began with a Linear layer (9 input features to 64 hidden units) plus a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions). The encoder consisted of 2 blocks, each containing LayerNorm(64) followed by 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with query/key/value/output Linear layers (64 to 64). This was followed by a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear layer (64 to 128), ReLU activation, a Linear layer (128 to 64), and a final residual connection. The head comprised a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear layer (64 to 6) for classification.

We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic Training, Identity Control), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights to ensure comparability. Evaluation was performed on held-out synthetic subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline).

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment was preregistered before data collection. The hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' We defined the primary decision rule based on the Primary block of seeds, with a confirmatory decision based on the Replication block. We did not pool the cohorts.

The Primary cohort utilized 43 specific seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The Confirmatory replication cohort utilized a distinct set of 43 seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for all metrics. The preregistered decision rule required the mean contrast to exceed 0.0125098 to support the hypothesis; otherwise, the hypothesis would be refuted. All analysis scripts were fixed prior to unblinding the results.

We report results for the Primary and Confirmatory Replication cohorts separately, adhering to the preregistered analysis plan.

**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition (EntropyMax) worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (Deterministic). The 95% CI was [-0.0714, -0.0324], with a paired randomisation p=0.0002 and Cohen's dz=-0.72. This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], compared to 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for the baseline. The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082, NegCtrl2: 0.909). Based on the preregistered decision rule, the decision is: direction_refuted.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1'. The 95% CI was [-0.0422, -0.0278], with a paired randomisation p=0.0002 and Cohen's dz=-1.41. This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], compared to 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] for the baseline. Negative controls remained stable (NegCtrl1: 0.908, NegCtrl2: 0.9088). Based on the preregistered decision rule, the decision is: direction_refuted.

Figure 1 and Figure 3 display the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the Primary and Replication cohorts, respectively. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition. The training curves indicate that the proposed method converged to a lower performance plateau compared to the baseline and negative controls in both cohorts.

=== discussion ===
The results of this study explicitly refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Both the primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy for the intervention compared to the deterministic baseline.

These findings contradict the expectation that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity would generalize well to attention-based architectures. Prior work suggests BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], yet our results align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Specifically, while Node-based BNNs highlight the potential for robustness [6], our implementation of entropy maximization within a Transformer architecture failed to replicate these benefits, suggesting the mechanism may not transfer directly to self-attention models without modification.

The negative outcome also relates to constraints identified in stochastic weight sharing and structured partial stochasticity, which note difficulties in convergence and posterior modes [7], [18]. The significant performance drop (Cohen's dz=-0.72 in Primary, -1.41 in Replication) suggests that maximizing entropy may actively disrupt the feature learning required for subject-disjoint generalization in this context. This contrasts with works proposing weight noise injection for robustness [15], indicating that the *objective* of the noise (entropy maximization vs. injection) is critical.

Regarding the literature on baselines, 1D convolutional neural networks are described as standard for various operations [10], and while we used a Transformer, the failure of the robustness method suggests that standard regularization might still outperform complex uncertainty objectives in this regime. Furthermore, while Bayesian optimization is discussed for tuning hyperparameters in robust Bayesian neural networks [11], our fixed hyperparameter setup suggests that the core objective function (entropy max) was the limiting factor, not just tuning. The results extend the understanding of BNN limitations [5], [12] by showing that even when uncertainty is explicitly maximized, it does not guarantee robustness gains and may incur a accuracy penalty. Practitioners should therefore be cautious about prioritizing entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in similar architectures.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations. First, we used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies; while this controls for variability, it may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. Second, the architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may not generalize to other architectures such as CNNs or RNNs. Third, we focused on subject-disjoint splits; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift) were not tested. Finally, the negative result limits our ability to explore *why* entropy maximization failed beyond the quantitative metrics; further ablation studies on the entropy term's magnitude would be required to understand the failure mode.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report investigated whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both primary and replication cohorts. The results refute the utility of this specific entropy maximization mechanism for this task, aligning with literature warning of poor performance in approximate Bayesian inference under shift [13]. Future work should investigate alternative uncertainty objectives or architectural modifications before deploying entropy-maximized weight noise in production robustness systems.

Hyperparameter tuning in robust contexts is also critical; Bayesian optimization is discussed for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Other works investigate convergence stability, such as momentum breakdown in ill-conditioned regression [1] and learning rate effects on synthetic non-linear data [2]. Structural constraints in BNNs include computational requirements and posterior mode difficulties [7], [18]. Entropy has been used to measure uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and BNNs have been developed specifically for data with limited observations [16]. This work builds on these foundations by testing entropy maximization specifically within a Transformer architecture for subject-disjoint generalization.
Method: We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of the attention mechanism. The goal was to explicitly maximize the entropy of the multiplicative weight noise distributions during training. We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), consisting of raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. The data included 6 classes and subject clusters, utilizing the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows to avoid external dependencies during the experimental phase.

The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder. It began with a Linear layer (9 input features to 64 hidden units) plus a learned positional embedding (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions). The encoder consisted of 2 blocks, each containing LayerNorm(64) followed by 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with query/key/value/output Linear layers (64 to 64). This was followed by a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear layer (64 to 128), ReLU activation, a Linear layer (128 to 64), and a final residual connection. The head comprised a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear layer (64 to 6) for classification.

We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic Training, Identity Control), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights to ensure comparability. Evaluation was performed on held-out synthetic subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline).

**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition (EntropyMax) worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (Deterministic). The 95% CI was [-0.0714, -0.0324], with a paired randomisation p=0.0002 and Cohen's dz=-0.72. This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], compared to 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for the baseline. The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082, NegCtrl2: 0.909). Based on the preregistered decision rule, the decision is: direction_refuted.

Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1'. The 95% CI was [-0.0422, -0.0278], with a paired randomisation p=0.0002 and Cohen's dz=-1.41. This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], compared to 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] for the baseline. Negative controls remained stable (NegCtrl1: 0.908, NegCtrl2: 0.9088). These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The results of this study explicitly refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Both the primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy for the intervention compared to the deterministic baseline.

These findings contradict the expectation that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity would generalize well to attention-based architectures. Prior work suggests BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], yet our results align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Specifically, while Node-based BNNs highlight the potential for robustness [6], our implementation of entropy maximization within a Transformer architecture failed to replicate these benefits, suggesting the mechanism may not transfer directly to self-attention models without modification.

The negative outcome also relates to constraints identified in stochastic weight sharing and structured partial stochasticity, which note difficulties in convergence and posterior modes [7], [18]. The significant performance drop (Cohen's dz=-0.72 in Primary, -1.41 in Replication) suggests that maximizing entropy may actively disrupt the feature learning required for subject-disjoint generalization in this context. This contrasts with works proposing weight noise injection for robustness [15], indicating that the *objective* of the noise (entropy maximization vs. injection) is critical.

Regarding the literature on baselines, 1D convolutional neural networks are described as standard for various operations [10], and while we used a Transformer, the failure of the robustness method suggests that standard regularization might still outperform complex uncertainty objectives in this regime. Furthermore, while Bayesian optimization is discussed for tuning hyperparameters in robust Bayesian neural networks [11], our fixed hyperparameter setup suggests that the core objective function (entropy max) was the limiting factor, not just tuning. The results extend the understanding of BNN limitations [5], [12] by showing that even when uncertainty is explicitly maximized, it does not guarantee robustness gains and may incur a accuracy penalty. Practitioners should therefore be cautious about prioritizing entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in similar architectures.
Limitations: This study has several limitations. First, we used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies; while this controls for variability, it may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. Second, the architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may not generalize to other architectures such as CNNs or RNNs. Third, we focused on subject-disjoint splits; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift) were not tested. Finally, the negative result limits our ability to explore *why* entropy maximization failed beyond the quantitative metrics; further ablation studies on the entropy term's magnitude would be required to understand the failure mode.

=== abstract ===

We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098 proportion. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise in a Transformer encoder and evaluated it against deterministic baselines and negative controls using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened accuracy. In the primary cohort, the contrast was -0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the replication cohort, the contrast was -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis and suggest that entropy-maximized weight noise may degrade robustness in attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly critical for deployment in safety-sensitive domains, yet basic neural networks do not inherently deliver this confidence [3]. Deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, leading practitioners to explore Bayesian statistics as a formalism to address this limitation [12]. While Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity, and node-based approaches have been proposed to mitigate these issues [6]. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, warning against uncritical adoption [13].

This work addresses a specific gap: while prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We investigate whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. This validates or refutes mechanisms related to stochastic weight sharing [7] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization.

We preregistered the following hypothesis: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' We report honest results against this preregistration, including unforeseen negative findings.

=== related_work ===

Bayesian Neural Networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify [12]. Regarding robustness, Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6]. However, Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets, providing context for architecture-specific shift behavior [8]. Batch Normalization addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training, a related form of internal shift [9].

Regarding noise and entropy, A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. Alignment Entropy Regularization uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14]. Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration and overfitting [17]. Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks and Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18].
