=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is often pursued to improve robustness under distribution shift, yet the efficacy of explicit entropy maximization in weight space remains unverified for subject-disjoint time-series tasks. This Registered Report tested whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves out-of-distribution accuracy compared to standard deterministic training in a Transformer architecture. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy with a mean paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. Across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts, the intervention significantly worsened accuracy relative to the baseline (Primary contrast: -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]; Replication contrast: -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). Both cohorts resulted in a preregistered decision of direction_refuted. These findings indicate that optimizing weight uncertainty for diversity via entropy maximization does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift and may actively degrade performance compared to deterministic regularization.

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in settings where confidence in predictions is critical, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. While Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this challenge in black-box deep learning methods [12], standard backpropagation suffers from disadvantages such as lack of calibration [17]. Consequently, researchers have explored uncertainty-inducing mechanisms to improve robustness, particularly under covariate shift where the distribution of layer inputs changes during training [9]. A prominent open problem is whether uncertainty mechanisms optimized for diversity, such as entropy maximization, generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift better than standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

This study addresses the gap where prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. We investigate whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. Our preregistered hypothesis predicted that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. This work validates or refutes the core mechanism of node-based Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) [6] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization.

=== related_work ===
The pursuit of robustness through uncertainty quantification is motivated by the intrinsic uncertainty neural networks introduce regarding which features are model-related versus data-driven [5]. While uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], implementing Bayesian methods often encounters constraints regarding computational requirements and convergence difficulties [7]. Specifically, while BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity compared to node-based approaches [6]. This struggle is compounded by evidence that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], suggesting that the method of uncertainty injection matters critically.

Within the space of noise-based regularization, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [15], and entropy has been used to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass [14]. However, systematic measurements of out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers have largely focused on NLP datasets [8], leaving time-series subject-disjoint tasks less explored. The literature thus presents a tension: while entropy regularization and noise injection are theoretically appealing for robustness [14, 15], weight-based Bayesian approaches face specific convergence and shift-performance dangers [6, 13]. This study contextualizes the failure of entropy maximization versus other noise methods within this broader context of Bayesian robustness, testing whether explicit entropy maximization can overcome the limitations previously observed in weight-based stochasticity [7].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection and learned positional embedding(128,64). The encoder contained 2 blocks, each comprising LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) feedforward network, and a final residual connection. A final LayerNorm(64) preceded mean-pooling over time and a Linear(64,6) classification head.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining structural fidelity to the raw inertial signals and official subject-disjoint split statistics. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights to ensure comparability. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic Training, Identity Control), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. Paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed to assess the hypothesis.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized two distinct cohorts of random seeds to ensure robustness of the findings. The Primary cohort consisted of 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The Confirmatory Replication cohort consisted of a disjoint set of 43 seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block first, then confirmed on the Replication block. The hypothesis stated that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We did not pool the cohorts; each was analyzed separately to maintain the integrity of the replication framework.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This was a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Primary cohort was direction_refuted. The Baseline condition achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912], while the Proposed condition achieved 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877]. Negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082, NegCtrl2: 0.909).

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 2). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This was a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Replication cohort was direction_refuted. The Baseline condition achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91], while the Proposed condition achieved 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877]. Negative controls again matched the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.908, NegCtrl2: 0.9088).

Figure 1 displays the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the Primary cohort, illustrating the separation between the Proposed and Baseline conditions. Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition, indicating that the performance degradation emerged early and persisted throughout training. The replication cohort exhibited consistent trends in Figures 3 and 4.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that entropy-maximized weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy when using the intervention compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the promise implied by node-based Bayesian neural networks [6], which suggest improved generalization under covariate shift, indicating that this benefit does not transfer to weight-based entropy maximization in attention architectures. Instead, our results align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

The failure of the intervention suggests that optimizing weight uncertainty for diversity via entropy maximization is distinct from effective robustness mechanisms. While weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [15], our negative controls (FixedNoise) outperformed the entropy-maximized variant, implying that the *optimization objective* (entropy maximization) rather than the noise itself caused the degradation. This supports the view that weight-based BNNs often struggle with convergence difficulties [7], potentially exacerbated by the entropy term conflicting with the classification loss. Furthermore, while entropy is used to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass [14], maximizing this entropy in weight space appears to disrupt the feature learning required for subject-disjoint time-series classification.

These findings extend the literature by demonstrating that mechanisms validated in node-based or posterior-fidelity contexts [6, 17] do not necessarily hold when explicitly maximizing entropy in weight parameters. The consistency between the Primary and Replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that deterministic training remains superior for this specific task configuration. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in similar Transformer-based time-series settings.

=== limitations ===
This study utilized synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration; results may differ in deeper models or different modalities such as NLP where Transformers have shown OOD robustness [8]. Additionally, we focused on subject-disjoint shifts; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift) were not tested. The negative controls used specific noise configurations (EntropyMin, FixedNoise) that may not represent all possible regularization baselines.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report provides rigorous evidence that explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise does not improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts with significant effect sizes. These results contradict the generalization promises of weight-based Bayesian approaches under shift [6, 13] and suggest that entropy maximization in weight space is detrimental to performance in this context. Future work should investigate whether node-based uncertainty methods [6] retain their advantages in Transformer architectures without resorting to weight-space entropy optimization.

These results contradict the generalization promises of weight-based Bayesian approaches under shift [4, 9] and suggest that entropy maximization in weight space is detrimental to performance in this context. === abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is often pursued to improve robustness under distribution shift, yet the optimal mechanism for inducing uncertainty remains debated. This Registered Report evaluates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated it against deterministic, entropy-minimized, and fixed-noise controls using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both the primary cohort (contrast = -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) and the confirmatory replication cohort (contrast = -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy-maximized weight uncertainty enhances generalization in this domain. The findings align with prior warnings regarding Bayesian inference performance under covariate shift [13] and suggest that weight-based stochasticity may degrade rather than improve robustness in attention-based architectures without careful calibration.

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks frequently lack calibrated confidence in their predictions, limiting their reliability in safety-critical applications [3]. While Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty, standard variational objectives often prioritize posterior fidelity via KL minimization rather than explicit diversity maximization [12]. Recent work suggests that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity, such as entropy maximization, might improve generalization under distribution shift [6]. However, it remains an open problem whether these mechanisms generalize to attention-based architectures under subject-disjoint distribution shifts compared to standard regularization.

This study addresses the gap between weight noise injection strategies and Bayesian uncertainty objectives in Transformers. While prior work explores weight noise and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives [5]. Validating or refuting this core mechanism is critical for guiding practitioners on whether to prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks [7].

We preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than deterministic training, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. This Registered Report protocol ensures that the refuted hypothesis and replication design are publishable regardless of the outcome, maintaining integrity against publication bias [13]. We strictly adhere to the declared scope regarding generalization beyond the specific testbed to ensure conclusions remain calibrated to the experimental conditions.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty quantification is increasingly recognized as essential for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4]. However, basic neural networks do not inherently deliver this confidence, necessitating specialized architectures or training objectives [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this, though deep learning methods often remain black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify [12]. Probabilistic backpropagation highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation, such as lack of calibration, motivating alternative uncertainty propagation methods [17].

Regarding robustness, pretrained Transformers have been shown to improve out-of-distribution robustness in NLP datasets, yet their behavior under weight stochasticity in time-series domains is less understood [8]. Weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness in diffractive neural networks, suggesting potential benefits of stochastic weights [15]. However, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity and may not guarantee improved generalization under covariate shift [6]. Indeed, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, warning against uncritical adoption of Bayesian averaging [13].

Specific constraints exist for stochastic weight methods. Stochastic Weight Sharing and Structured Partial Stochasticity identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18]. While Batch Normalization addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training, it does not resolve the optimization instability introduced by explicit entropy maximization on weights [9]. Furthermore, 1D convolutional neural networks remain standard for various operations in time-series, providing a baseline context for Transformer applications [10]. Our work specifically tests whether entropy maximization overcomes these known convergence and shift-performance dangers in a subject-disjoint setting.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). The final layer involved LayerNorm(64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear(64,6) classification head.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while preserving domain characteristics. The data utilized the official subject-disjoint split statistics (7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows) [DOI 10.24432/C54S4K]. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights to ensure comparability.

We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic Training, Identity Control), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects using held-out classification accuracy as the primary metric. Paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed per seed. We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block, without pooling cohorts.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized two independent cohorts of seeds to ensure reproducibility. The Primary cohort consisted of 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, ...). The Confirmatory Replication cohort consisted of 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, ...). All seeds were fixed prior to data generation and training.

We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for each condition. The preregistered hypothesis predicted the intervention would exceed the baseline by a margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The decision rule classified the hypothesis as supported only if the lower bound of the 95% CI for the contrast exceeded this margin; otherwise, it was refuted. All analysis scripts were locked before unblinding the results.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 1, Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The training trajectory showed consistent separation between conditions over steps (Figure 2). Based on the preregistered decision rule, the decision is: direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 2, Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The training trajectory replicated the primary cohort's separation (Figure 4). Based on the preregistered decision rule, the decision is: direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

=== discussion ===
The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. In both cohorts, the intervention reduced accuracy by approximately 3.5% to 4.8% compared to deterministic baselines. This finding directly contradicts the assumption that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms inherently enhance robustness in this architecture.

Reflecting on the literature, these results confirm warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. While node-based BNNs have been proposed to tackle covariate shift, our results suggest weight-based stochasticity without node-specific conditioning may struggle to maintain performance [6]. The observed degradation aligns with identified constraints regarding convergence difficulties in stochastic weight sharing methods [7]. The entropy maximization objective likely introduced optimization instability that outweighed any regularization benefit, consistent with concerns that weight-based BNNs face specific convergence and shift-performance dangers [7, 13].

We note that Batch Normalization addresses internal covariate shift but does not mitigate the performance degradation caused by explicit weight entropy maximization under distribution shift [9]. Similarly, while uncertainty propagation is core for detecting uncertain data, maximizing entropy did not improve the actual classification accuracy on held-out subjects [4]. The results extend the findings of Hendrycks et al. by showing that pretrained-style robustness does not automatically transfer to entropy-maximized weight noise in time-series Transformers [8].

These findings guide practitioners to prioritize standard regularization over entropy maximization for robustness tasks in subject-disjoint time-series classification. The core mechanism of Node-based BNNs may require specific architectural conditioning rather than global weight entropy maximization to validate its utility in modern architectures [6]. We strictly adhere to the declared scope; these conclusions apply to the specific testbed of subject-disjoint time-series data and should not be generalized to all distribution shift scenarios without further evidence.

=== limitations ===
This study utilized synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration; results may differ with deeper models or different attention mechanisms. We evaluated only subject-disjoint shifts; other shift types (e.g., sensor drift, activity definition changes) were not tested. The entropy maximization hyperparameters were fixed; adaptive schedules might yield different outcomes, though this was not part of the preregistered plan.

=== conclusion ===
We tested whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic training. These results confirm prior literature warnings regarding Bayesian inference performance under covariate shift and highlight convergence difficulties associated with weight-based stochasticity. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks in this domain without further evidence of stability.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robust deployment, yet standard methods often fail to deliver calibrated confidence under distribution shift. This Registered Report preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters would improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated it on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline in both cohorts. In the primary cohort, the paired contrast was −0.04805 (95% CI [−0.0714, −0.0324], p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=−0.72). In the replication cohort, the contrast was −0.03482 (95% CI [−0.0422, −0.0278], p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=−1.41). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy-maximized weight uncertainty enhances generalization in this setting, suggesting that diversity-driven objectives may conflict with optimization stability in attention-based architectures.

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in settings where confidence in predictions is as important as accuracy, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to address this challenge, treating deep learning methods not as black boxes but as probabilistic models where uncertainty can be quantified [12]. While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based implementations often struggle with high computational complexity and convergence difficulties [6, 18]. Recent work has explored weight noise injection to achieve robustness [15], and pretrained Transformers have shown improved out-of-distribution robustness in NLP tasks [8]. However, it remains an open problem whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

This study addresses the gap where prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report the results of a robust design with clear statistical reporting, separating primary and confirmatory replication cohorts to ensure validity.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty quantification is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], yet standard backpropagation suffers from disadvantages such as lack of calibration [17]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this, though neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features are model-related [5]. Research into robustness indicates that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Specifically, while node-based BNNs tackle covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with complexity [6].

Regarding optimization and architecture, Batch Normalization addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], but constraints regarding computational requirements and convergence difficulties persist in stochastic weight sharing schemes [7, 18]. While 1D convolutional neural networks are standard for various operations in time-series [10], Transformers are increasingly used for sequence modeling. Pretrained Transformers have been systematically measured for out-of-distribution generalization on NLP datasets [8]. Weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [15], and entropy has been used to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14]. However, convergence stability and learning rate effects remain critical in optimization [1, 2]. This work tests whether explicit entropy maximization of weight noise improves robustness in a Transformer architecture, contrasting with standard variational objectives.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) feedforward network, and a final residual. The final layer used LayerNorm(64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear(64,6) classification head.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining realistic structure. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects.

=== experimental_setup ===
We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). The experiment was divided into a Primary block and a Confirmatory Replication block. The Primary cohort used 43 specific seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The Confirmatory Replication cohort used 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block first, then confirmed on the Replication block. The preregistered hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' We report held-out classification accuracy as the primary metric.

=== results ===
We report results separately for the Primary and Confirmatory Replication cohorts. We do not pool the cohorts.

**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [−0.0714, −0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=−0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 2). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [−0.0422, −0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=−1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

Figure 1 and Figure 3 display the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the Primary and Replication cohorts, respectively. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding aligns with prior work warning that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. While weight noise injection has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [15], our results suggest that maximizing entropy of the noise distribution specifically may introduce optimization instability that outweighs regularization benefits.

The negative contrast supports the observation that weight-based BNNs often struggle with complexity and convergence difficulties [6, 18]. Although Batch Normalization addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], it did not mitigate the performance drop associated with entropy maximization in this architecture. The results contradict the expectation that diversity-driven objectives generalize better than posterior fidelity objectives in this context. Furthermore, while pretrained Transformers improve out-of-distribution robustness in NLP [8], our findings indicate that modifying weight uncertainty mechanisms within the Transformer attention layers requires careful calibration to avoid degrading standard generalization. The consistency between the Primary and Replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this is a robust negative result rather than a sampling artifact.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder with fixed hyperparameters (2 blocks, 4 heads); results may differ in deeper models or with different attention mechanisms. The training duration was fixed at 50 epochs, and longer training schedules might interact differently with entropy maximization. Finally, we evaluated subject-disjoint generalization on synthetic clusters; real-world domain shift may present different challenges.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a preregistered experiment to test whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening held-out classification accuracy. These findings suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting without further evidence. Future work should investigate whether alternative uncertainty objectives or architectural modifications can stabilize entropy-driven weight noise.

Introduction: Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in settings where confidence in predictions is as important as accuracy, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to address this challenge, treating deep learning methods not as black boxes but as probabilistic models where uncertainty can be quantified [11]. While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based implementations often struggle with high computational complexity and convergence difficulties [6, 16]. Recent work has explored weight noise injection to achieve robustness [14], and pretrained Transformers have shown improved out-of-distribution robustness in NLP tasks [8]. However, it remains an open problem whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

This study addresses the gap where prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report the results of a robust design with clear statistical reporting, separating primary and confirmatory replication cohorts to ensure validity.

Discussion: The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding aligns with prior work warning that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [12]. While weight noise injection has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [14], our results suggest that maximizing entropy of the noise distribution specifically may introduce optimization instability that outweighs regularization benefits.

The negative contrast supports the observation that weight-based BNNs often struggle with complexity and convergence difficulties [6, 16]. Although Batch Normalization addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], it did not mitigate the performance drop associated with entropy maximization in this architecture. The results contradict the expectation that diversity-driven objectives generalize better than posterior fidelity objectives in this context. Furthermore, while pretrained Transformers improve out-of-distribution robustness in NLP [8], our findings indicate that modifying weight uncertainty mechanisms within the Transformer attention layers requires careful calibration to avoid degrading standard generalization. The consistency between the Primary and Replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this is a robust negative result rather than a sampling artifact.

Conclusion: We conducted a preregistered experiment to test whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening held-out classification accuracy. These findings suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting without further evidence. Future work should investigate whether alternative uncertainty objectives or architectural modifications can stabilize entropy-driven weight noise.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robust deployment under distribution shift. While Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) aim to improve generalization, it remains unclear whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters outperforms standard deterministic training in subject-disjoint time-series tasks. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than deterministic baselines, exceeding a worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. We evaluated this using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened accuracy compared to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary contrast: -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]; Replication contrast: -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). These results refute the prediction that entropy maximization improves subject-disjoint robustness in this architecture, aligning instead with warnings regarding approximate Bayesian inference under covariate shift.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important for safety-critical applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. Deep learning methods are often described as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, though Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) have been proposed to manage this uncertainty, observing that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features are model-related versus data-driven [5]. However, constraints regarding computational requirements and convergence difficulties persist in stochastic weight sharing schemes [7].

This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We investigate whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training.

We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. This Registered Report validly executes the preregistered protocol, and the refuted hypothesis is a publishable outcome under the registered report framework.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. Bayesian Neural Networks observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17].

Regarding robustness and optimization, Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks and Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18]. Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. Alignment Entropy Regularization uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14]. Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer architecture. The model used was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and final residual. The head consisted of final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6).

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining domain relevance. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) and applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The dataset mimicked the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). The primary cohort utilized 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The confirmatory replication cohort utilized 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). The metric was held-out classification accuracy. Baselines included Deterministic Training (Identity Control). Training was fixed at 50 epochs using SGD.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Figure 1 and Figure 2). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

Table 1 presents the final metric values per condition. The 'proposed' condition achieved 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. Negative controls 'negative_control_1' and 'negative_control_2' achieved 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] and 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] respectively.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Figure 3 and Figure 4). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

Table 2 presents the final metric values per condition. The 'proposed' condition achieved 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. Negative controls 'negative_control_1' and 'negative_control_2' achieved 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] and 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] respectively.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that entropy-maximized weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention reduced accuracy by approximately 3.5% to 4.8% compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the promise of improved generalization under covariate shift stated by node-based Bayesian neural networks [6]. While [6] suggests BNNs may handle shift, our results indicate that entropy maximization specifically—distinct from posterior fidelity objectives—degrades performance in this architecture.

Our findings align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. The significant negative effect size (dz=-0.72 Primary, dz=-1.41 Replication) suggests this is not a variance artifact but a systematic failure of the entropy maximization objective in this context. This extends the constraints identified in stochastic weight sharing schemes [7], demonstrating that diversity-focused objectives may conflict with accuracy goals in subject-disjoint time-series classification.

The negative controls (EntropyMin, FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Deterministic baseline, indicating that the performance drop is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se. This suggests that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in Transformer-based time-series models. The results validate the concern that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration with 2 blocks; results may differ in deeper models or different attention mechanisms. Training was fixed at 50 epochs; longer training schedules might interact differently with the entropy regularization. The study focused on subject-disjoint splits; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift) were not evaluated.

=== conclusion ===
We tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The preregistered hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These results contradict claims that BNNs inherently improve generalization under covariate shift [6] and support warnings regarding approximate Bayesian inference under shift [13]. We conclude that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting.

Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robust deployment under distribution shift, yet the optimal mechanism for inducing uncertainty remains debated. This Registered Report tests whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated it against deterministic, entropy-minimized, and fixed-noise controls using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. === introduction ===
Deep neural networks often lack calibrated confidence in their predictions, limiting their reliability in safety-critical applications where distribution shift is common [3]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty, treating weights as distributions rather than point estimates [12]. While standard variational objectives minimize divergence to approximate posteriors, alternative mechanisms propose maximizing entropy to encourage diversity in weight configurations [14]. Theoretical work suggests that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity might generalize better under covariate shift [6]. However, empirical evidence regarding entropy maximization in modern attention-based architectures remains limited.

This study addresses the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. Specifically, we investigate whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. The core mechanism of node-based BNNs suggests improved generalization under covariate shift, yet weight-based approaches often struggle with computational complexity or convergence [6]. Validating or refuting the core mechanism of node-based BNNs in modern architectures guides whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization.

We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. This Registered Report presents the results of the experiment exactly as run, adhering to the approved protocol. We report both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts separately to ensure robustness of the findings.

Deep learning methods are often described as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, and Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. Neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features are model-related versus data-related [5]. Uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], and standard backpropagation lacks calibration compared to probabilistic alternatives [17].

Approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, warning against uncritical adoption of Bayesian Model Averaging [13]. Internal covariate shift during training is addressed by normalization techniques, which stabilize layer input distributions [9]. Weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness in diffractive neural networks [15].

The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We report means with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds.

| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

The results consistently refute the preregistered hypothesis across both primary and replication cohorts. Explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters degraded out-of-distribution accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-focused regularization enhances generalization in this setting.

**Relation to Prior Work**
These results relate directly to the literature on BNNs and covariate shift. While node-based BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], our results suggest that weight-based entropy maximization does not replicate this benefit in Transformers. Prior work uses entropy to measure uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sets of allowed alignments [14]. === abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robustness under distribution shift, yet standard variational objectives often prioritize posterior fidelity over diversity. This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it against deterministic, entropy-minimized, and fixed-noise baselines using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy. In the primary cohort (43 seeds), the proposed method decreased accuracy by 0.04805 proportion (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to baseline. This direction of effect was confirmed in the replication cohort (43 seeds), with a decrease of 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy-maximized weight noise enhances subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, suggesting that diversity-inducing mechanisms may interfere with feature learning when not balanced by posterior fidelity constraints.

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks frequently exhibit overconfidence in predictions, failing to capture uncertainty inherent in data or model parameters [3]. This limitation is particularly acute in safety-critical applications where distribution shifts, such as subject-disjoint splits in time-series classification, can degrade performance [6]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty, yet standard approaches often minimize divergence (e.g., KL divergence) to approximate a posterior, potentially constraining the diversity of predictive functions [12]. Recent work suggests that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity might improve robustness [15]. However, it remains unclear whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters generalizes to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

This study addresses the gap where prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than deterministic training, exceeding a worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results of a primary experiment and a confirmatory replication, adhering strictly to the preregistered analysis plan.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty quantification is increasingly recognized as essential for reliable deep learning, yet basic neural networks do not deliver calibrated confidence [3]. Deep learning methods are often treated as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, prompting the adoption of Bayesian statistics to address this limitation [12]. Bayesian Neural Networks intrinsically increase uncertainty regarding which features are model-related versus data-driven [5]. While uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], standard backpropagation lacks calibration [17].

Regarding robustness, BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Furthermore, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Pretrained Transformers have been measured for out-of-distribution generalization in NLP, but less is known about weight noise mechanisms in Transformer encoders for time-series data [8]. Internal covariate shift during training is typically addressed by normalization layers [9], while weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness in other architectures [15].

Optimization strategies vary in their approach to uncertainty. Convolutional neural networks are standard for various operations in time-series processing [10]. Bayesian optimization discusses tuning hyperparameters of machine learning algorithms [11]. However, constraints regarding computational requirements and convergence difficulties exist for stochastic weight sharing methods [7]. Some approaches use entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], but the effect of maximizing weight noise entropy specifically for subject-disjoint robustness remains empirically unverified.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a linear input projection (9 to 64 channels), learned positional embeddings (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions), and two encoder blocks. Each block included LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps (query/key/value/output linear projections 64 to 64), a residual connection, LayerNorm, and a feed-forward network (Linear 64->128->ReLU->Linear 128->64) with a residual connection. The final layer involved LayerNorm, mean-pooling over time, and a linear projection to 6 classes.

To avoid external dependencies while maintaining ecological validity, we generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), comprising 9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, and subject clusters. We initialized identical model weights for each seed to ensure comparability. We ran four conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs using SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. Paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed to test the hypothesis.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized 43 seeds for the primary cohort and 43 seeds for the confirmatory replication cohort, as preregistered. The primary seeds included values such as 497360171578835126 and 619747419151856849, while replication seeds included 460845256865125083 and 168360166801404394. The metric of interest was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered decision rule required the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast $H_s$ to exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in the primary block to claim support, followed by confirmation in the replication block. We applied bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for all metric estimates. Figure 1 displays final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, and Figure 2 shows mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. Table 1 details the accuracy per condition.

| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. Table 2 details the accuracy per condition.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformer encoders. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in held-out accuracy compared to deterministic training, with effect sizes of dz=-0.72 and dz=-1.41 respectively. This finding contradicts the promise of BNNs for improved generalization under covariate shift in this specific configuration [6]. While weight noise injection has been proposed to achieve robustness [15], our results suggest that maximizing entropy of the noise distribution without posterior fidelity constraints may degrade feature learning.

These findings align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the deterministic baseline, indicating that the performance drop is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se. This extends the understanding of stochastic weight sharing constraints [7], suggesting that computational or optimization difficulties may manifest as accuracy loss when diversity is prioritized over fidelity. The results do not support prioritizing entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting.

=== limitations ===
This study utilized synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to ensure control over subject disjointness, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. payload.content:
=== abstract ===
This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise on a Transformer encoder architecture and evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects mimicking UCI HAR statistics. The preregistered hypothesis predicted that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. In the Primary cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened the contrast by 0.03482 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts yielded a preregistered decision of direction_refuted. These results indicate that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise harms subject-disjoint generalization in this setting compared to deterministic training.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. Deep learning methods are often described as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, though Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. While Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Furthermore, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. This study addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

We preregistered the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training would improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. Specifically, the intervention was predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This work validates or refutes the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [7] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. We report the results of the experiment exactly as run, adhering to the preregistered analysis plan.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. Uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], and standard backpropagation lacks calibration [17]. To address robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [15]. However, constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes exist in BNNs [7].

Regarding architecture-specific robustness, Convolutional neural networks are standard for various operations in time-series processing [10]. In the context of Transformers, prior work systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Additionally, batch normalization addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9]. Less is known about weight noise mechanisms in Transformer encoders for time-series data. This gap motivates our investigation into entropy-maximized weight noise in this specific architectural context.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer. We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual connection. The head consisted of final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6).

We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for fixed epochs (50) with SGD. We evaluated on held-out synthetic subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block. We did not pool the cohorts.

=== experimental_setup ===
We used the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset statistics (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows) to guide synthetic data generation. The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We utilized 43 seeds for the Primary cohort and 43 seeds for the Confirmatory Replication cohort. The preregistered decision rule required the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s to exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for all metric values.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition achieved 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Primary cohort is direction_refuted.

In the Confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition achieved 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Replication cohort is direction_refuted.

Training dynamics showed consistent separation between conditions over steps (see Figure 2 and Figure 4). The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline in both cohorts, indicating that the performance degradation was specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection generally.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that entropy-maximized weight noise improves out-of-distribution accuracy. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would generalize better under distribution shift.

Relating these quantitative findings to prior work, our results align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity and convergence [6]. Our data suggests that explicitly maximizing entropy in weight noise parameters exacerbates this struggle in Transformer encoders, leading to lower accuracy than deterministic baselines. This extends the findings of [6] by demonstrating that weight-based uncertainty mechanisms can actively harm performance in attention-based architectures under subject-disjoint shift, not merely struggle with complexity.

The negative controls (FixedNoise) performed comparably to the Baseline, suggesting that simple noise injection does not incur the same penalty as entropy-maximized noise. This distinguishes our findings from general weight noise injection training proposed for robustness [15], indicating that the optimization objective (entropy maximization) is the critical factor driving the performance drop. Consequently, practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration; results may vary with deeper models or different attention heads. The margin of 0.0125098 was fixed preregistered; while the effect was negative and significant, different margins might alter binary decisions in borderline cases (though not here). Finally, we focused on subject-disjoint shifts; other distribution shifts (e.g., sensor drift) were not evaluated.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a Registered Report to test whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. The hypothesis was refuted in both Primary and Replication cohorts. The intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training. These results suggest that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters is not a viable strategy for improving out-of-distribution accuracy in this context and may actively degrade performance.

Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robust deployment, yet standard variational objectives often prioritize posterior fidelity over diversity. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it against deterministic, entropy-minimized, and fixed-noise baselines using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Preregistered analysis across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts tested the hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a worthwhile accuracy margin of 0.0125098.
