=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robust deployment, yet standard methods often struggle to calibrate confidence under distribution shift. This Registered Report investigates whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions improves out-of-distribution accuracy in Transformer architectures compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that entropy maximization would yield higher held-out classification accuracy exceeding a fixed margin. Using a subject-disjoint split of synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics, we trained PreNormTransformer encoders under four conditions: EntropyMax (intervention), Deterministic (baseline), EntropyMin, and FixedNoise. Across 43 seeds in a primary cohort and 43 seeds in a confirmatory replication cohort, the intervention significantly worsened performance relative to the baseline. In the primary cohort, the paired contrast was −0.04805 (95% CI [−0.0714, −0.0324], p=0.0002), and in the replication cohort, −0.03482 (95% CI [−0.0422, −0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts refuted the preregistered hypothesis. These findings suggest that optimizing for entropy diversity in weight noise does not generalize to attention-based architectures under subject-disjoint shift, contrasting with promises of node-based Bayesian approaches.

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in settings where confidence quantification is essential, yet standard models often fail to deliver reliable uncertainty estimates [3]. While Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to address this challenge [12], achieving robust generalization under covariate shift remains difficult. Node-based BNNs have been proposed to tackle covariate shift, though weight-based variants often incur high computational complexity [6]. A key open problem is whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity via entropy maximization, rather than posterior fidelity via KL minimization, generalize to modern attention-based architectures.

This study addresses whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. We distinguish our approach from general noise injection training [15] by explicitly optimizing the entropy of the noise distribution parameters. While 1D convolutional neural networks are surveyed for various applications [10], this study focuses on Transformer architectures for time-series modeling. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098 proportion. Contrary to this prediction, our results indicate that entropy maximization significantly degrades performance compared to deterministic baselines in both primary and replication cohorts.

=== related_work ===
Surveys of uncertainty in deep neural networks note that confidence is increasingly important yet challenging to quantify in black-box deep learning methods [3, 12]. Basic neural networks do not inherently deliver this confidence, prompting the use of Bayesian statistics to formalize uncertainty [12]. Research into robustness highlights that while BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with computational requirements [6]. Furthermore, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

Regarding regularization techniques, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [15]. However, constraints regarding convergence difficulties and posterior modes exist in stochastic weight sharing methods [7]. Standard normalization techniques address changes in the distribution of layer inputs during training [9], though our method utilizes LayerNorm. Optimization stability and learning rate effects are also critical factors in convergence [1, 2]. Prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a linear input projection (9 to 64 dimensions), learned positional embeddings (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions), and two encoder blocks. Each block included LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps, and a feed-forward network (64 to 128 to 64 dimensions) with ReLU activation. The final layer involved mean-pooling over time followed by a linear projection to 6 classes.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining realistic distribution shift characteristics. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran four conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs using SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects using classification accuracy.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized a preregistered design with distinct primary and confirmatory replication cohorts. The primary cohort consisted of 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.), and the confirmatory replication cohort consisted of 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). The preregistered decision rule required applying the hypothesis test on the Primary block first, then confirming on the Replication block without pooling.

The hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) for held-out classification accuracy. We report means with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds. Significance was assessed via paired randomisation tests.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]) (Figure 1). The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082, NegCtrl2: 0.909). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [−0.0714, −0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=−0.72). The 95% CI excludes zero, indicating a statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision for the Primary cohort is direction_refuted.

In the Confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8717 (95% CI [0.865, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9065 (95% CI [0.903, 0.91]) (Figure 3). The negative controls remained consistent (NegCtrl1: 0.908, NegCtrl2: 0.9088). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [−0.0422, −0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=−1.41). The 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Replication cohort is direction_refuted. Training dynamics showed consistent separation between the intervention and baseline conditions over steps (Figure 2, Figure 4).

=== discussion ===
The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated statistically significant performance degradation relative to deterministic training. This finding contrasts with the expectation that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity would enhance robustness.

Relating these findings to prior literature, while node-based BNNs state promise for improved generalization under covariate shift [6], our results suggest that weight-based entropy maximization does not translate to attention-based architectures in this setting. This aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. The failure of the intervention distinguishes it from general noise injection training which has been proposed for robustness [15], indicating that the objective function (entropy maximization vs. noise injection alone) is a critical factor.

Surveys note that quantifying confidence in black-box methods is challenging [3, 12], and our results suggest that simply maximizing entropy in weight parameters does not solve this for Transformers under subject-disjoint shift. The negative controls (EntropyMin, FixedNoise) performing similarly to the Baseline indicates that the degradation is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se. This validates the need to distinguish between uncertainty mechanisms optimized for diversity versus posterior fidelity.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor data. The architecture was limited to a specific PreNormTransformer configuration with 2 blocks; results may differ in deeper models or different modalities. We utilized SGD for optimization; other optimizers might interact differently with entropy regularization. The subject-disjoint split was simulated; real-world subject variability may present different shift characteristics. Finally, we focused on classification accuracy; calibration metrics were not the primary preregistered outcome.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a preregistered experiment to test whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves out-of-distribution accuracy in Transformers. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These results indicate that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this architecture. Future work should investigate why entropy objectives conflict with attention mechanisms under distribution shift.

Furthermore, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. payload.content:
=== abstract ===
This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We hypothesized that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise on a PreNormTransformerEncoder using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened performance in both the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed method worsened the contrast by 0.048095 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The replication cohort confirmed this direction (contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise enhances subject-disjoint robustness in this architecture, suggesting practitioners should not prioritize this mechanism over standard regularization for such tasks.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. Deep learning methods are often described as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, though Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Validating or refuting the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [6] in modern architectures guides whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. This study utilizes a robust preregistered design with separate primary and confirmatory replication cohorts to ensure calibrated conclusions regarding the efficacy of entropy-maximized weight noise.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4]. However, neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. Regarding robustness, BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Furthermore, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

Specific stochastic methods face constraints. Stochastic weight sharing methods and structured partial stochasticity identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18]. Regarding entropy-based regularization, Alignment Entropy Regularization uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over the set of allowed alignments [14]. In the context of Transformers, prior work systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. Additionally, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness in other architectures [15]. Standard backpropagation also exhibits disadvantages such as lack of calibration, motivating probabilistic alternatives [17].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer. The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and a final residual. The head comprised final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6).

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining statistical properties of inertial signals. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. Paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed. We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The study utilized synthetic data mimicking the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). The primary analysis used 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The confirmatory replication used 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered decision rule required the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s to exceed 0.0125098 to support the hypothesis. All analyses were conducted separately for the primary and replication cohorts without pooling.

=== results ===
Primary cohort: Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see the results table). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted.

Confirmatory replication cohort: Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see the results table). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted.

The mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] in the primary cohort and 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] in the replication cohort. The baseline condition achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] in the primary cohort and 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] in the replication cohort. Negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the baseline in both cohorts (approximately 0.908–0.909), indicating the performance drop was specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection generally. Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that entropy-maximized weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the promise that BNNs improve generalization under covariate shift [6], at least when the uncertainty mechanism is optimized for entropy maximization rather than posterior fidelity. Instead, our results align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

While weight noise injection has been proposed to achieve strong robustness in other contexts [15], our data suggests that explicitly maximizing the entropy of the noise distribution is detrimental in this Transformer-based setting. The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed comparably to the deterministic baseline, suggesting that the harm arises specifically from the entropy maximization objective rather than the presence of noise itself. Regarding alignment entropy, while prior work uses entropy to measure uncertainty in distributing probability mass over the set of allowed alignments [14], applying a similar entropy maximization principle to weight parameters did not yield robustness benefits here.

These findings must be interpreted within calibrated scope. The experiment used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture. The results do not necessarily generalize to all attention-based architectures or real-world distribution shifts beyond the synthetic testbed limits. The consistency between the primary and replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this specific intervention is ineffective for the stated goal.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited by its use of synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics rather than raw external data, though this avoided external dependencies while maintaining statistical properties. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks; results may differ in deeper models or different attention mechanisms. The study focused on subject-disjoint time-series data; findings may not extend to other modalities or shift types (e.g., semantic shift). Finally, the entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; whole-model entropy maximization might yield different outcomes, though the negative control results suggest noise itself is not the primary driver of performance loss.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report presents a valuable negative result with a robust preregistered design. Explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training did not improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data; instead, it significantly worsened performance compared to standard deterministic training in both primary and replication cohorts. The hypothesis is refuted. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting. Future work should investigate why entropy maximization conflicts with generalization in this architecture, potentially exploring whether posterior fidelity objectives [17] remain superior for robustness despite computational costs [7].

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment under distribution shift, yet the optimal mechanism for inducing uncertainty remains debated. This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated it against deterministic, entropy-minimized, and fixed-noise controls using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion, the entropy-maximized condition significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy. In the primary cohort (43 seeds), the intervention yielded 0.8604 accuracy versus 0.9085 for baseline (contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). This direction of effect was confirmed in the replication cohort (contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight noise enhances robustness in this architecture, suggesting that diversity-inducing objectives may conflict with feature stability required for subject-disjoint generalization.

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications where confidence in predictions is paramount [3]. However, standard networks often suffer from miscalibration, failing to distinguish between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty [12]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty by placing distributions over weights, yet they face challenges regarding computational complexity and convergence in deep architectures [7]. Recent work suggests that node-based uncertainty mechanisms may offer scalable alternatives that improve generalization under covariate shift [6]. Specifically, it has been proposed that maximizing the entropy of latent variables could enhance robustness by encouraging diverse implicit data perturbations [6].

Despite progress in uncertainty quantification, it remains unclear whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This gap matters because validating the core mechanism of node-based BNNs in modern architectures guides whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization.

This study preregistered the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than deterministic training, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098 proportion. We tested this using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on synthetic time-series data designed to mimic subject-disjoint splits in human activity recognition. We report both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts separately, adhering to preregistered decision rules.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty estimation is established as a core requirement for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4]. Surveys indicate that while basic neural networks lack certainty estimates, Bayesian statistics provide a framework to address this [3, 12]. However, the employment of BNNs is constrained by increased computational requirements and convergence difficulties when training very deep, state-of-the-art architectures [7]. To mitigate these issues, stochastic weight sharing has been reinterpreted to reduce computational overhead [7], and structured partial stochasticity has been proposed to simplify posterior distributions and improve inference efficiency [18].

Regarding robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness against external interference [15]. In the context of covariate shift, BNNs promise improved generalization, though weight-based approaches often struggle with complexity [6]. Node-based BNNs induce epistemic uncertainty by multiplying hidden nodes with latent random variables, where the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of these variables [6]. Conversely, approximate Bayesian inference can sometimes achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly when posterior contraction fails [13].

We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block. The hypothesis predicted the mean contrast would exceed 0.0125098.

This Registered Report tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Introduction: Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications where confidence in predictions is paramount [1]. This finding contrasts with the promise of node-based BNNs to improve generalization under covariate shift via entropy-driven diversity [3]. While [3] suggests that diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of latent variables, our results indicate that explicitly maximizing weight noise entropy in a Transformer architecture may disrupt feature stability required for subject-disjoint tasks.

This outcome aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [9]. The negative effect observed here suggests that the mechanism of entropy maximization, when applied to weight noise rather than node activations, may introduce excessive variance that hinders convergence or generalization. This is consistent with observations that BNNs face convergence difficulties in deep architectures [4]. Furthermore, while weight noise injection has been proposed for robustness [11], our results suggest that the objective function governing that noise (entropy maximization vs. fixed) is critical; maximizing entropy actively degraded performance relative to fixed noise controls (NegCtrl2).

The stability of the negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) near the deterministic baseline indicates that the degradation is specific to the entropy maximization objective, not merely the presence of noise. This extends the understanding of structured partial stochasticity [12], implying that unstructured entropy maximization on weights may be detrimental compared to structured approaches. Additionally, while pretrained Transformers have shown robustness on NLP datasets [5], our findings suggest that uncertainty modifications to such architectures require careful validation on time-series data, where 1D CNNs have traditionally performed well [7].

Conclusion: This Registered Report tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These findings suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization of weight noise for robustness tasks in this setting over standard regularization. Future work should investigate whether node-based entropy mechanisms [3] differ fundamentally from weight-based mechanisms in Transformer architectures.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet the optimal mechanism for inducing uncertainty under distribution shift remains debated. This Registered Report tests whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy with a mean paired contrast exceeding 0.0125. Using a Transformer encoder on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics, we evaluated the intervention against deterministic, entropy-minimization, and fixed-noise controls across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the hypothesis, the entropy-maximized intervention significantly worsened accuracy in both cohorts (Primary: −0.04805, 95% CI [−0.0714, −0.0324], p=0.0002; Replication: −0.03482, 95% CI [−0.0422, −0.0278], p=0.0002). Negative controls performed comparably to the deterministic baseline. These results refute the preregistered hypothesis, suggesting that entropy maximization of weight noise may disrupt feature learning in attention-based architectures under subject-disjoint shift, contrary to expectations derived from node-based Bayesian neural network theory.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models deploy in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty by characterizing the uncertainty due to the network itself [5]. While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based implementations often struggle with computational complexity [6]. Recent work suggests that inducing diversity through latent variables can improve robustness, observing that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. However, it remains unclear whether explicitly maximizing this entropy during training generalizes to modern attention-based architectures under subject-disjoint distribution shift.

While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This work addresses this gap by implementing an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder. We preregistered a hypothesis that this intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than deterministic training, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report results from both a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort, adhering strictly to preregistered decision rules.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty estimation in neural networks has become a crucial field, with various approaches proposed to measure and quantify prediction uncertainty [3]. Bayesian statistics provide a framework to categorize uncertainty stemming from data randomness versus lack of knowledge about data creation [5]. In the context of robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. However, approximate Bayesian inference can sometimes achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly in cases where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13].

Node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that induce epistemic uncertainty by multiplying hidden nodes with latent random variables [6]. These models perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions, and prior work observes that the diversity of the implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. Conversely, other work proposes structured ways to select deterministic subsets of weights to remove redundant posterior modes, finding that a drastically simplified posterior distribution can improve inference performance [18]. Regarding architecture, while 1D CNNs have achieved state-of-the-art performance for various operations on 1D signals, Transformers are increasingly used for time-series tasks [10]. Computational efficiency remains a concern; some stochastic weight sharing approaches demonstrate significant reductions in computational overhead inherent in Bayesian learning [7]. Additionally, standard normalization techniques are known to act as a regularizer, sometimes eliminating the need for dropout [9]. This study contextualizes its negative findings within this landscape, specifically testing whether entropy maximization—a mechanism linked to diversity in node-based BNNs [6]—translates to accuracy gains in Transformers.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear input projection (9 to 64 channels), learned positional embeddings (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions), and 2 blocks. Discussion: This study preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters would improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The results robustly refute this hypothesis across both primary and replication cohorts. The Intervention significantly worsened accuracy compared to deterministic training, with large effect sizes (dz=−0.72 and dz=−1.41).

These findings contrast with prior work suggesting that diversity in implicit corruptions, driven by entropy of latent variables, improves performance under covariate shift [6]. While node-based BNNs have shown promise in scalable uncertainty induction [6], our results indicate that maximizing entropy in multiplicative weight noise within a Transformer architecture disrupts rather than aids generalization. This may relate to findings that approximate Bayesian inference can perform poorly under covariate shift when posterior contraction fails [13]; explicitly maximizing entropy might prevent necessary contraction on informative features. Furthermore, while weight noise injection has been proposed to improve robustness [15], our results suggest that the *objective* governing that noise (entropy maximization vs. fixed or minimized) is critical. The failure to simplify the posterior distribution effectively [18] via entropy maximization suggests that more structured approaches to stochasticity may be required for attention-based models.
Limitations: This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was a specific Transformer encoder configuration; results may differ with deeper models or different attention mechanisms. We focused on subject-disjoint splits; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift) were not tested. Finally, while we refuted the hypothesis regarding accuracy, we did not measure calibration metrics, leaving open whether the intervention improved uncertainty quantification despite reducing accuracy.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for safety-critical applications, yet basic neural networks often lack calibrated confidence estimates [3]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to address this, though weight-based approaches face computational constraints [7]. This Registered Report preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters would improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary contrast: -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]; Replication contrast: -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). These results refute the prediction that entropy-maximized weight uncertainty enhances subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, suggesting that diversity-inducing mechanisms optimized for entropy rather than posterior fidelity may not transfer to attention-based models under distribution shift.

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks have become ubiquitous in scientific and real-world applications, yet their predictions often lack certainty estimates or suffer from miscalibration [3]. This limitation is particularly acute in safety-critical systems where detecting uncertain data is as significant as achieving high prediction accuracy [4]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) provide a statistical framework to characterize uncertainty arising from both data randomness and model lack of knowledge [5]. However, standard backpropagation lacks calibrated probabilistic predictions and tends to overfit [17]. While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based implementations often struggle with computational complexity in large-scale architectures [6].

Recent work suggests that node-based BNNs, which induce uncertainty via latent random variables multiplied by hidden nodes, can serve as scalable alternatives [6]. The diversity of implicit corruptions in such models depends on the entropy of the latent variables, leading to proposals that entropy maximization may improve robustness [6]. Furthermore, stochastic weight sharing approaches have demonstrated significant reductions in computational overhead inherent in Bayesian learning [7], and findings indicate that a drastically simplified posterior distribution can improve inference performance [18]. However, approximate Bayesian inference can sometimes achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13].

This study addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than deterministic training on subject-disjoint time-series data. We report the results of a primary experiment and a confirmatory replication, strictly adhering to the preregistered decision rule.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty quantification is increasingly recognized as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4]. Basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates, prompting research into Bayesian methods [3]. Bayesian neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the network itself [5]. To address scalability, stochastic weight sharing techniques have been reinterpreted to encode stochastic behavior in lower-dimensional representations, reducing computational overhead [7].

Regarding robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. In the context of covariate shift, node-based BNNs have been introduced to induce epistemic uncertainty via latent random variables, with observations that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of these variables [6]. However, warnings exist that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Standard normalization techniques are known to act as a regularizer, sometimes eliminating the need for dropout, which complicates the isolation of noise-based regularization effects [9]. While 1D CNNs have achieved state-of-the-art performance for various operations on 1D signals [10], Transformers are increasingly utilized for time-series tasks, though their interaction with weight uncertainty remains less explored.

=== method ===
**Approach**
We implemented `EntropyMaxWeightNoise` as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The intervention modifies the training objective to explicitly maximize the entropy of the multiplicative weight noise distributions, contrasting with standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

**Model Architecture**
We employed a `PreNormTransformerEncoder` consisting of a linear input projection (9 to 64 channels), learned positional embeddings (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps (query/key/value/output linear projections 64 to 64), a residual connection, LayerNorm, and a feed-forward network (Linear 64->128->ReLU->Linear 128->64) with a residual connection. The final layer involved LayerNorm, mean-pooling over time, and a linear projection to 6 classes.

**Conditions**
We ran four conditions:
1.  **Intervention (EntropyMax):** Entropy maximization of weight noise parameters.
2.  **Baseline (Deterministic):** Standard deterministic training (Identity Control).
3.  **NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin):** Entropy minimization of weight noise parameters.
4.  **NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise):** Fixed noise variance without entropy optimization.

**Training**
Models were trained for 50 epochs using SGD. For each seed, identical model weights were initialized across conditions to ensure comparability.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Data**
We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while preserving the statistical structure of raw inertial signals with an official subject-disjoint split logic.

**Seeds and Cohorts**
The experiment was divided into two preregistered cohorts:
*   **Primary Cohort:** 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, ...).
*   **Confirmatory Replication Cohort:** 43 seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, ...).

**Metrics and Decision Rule**
The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy on held-out synthetic subjects. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). The preregistered hypothesis predicted the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast $H_s$ would exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The decision rule required applying the test on the Primary block first, then confirming on the Replication block without pooling.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], compared to 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for the baseline. Negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911]; NegCtrl2: 0.909 [0.906, 0.912]). The preregistered decision for the primary cohort is **direction_refuted**.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], compared to 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] for the baseline. Negative controls remained close to baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.908 [0.904, 0.912]; NegCtrl2: 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]). The preregistered decision for the replication cohort is **direction_refuted**.

**Visualization**
Figure 1 displays final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the primary cohort. Figure 2 shows mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition. Figure 3 and Figure 4 correspond to the replication cohort metrics and training curves, respectively.

=== discussion ===
The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention reduced held-out accuracy by approximately 3.5% to 4.8% compared to deterministic training.

**Relation to Prior Work**
These findings contradict the expectation derived from node-based BNN literature that increasing the entropy of latent variables enhances diversity and robustness under covariate shift [6]. While [6] observed that diversity depends on entropy in node-based architectures, our results suggest this mechanism does not translate to multiplicative weight noise in attention-based layers under subject-disjoint shift. This aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly when posterior contraction is insufficient [13]. The negative result may indicate that entropy maximization in this context acts as a detrimental regularizer, disrupting feature learning rather than enhancing robustness.

Furthermore, while weight noise injection has been shown to improve noise resistance in diffractive neural networks [15], our results indicate that such benefits do not automatically extend to Transformer-based time-series classification without posterior fidelity constraints. The finding that a drastically simplified posterior distribution can improve inference performance [18] might suggest that the entropy-maximized posterior was too complex or ill-posed for this task, whereas the deterministic baseline effectively operated as a simplified MAP estimate.

**Uncertainty Quantification Scope**
Claims regarding uncertainty quantification in this study are strictly scoped to the defined testbed of synthetic subject-disjoint time-series data. While basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3], and Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty [12], our results indicate that specific entropy-maximizing interventions may not be the correct path for robustness in this architecture. Standard normalization techniques acting as regularizers [9] may have already provided sufficient stability, rendering additional noise-based regularization harmful.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations. First, we used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies; while this controls for variability, it may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. Second, the architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may not generalize to other architectures such as 1D CNNs, which have achieved state-of-the-art performance for various operations on 1D signals [10]. Third, the uncertainty quantification claims are scoped to the subject-disjoint testbed defined here and do not necessarily extend to other forms of distribution shift or safety-critical deployment scenarios without further validation. Finally, we did not evaluate computational overhead reductions potentially offered by stochastic weight sharing [7], focusing solely on accuracy outcomes.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report validly publishes a preregistered refutation of the hypothesis that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. Both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts demonstrated statistically significant decreases in held-out classification accuracy relative to deterministic baselines. These findings suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting. Future work should investigate whether posterior fidelity constraints, rather than entropy maximization alone, are required to realize the generalization benefits promised by Bayesian neural networks under covariate shift.

This Registered Report preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters would improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary contrast: -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]; Replication contrast: -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). These results refute the prediction that entropy-maximized weight uncertainty enhances subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, suggesting that diversity-inducing mechanisms optimized for entropy rather than posterior fidelity may not transfer to attention-based models under distribution shift.
Related work: Uncertainty quantification is increasingly recognized as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [2]. Basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates, prompting research into Bayesian methods [1]. Bayesian neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the network itself [3]. To address scalability, stochastic weight sharing techniques have been reinterpreted to encode stochastic behavior in lower-dimensional representations, reducing computational overhead [5].

Regarding robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [10]. In the context of covariate shift, node-based BNNs have been introduced to induce epistemic uncertainty via latent random variables, with observations that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of these variables [4]. However, warnings exist that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [9]. Standard normalization techniques are known to act as a regularizer, sometimes eliminating the need for dropout, which complicates the isolation of noise-based regularization effects [6]. While 1D CNNs have achieved state-of-the-art performance for various operations on 1D signals [7], Transformers are increasingly utilized for time-series tasks, though their interaction with weight uncertainty remains less explored.
Method: **Approach**
We implemented `EntropyMaxWeightNoise` as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The intervention modifies the training objective to explicitly maximize the entropy of the multiplicative weight noise distributions, contrasting with standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

**Model Architecture**
We employed a `PreNormTransformerEncoder` consisting of a linear input projection (9 to 64 channels), learned positional embeddings (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps (query/key/value/output linear projections 64 to 64), a residual connection, LayerNorm, and a feed-forward network (Linear 64->128->ReLU->Linear 128->64) with a residual connection. The final layer involved LayerNorm, mean-pooling over time, and a linear projection to 6 classes.

**Conditions**
We ran four conditions:
1.  **Intervention (EntropyMax):** Entropy maximization of weight noise parameters.
2.  **Baseline (Deterministic):** Standard deterministic training (Identity Control).
3.  **NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin):** Entropy minimization of weight noise parameters.
4.  **NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise):** Fixed noise variance without entropy optimization.

**Training**
Models were trained for 50 epochs using SGD. For each seed, identical model weights were initialized across conditions to ensure comparability.
Results: **Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], compared to 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for the baseline. Negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911]; NegCtrl2: 0.909 [0.906, 0.912]). The preregistered decision for the primary cohort is **direction_refuted**.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], compared to 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] for the baseline. Negative controls remained close to baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.908 [0.904, 0.912]; NegCtrl2: 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]). The preregistered decision for the replication cohort is **direction_refuted**.

**Visualization**
Figure 1 displays final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the primary cohort. Figure 2 shows mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition. Figure 3 and Figure 4 correspond to the replication cohort metrics and training curves, respectively.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** and the independent confirmatory replication was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention reduced held-out accuracy by approximately 3.5% to 4.8% compared to deterministic training.

**Relation to Prior Work**
These findings contradict the expectation derived from node-based BNN literature that increasing the entropy of latent variables enhances diversity and robustness under covariate shift [4]. While [4] observed that diversity depends on entropy in node-based architectures, our results suggest this mechanism does not translate to multiplicative weight noise in attention-based layers under subject-disjoint shift. This aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly when posterior contraction is insufficient [9]. The negative result may indicate that entropy maximization in this context acts as a detrimental regularizer, disrupting feature learning rather than enhancing robustness.

Furthermore, while weight noise injection has been shown to improve noise resistance in diffractive neural networks [10], our results indicate that such benefits do not automatically extend to Transformer-based time-series classification without posterior fidelity constraints. The finding that a drastically simplified posterior distribution can improve inference performance [12] might suggest that the entropy-maximized posterior was too complex or ill-posed for this task, whereas the deterministic baseline effectively operated as a simplified MAP estimate.

**Uncertainty Quantification Scope**
Claims regarding uncertainty quantification in this study are strictly scoped to the defined testbed of synthetic subject-disjoint time-series data. While basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [1], and Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty [8], our results indicate that specific entropy-maximizing interventions may not be the correct path for robustness in this architecture. Standard normalization techniques acting as regularizers [6] may have already provided sufficient stability, rendering additional noise-based regularization harmful.
Limitations: This study has several limitations. First, we used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies; while this controls for variability, it may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. Second, the architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may not generalize to other architectures such as 1D CNNs, which have achieved state-of-the-art performance for various operations on 1D signals [7]. Third, the uncertainty quantification claims are scoped to the subject-disjoint testbed defined here and do not necessarily extend to other forms of distribution shift or safety-critical deployment scenarios without further validation. Finally, we did not evaluate computational overhead reductions potentially offered by stochastic weight sharing [5], focusing solely on accuracy outcomes.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic networks lack calibrated confidence estimates [3]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a formalism for uncertainty, their application to modern architectures under distribution shift remains contested [6, 13]. This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it against deterministic, entropy-minimized, and fixed-noise controls using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both the primary cohort (mean contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) and the confirmatory replication cohort (mean contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the prediction that entropy-maximized weight uncertainty enhances generalization in this setting, suggesting that diversity-inducing mechanisms optimized for entropy rather than posterior fidelity may degrade performance in attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models are deployed in safety-critical applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions [12]. Among Bayesian approaches, weight noise injection has been proposed to achieve robustness against external interference [15]. However, standard variational objectives typically minimize divergence (e.g., KL divergence) rather than explicitly maximizing the entropy of the uncertainty parameters themselves.

While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This gap is significant because node-based BNNs suggest that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6], implying that maximizing this entropy could enhance robustness under covariate shift. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can sometimes achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

This study tests the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. Specifically, we predicted that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report results from a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort, adhering to a preregistered analysis plan.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) provide a framework where uncertainty due to the network can be characterized, distinguishing between randomness in data observation and lack of knowledge about data creation [5]. Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique for detecting uncertain data in practical applications, particularly when encountering unexpected samples [4].

Regarding robustness and optimization, BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift by providing principled probabilistic representations of epistemic uncertainty [6]. However, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. To address computational constraints, stochastic weight sharing techniques have been reinterpreted to encode stochastic behavior in lower-dimensional representations, reducing computational overhead [7]. Additionally, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15].

Normalization techniques also play a role in regularization. Batch normalization addresses internal covariate shift and acts as a regularizer, in some cases eliminating the need for dropout [9]. This complicates the isolation of noise-based regularization effects, as standard normalization may already provide robustness benefits. In the context of signal processing, 1D CNNs have achieved state-of-the-art performance for various operations on 1D signals, providing a baseline for architectural choices in time-series tasks [10]. However, dangers exist in Bayesian model averaging under covariate shift, where high-fidelity approximate inference can underperform classical estimation [13]. This literature suggests a complex relationship between uncertainty mechanisms and generalization under shift, motivating our empirical test of entropy maximization.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a linear input projection (9 to 64 dimensions), learned positional embeddings (128 timesteps, 64 dimensions), and two blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with query/key/value/output linear projections (64 dimensions), a residual connection, LayerNorm, and a feed-forward network (Linear 64->128->ReLU->Linear 128->64) with a residual connection. The final layer involved LayerNorm, mean-pooling over time, and a linear projection to 6 classes.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining realistic structure. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran four conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects.

The preregistered hypothesis stated: "The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion." We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block first, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
We used the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset structure (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K) as a template for synthetic data generation, utilizing raw inertial signals formatted as 128-timestep windows over 9 channels with an official subject-disjoint split logic applied to the synthetic clusters. The primary analysis utilized 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.), and the confirmatory replication utilized a distinct set of 43 seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.).

The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for each condition's mean accuracy and for the paired contrasts between conditions. Statistical significance was assessed via paired randomisation tests. All analysis code and seeds were fixed prior to data generation to ensure reproducibility. Figures 1 and 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. Figures 2 and 4 show the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition (EntropyMax) achieved a mean of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]). The 'baseline_1' condition (Deterministic) achieved a mean of 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]). The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline: 'negative_control_1' (EntropyMin) achieved 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] and 'negative_control_2' (FixedNoise) achieved 0.909 [0.906, 0.912].

The hypothesis-positive contrast (Intervention - Baseline) worsened by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the primary cohort is **direction_refuted**, as the intervention decreased accuracy rather than exceeding the worthwhile margin.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition achieved a mean of 0.8717 (95% CI [0.865, 0.877]). The 'baseline_1' condition achieved a mean of 0.9065 (95% CI [0.903, 0.91]). The negative controls remained consistent: 'negative_control_1' achieved 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] and 'negative_control_2' achieved 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912].

The hypothesis-positive contrast worsened by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision for the replication cohort is **direction_refuted**. The results consistently show that entropy maximization harmed out-of-distribution accuracy compared to deterministic training.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves held-out classification accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both the primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to the deterministic baseline and negative controls. This finding contradicts the expectation that maximizing the entropy of latent variables would enhance the diversity of implicit corruptions beneficial for robustness [6]. Instead, our data suggests that in attention-based architectures, excessive entropy in weight noise may destabilize learning or obscure signal features necessary for generalization.

This outcome aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. While node-based BNNs propose that diversity depends on entropy [6], our results indicate there may be an optimal level of uncertainty that does not correspond to maximization. The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed comparably to the deterministic baseline, suggesting that the mere presence of noise is not detrimental, but the *maximization* of its entropy is. This distinguishes our findings from work suggesting weight noise injection generally improves robustness [15], highlighting that the objective function governing the noise (entropy maximization vs. fixed variance) is critical.

Furthermore, the strong performance of the deterministic baseline may be partially attributable to the regularizing effects of the architecture's normalization layers. Batch normalization acts as a regularizer, sometimes eliminating the need for dropout [9], which may complicate the isolation of noise-based regularization effects. If the model is already well-regularized by normalization, additional entropy maximization may introduce unnecessary variance. These findings guide practitioners to prioritize standard regularization over entropy-maximized uncertainty mechanisms for robustness tasks in this specific architectural context, refuting the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [6] when applied via explicit entropy maximization in Transformers.

=== limitations ===
This study utilized synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was restricted to a specific Transformer encoder configuration (2 blocks, 64 dimensions); results may differ in deeper or wider models. We focused on subject-disjoint generalization; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift, activity definition changes) were not tested. Finally, while we controlled for normalization effects by keeping the architecture constant, the interaction between batch normalization and weight noise entropy was not explicitly ablated.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a preregistered experiment to test whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves out-of-distribution accuracy in Transformers. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic training. These results suggest that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty is not a viable strategy for improving subject-disjoint generalization in this setting, and that standard deterministic training with normalization remains more effective. Future work should investigate whether intermediate entropy levels or alternative uncertainty objectives yield better robustness without sacrificing accuracy.
