payload.content:
=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment under distribution shift, yet standard regularization techniques often fail to improve out-of-distribution generalization in attention-based architectures. This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves subject-disjoint accuracy compared to deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it on held-out subjects from the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset across 43 preregistered seeds in a primary cohort and 43 seeds in a confirmatory replication cohort. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy. In the primary cohort, the intervention yielded a mean accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]) versus 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]) for the baseline, a paired contrast of -0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). The replication cohort confirmed this negative effect with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy-maximized weight uncertainty enhances robustness in this setting, suggesting that diversity-inducing objectives may conflict with feature stability required for subject-disjoint generalization.

=== introduction ===
Neural networks are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications where confidence in predictions is paramount, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates and often suffer from calibration issues [3]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty, deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify without specialized training objectives [12]. A key open problem is whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity, such as entropy maximization, generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift better than standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

This study addresses the gap where prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. We focus on subject-disjoint time-series data, a setting where covariate shift is prevalent. While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Consequently, practitioners seek efficient regularization methods, such as batch normalization, which addresses internal covariate shift and acts as a regularizer, in some cases eliminating the need for dropout [9]. Additionally, 1D CNNs have achieved state-of-the-art performance for various operations on 1D signals, providing a baseline for architectural choices in time-series tasks [10], though Transformers are increasingly preferred for long-range dependencies.

We preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than deterministic training, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. This work validates or refutes the core mechanism of node-based uncertainty approaches [6] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty quantification remains a central challenge in deep learning. Surveys indicate that while confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, standard models lack calibrated uncertainty estimates [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this, characterizing uncertainty stemming from both data randomness and model lack of knowledge [5]. However, scalable learning of Bayesian neural networks often faces disadvantages such as lack of calibrated probabilistic predictions and tendencies to overfit [17]. To mitigate computational costs, stochastic weight sharing techniques have been reinterpreted to encode stochastic behavior in lower-dimensional representations, reducing computational overhead [7].

Regarding robustness under distribution shift, approximate Bayesian inference is often considered robust, yet Bayesian model averaging can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Node-based BNNs have been proposed as scalable alternatives that induce epistemic uncertainty via latent random variables, where the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. Complementary to Bayesian approaches, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. However, the interaction between explicit entropy maximization of weight noise and Transformer architectures under subject-disjoint shifts remains unexplored.

Optimization stability also influences robustness. Convergence stability can degrade under specific precision conditions, affecting momentum-based optimizers [1]. Furthermore, pretrained Transformers have been shown to improve out-of-distribution robustness compared to previous models, though larger models are not necessarily more robust [8]. These findings suggest that architectural choices and optimization dynamics interact complexly with uncertainty mechanisms, necessitating empirical validation of entropy-maximized noise injection.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The intervention modifies the training objective to explicitly maximize the entropy of the multiplicative weight noise distributions applied to the query weights, contrasting with standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection and learned positional embedding(128,64). The encoder contained 2 blocks, each comprising LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) projection, ReLU activation, Linear(128,64) projection, and a final residual connection. A final LayerNorm(64) preceded mean-pooling over time and a Linear(64,6) classification head.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies during development, but evaluated on the official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated held-out classification accuracy on held-out synthetic subjects during development and the official held-out windows for the final report. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline).

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized 43 seeds for the primary cohort and 43 seeds for the confirmatory replication cohort. Primary seeds included 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, and 41 others as preregistered. Replication seeds included 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, and 41 others. We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block first, then confirmed on the Replication block. The hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

Metrics included held-out classification accuracy. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for all metrics. Figure 1 displays final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the primary cohort, and Figure 3 displays the same for the replication cohort. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition in the primary and replication cohorts, respectively. We did not pool primary and replication cohorts; each was analyzed separately to maintain statistical integrity.

=== results ===
The preregistered hypothesis was refuted in both the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts. The intervention did not yield higher held-out classification accuracy; instead, it significantly worsened performance compared to the deterministic baseline.

**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention (EntropyMax) achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]). The baseline (Deterministic) achieved 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]). The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline: NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin) achieved 0.9082 (95% CI [0.905, 0.911]) and NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise) achieved 0.909 (95% CI [0.906, 0.912]).

The hypothesis-positive paired contrast (Intervention - Baseline) was -0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]). This difference was statistically significant (paired randomisation p=0.0002) with a large effect size (Cohen's dz=-0.72). The 95% CI excludes zero and falls below the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. These results are visualized in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8717 (95% CI [0.865, 0.877]). The baseline achieved 0.9065 (95% CI [0.903, 0.91]). Negative controls remained stable: NegCtrl1 achieved 0.908 (95% CI [0.904, 0.912]) and NegCtrl2 achieved 0.9088 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]).

The hypothesis-positive paired contrast was -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). This difference was statistically significant (paired randomisation p=0.0002) with a very large effect size (Cohen's dz=-1.41). The 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. These results are visualized in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

=== discussion ===
The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention reduced accuracy by approximately 3.5% to 4.8% compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-inducing objectives inherently enhance robustness under distribution shift.

These results relate directly to prior literature on Bayesian methods under covariate shift. While node-based BNNs have been proposed to improve generalization under covariate shift by inducing epistemic uncertainty [6], our weight-based entropy maximization failed to replicate this benefit in a Transformer architecture. This aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. The negative outcome suggests that maximizing entropy of weight noise may introduce excessive instability that outweighs the benefits of uncertainty diversity in this specific setting.

Furthermore, while weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15], our implementation focused on entropy maximization rather than noise resistance per se. The failure of the intervention implies that the mechanism of robustness in noise injection may rely on specific noise distributions or magnitudes not captured by entropy maximization alone. The stability of the negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) near baseline levels indicates that the performance drop is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than the presence of noise itself.

The findings also contextualize the role of architectural choices. While pretrained Transformers improve out-of-distribution robustness [8], our results suggest that modifying their internal uncertainty mechanisms via entropy maximization may be detrimental without pretraining or additional regularization. This validates the concern that basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3], but indicates that simple entropy maximization is not the correct remedy for subject-disjoint generalization in this context.

=== limitations ===
This study has several limitations. First, while we used the official subject-disjoint split of the UCI HAR dataset, the initial development utilized synthetic data mimicking UCI statistics, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. Second, the experiment was limited to a specific Transformer architecture (2-block PreNormEncoder) and may not generalize to deeper models or different attention mechanisms. Third, the entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; applying it to all linear layers might yield different results, though computational costs would increase. Finally, the negative result is specific to subject-disjoint shifts; performance under other types of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift) remains untested.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report provides rigorous evidence refuting the hypothesis that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. Across 86 total seeds in primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly decreased held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These findings caution against prioritizing entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting and highlight the need for further research into uncertainty mechanisms that align with feature stability under covariate shift.

Consequently, practitioners seek efficient regularization methods, such as batch normalization, which addresses internal covariate shift and acts as a regularizer, in some cases eliminating the need for dropout [7]. The negative outcome suggests that maximizing entropy of weight noise may introduce excessive instability that outweighs the benefits of uncertainty diversity in this specific setting.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robustness under distribution shift, yet standard deterministic models often lack calibrated confidence estimates. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across 43 seeds in a primary cohort and 43 seeds in a confirmatory replication cohort. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline. In the primary cohort, the mean contrast was -0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002), and in the replication cohort, -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters enhances generalization in this setting, suggesting that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not transfer effectively to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications where confidence in predictions is paramount. However, basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from over- or under-confidence, meaning they are badly calibrated [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions, characterizing uncertainty stemming from both data randomness and model lack of knowledge [5]. Despite this, scalable learning of Bayesian neural networks often faces disadvantages such as lack of calibrated probabilistic predictions and tendencies to overfit [12].

Recent work suggests that Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift by providing principled probabilistic representations of epistemic uncertainty [6]. Specifically, node-based approaches induce uncertainty by multiplying hidden nodes with latent random variables, where the diversity of the implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. This raises the question of whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves robustness in modern architectures. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13].

This study addresses the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report the results of a primary experiment and a confirmatory replication, adhering strictly to the preregistered analysis plan.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems, particularly for detecting uncertain data in safety-critical systems [4]. While Bayesian neural networks have attracted attention as a method to characterize uncertainty due to the network, their employment is still constrained by increased computational requirements and convergence difficulties when training very deep, state-of-the-art architectures [7]. To mitigate computational overhead, some approaches reinterpret weight-sharing quantization techniques from a stochastic perspective, enabling efficient Bayesian learning [7].

Regarding robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. However, systematic measurements of out-of-distribution generalization indicate that larger models are not necessarily more robust [8]. Furthermore, while batch normalization addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training, known as internal covariate shift [9], this phenomenon differs from the covariate shift encountered in out-of-distribution evaluation.

Specific to Bayesian methods under shift, node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. Conversely, research warns that Bayesian neural networks with high-fidelity approximate inference can achieve poor generalization under covariate shift, even underperforming classical estimation [13]. This suggests that the mechanism of uncertainty induction requires careful validation in specific architectural contexts, such as Transformers, where pretrained models show smaller performance declines under distribution shifts compared to previous models [8].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and a final residual. The head comprised final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6).

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics, featuring 9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, and subject clusters. This approach avoided external dependencies while maintaining statistical properties of the raw inertial signals and official subject-disjoint split structure. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights to ensure comparability across conditions.

We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic Training, Identity Control), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. Paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed for each seed. We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized 43 seeds for the primary cohort and 43 seeds for the confirmatory replication cohort. The primary seeds ranged from 497360171578835126 to 3754669615394449950, and replication seeds ranged from 460845256865125083 to 2718212184032681684. The metric of interest was held-out classification accuracy.

The preregistered hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' The decision rule required the mean contrast to exceed this margin to support the hypothesis. Any result failing to exceed this margin, or showing a negative contrast, would refute the hypothesis. We did not pool primary and replication cohorts; each was analyzed separately to maintain the integrity of the confirmatory design.

=== results ===
In the primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. Figure 1 displays the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds, and Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8717 (95% CI [0.865, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9065 (95% CI [0.903, 0.91]). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. Figure 3 displays the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the replication, and Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps. The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline in both cohorts (Table 1).

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. Both the primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy for the Intervention compared to the Baseline. This finding contradicts the expectation derived from prior work suggesting that increasing the entropy of latent variables enhances the diversity of implicit corruptions and robustness [6]. While [6] proposes that diversity depends on entropy, our results indicate that maximizing this entropy in a Transformer architecture under subject-disjoint shift may introduce detrimental noise rather than useful regularization.

Our findings align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. The significant negative contrast suggests that the mechanism of entropy maximization, when decoupled from posterior fidelity (KL minimization), may not generalize to attention-based architectures. This supports the view that Bayesian neural networks can struggle under covariate shift, particularly when inference procedures do not account for specific data dependencies [13]. Furthermore, the result underscores that larger or more complex uncertainty mechanisms are not necessarily more robust [8].

The negative controls performed comparably to the deterministic baseline, indicating that the performance drop is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se. This distinguishes our findings from work proposing weight noise injection training for robustness [15], suggesting that the optimization objective (entropy maximization vs. noise injection) is the critical factor. The consistency between primary and replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this is a reliable negative result rather than a statistical artifact.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may limit generalizability to real-world sensor data despite statistical matching. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may differ in other architectures such as CNNs, which are standard for various operations on 1D signals [10]. The experiment was limited to 50 epochs and specific hyperparameters; different training regimes might yield different interactions between entropy maximization and convergence. Additionally, while we addressed covariate shift via subject-disjoint splits, other forms of distribution shift were not explored.

=== conclusion ===
We investigated whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both primary and replication cohorts. These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization enhances robustness in this setting and suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization over standard regularization for subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. The findings highlight the importance of validating uncertainty mechanisms in specific architectural contexts, as mechanisms promising improved generalization under covariate shift may fail when optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity.

Introduction: Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications where confidence in predictions is paramount. However, basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from over- or under-confidence, meaning they are badly calibrated [1]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions, characterizing uncertainty stemming from both data randomness and model lack of knowledge [3]. Despite this, scalable learning of Bayesian neural networks often faces disadvantages such as lack of calibrated probabilistic predictions and tendencies to overfit [9].

Recent work suggests that Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift by providing principled probabilistic representations of epistemic uncertainty [4]. Specifically, node-based approaches induce uncertainty by multiplying hidden nodes with latent random variables, where the diversity of the implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [4]. This raises the question of whether explicitly maximizing the entropy of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves robustness in modern architectures. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [10].

This study addresses the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report the results of a primary experiment and a confirmatory replication, adhering strictly to the preregistered analysis plan.

Both the primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy for the Intervention compared to the Baseline. This finding contradicts the expectation derived from prior work suggesting that increasing the entropy of latent variables enhances the diversity of implicit corruptions and robustness [4]. While [4] proposes that diversity depends on entropy, our results indicate that maximizing this entropy in a Transformer architecture under subject-disjoint shift may introduce detrimental noise rather than useful regularization.

Our findings align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [10]. The significant negative contrast suggests that the mechanism of entropy maximization, when decoupled from posterior fidelity (KL minimization), may not generalize to attention-based architectures. This supports the view that Bayesian neural networks can struggle under covariate shift, particularly when inference procedures do not account for specific data dependencies [10]. Furthermore, the result underscores that larger or more complex uncertainty mechanisms are not necessarily more robust [6].

The negative controls performed comparably to the deterministic baseline, indicating that the performance drop is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se. This distinguishes our findings from work proposing weight noise injection training for robustness [11], suggesting that the optimization objective (entropy maximization vs. noise injection) is the critical factor. The consistency between primary and replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this is a reliable negative result rather than a statistical artifact.

Conclusion: We investigated whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both primary and replication cohorts. These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization enhances robustness in this setting and suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization over standard regularization for subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. The findings highlight the importance of validating uncertainty mechanisms in specific architectural contexts, as mechanisms promising improved generalization under covariate shift may fail when optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity.

=== abstract ===
This Registered Report evaluates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution (OOD) accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. While node-based Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) suggest entropy relates to robustness under covariate shift, it remains unclear whether entropy-maximized weight noise generalizes to attention-based architectures. We trained a PreNormTransformerEncoder on synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics under four conditions: EntropyMax (intervention), Deterministic (baseline), EntropyMin, and FixedNoise. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy with a mean contrast exceeding 0.0125. In the primary cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened accuracy by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to baseline. The confirmatory replication cohort (43 seeds) refuted the hypothesis again, with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results indicate that entropy maximization of weight noise does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this setting and may degrade performance.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly critical as models deploy in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks often lack calibrated uncertainty estimates [3]. Deep learning methods frequently operate as black boxes where quantifying uncertainty is challenging, prompting interest in Bayesian statistics to formalize prediction uncertainty [12]. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a framework to characterize uncertainty arising from the network itself versus the data [5]. Among various uncertainty-inducing mechanisms, weight noise injection has been proposed to improve robustness against external interference by making weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. However, systematic measurements of out-of-distribution generalization indicate that architectural choices alone, such as model size, do not guarantee robustness [8].

Recent work on node-based BNNs suggests that inducing epistemic uncertainty via latent random variables can improve generalization under covariate shift, with performance diversity depending on the entropy of these variables [6]. This raises the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity via entropy maximization, rather than posterior fidelity via KL minimization, generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This study tests the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard deterministic training.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty quantification is essential for detecting uncertain data in practical applications, yet standard backpropagation lacks calibrated probabilistic predictions [4, 17]. Bayesian neural networks address this by treating weights as distributions, though they often face computational constraints and convergence difficulties in deep architectures [7]. Approximate Bayesian inference is frequently considered a robust alternative to standard training, but evidence suggests it can achieve poor generalization under covariate shift, sometimes underperforming classical estimation [13]. Specifically, Bayesian model averaging can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13].

Regarding robustness mechanisms, weight noise injection training has been shown to reduce the impact of external interference in diffractive neural networks [15]. In the context of covariate shift, node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that induce epistemic uncertainty by multiplying hidden nodes with latent random variables [6]. These node-based approaches perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions, and the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. However, systematic measurements of out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers show that performance declines under distribution shift are substantial, and larger models are not necessarily more robust [8]. This motivates the investigation of whether explicit entropy maximization of weight noise, distinct from node-based latent variables, can improve robustness in Transformer-based time-series classification.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) feedforward network, and a final residual connection. The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooled over time, and projected via Linear(64,6) for classification.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset structure (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows) adapted for synthetic generation. The primary analysis used 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The confirmatory replication analysis used a distinct set of 43 seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). The preregistered hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' The metric was held-out classification accuracy. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for all metrics.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention did not improve accuracy. On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This was a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' was 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] (Figure 1). The preregistered decision was direction_refuted.

In the Confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the result was consistent. On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This was a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' was 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] (Figure 3). The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. Training curves showed stable convergence for all conditions, with the intervention consistently underperforming the baseline throughout training steps (Figure 2, Figure 4). Negative controls (EntropyMin, FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Deterministic baseline in both cohorts (Table 1, Table 2).

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in held-out accuracy for the intervention compared to deterministic training. This finding aligns with prior work warning that approximate Bayesian inference, often considered robust, can achieve poor generalization under covariate shift [13]. Specifically, the failure of the entropy-maximized weight noise suggests that mechanisms effective for node-based BNNs do not necessarily transfer to weight-based uncertainty in attention architectures. While node-based BNNs leverage latent variable entropy to handle input corruptions [6], our results indicate that maximizing entropy in multiplicative weight noise parameters may disrupt feature learning rather than enhance robustness.

Furthermore, the results support evidence that pretrained Transformers do not inherently guarantee out-of-distribution robustness [8]. The negative contrast observed here (-0.04805 in primary, -0.03482 in replication) exceeds the preregistered worthwhile margin in the opposite direction, indicating a meaningful degradation. This contradicts the assumption that diversity-inducing regularization via entropy maximization is universally beneficial for robustness tasks. Instead, it suggests that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness over standard regularization in this specific architectural context without further evidence. The consistency between primary and replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this is a reliable negative result rather than a statistical artifact.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks; results may not generalize to deeper Transformers or different modalities. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; applying it to all weight matrices might yield different outcomes. Additionally, the study focused on subject-disjoint splits; other distribution shifts (e.g., sensor drift) were not explicitly tested.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report investigated whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis predicted a positive contrast exceeding 0.0125. Instead, the intervention significantly worsened accuracy by 0.04805 in the primary cohort and 0.03482 in the replication cohort. These results refute the hypothesis and indicate that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise does not improve subject-disjoint robustness in this setting. The findings align with literature suggesting Bayesian methods can fail under covariate shift [13] and that Transformer robustness is not guaranteed by architecture alone [8]. Future work should investigate why node-based entropy mechanisms [6] do not translate to weight-based entropy in Transformers.

However, systematic measurements of out-of-distribution generalization indicate that architectural choices alone, such as model size, do not guarantee robustness [6].

This raises the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity via entropy maximization, rather than posterior fidelity via KL minimization, generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This contradicts the assumption that diversity-inducing regularization via entropy maximization is universally beneficial for robustness tasks. Instead, it suggests that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness over standard regularization in this specific architectural context without further evidence. The consistency between primary and replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this is a reliable negative result rather than a statistical artifact.

The hypothesis predicted a positive contrast exceeding 0.0125. Instead, the intervention significantly worsened accuracy by 0.04805 in the primary cohort and 0.03482 in the replication cohort. These results refute the hypothesis and indicate that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise does not improve subject-disjoint robustness in this setting. The findings align with literature suggesting Bayesian methods can fail under covariate shift [8] and that Transformer robustness is not guaranteed by architecture alone [6]. Future work should investigate why node-based entropy mechanisms [4] do not translate to weight-based entropy in Transformers.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic models lack calibrated confidence estimates. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise distributions improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise on a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated performance on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline. In the primary cohort, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The replication cohort confirmed this direction of effect with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters enhances generalization in this architecture, suggesting that standard deterministic training remains more effective for subject-disjoint time-series classification than this specific uncertainty-inducing mechanism.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models are deployed in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions [12]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with computational complexity, leading to alternatives like node-based approaches [6]. However, approximate Bayesian inference can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity via entropy maximization, rather than posterior fidelity via KL minimization, generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. Specifically, we test the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification highlights that deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify [12]. Surveys of the field note that basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates, motivating approaches to measure and quantify uncertainty [3]. Regarding robustness, systematic measurements of out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers show that performance declines under distribution shift occur, though they are substantially smaller than previous models [8]. Furthermore, larger models are not necessarily more robust [8].

In the context of Bayesian methods, node-based approaches perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. The diversity of implicit corruptions in these models depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. However, Bayesian model averaging can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Alternative robustness strategies include weight noise injection training, which has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input layer, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and a final residual connection. A final LayerNorm(64) preceded mean-pooling over time and a Linear(64,6) output layer.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. Paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed to test the hypothesis.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset structure (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows) adapted for synthetic generation. The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We preregistered a decision rule to apply on the Primary block, then confirm on the Replication block. The hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

The Primary cohort used 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, ...). The Confirmatory replication cohort used 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, ...). We report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus baseline_1 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This was a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. Mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], compared to 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for baseline_1. Negative controls performed similarly to the baseline: negative_control_1 achieved 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] and negative_control_2 achieved 0.909 [0.906, 0.912].

In the Confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus baseline_1 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This was a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. Mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], compared to 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] for baseline_1. Negative controls remained consistent: negative_control_1 achieved 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] and negative_control_2 achieved 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]. Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy in this setting. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy for the intervention compared to deterministic training. This finding contrasts with prior work suggesting node-based approaches perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. While [6] observed that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables, our application of entropy maximization to multiplicative weight noise in Transformers did not yield similar benefits.

The failure of the intervention may relate to challenges identified in Bayesian methods under shift. Bayesian model averaging can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Although our method did not use full Bayesian model averaging, the optimization of entropy may have interacted poorly with the subject-disjoint shift similar to posterior contraction issues. Furthermore, systematic measurements of out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers show that performance declines under distribution shift are observed, and larger models are not necessarily more robust [8]. Our results suggest that adding entropy-maximized noise does not mitigate these declines in this architecture.

Weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making weights insensitive to changes [15]. However, our negative controls (FixedNoise) performed similarly to the deterministic baseline, while the EntropyMax condition performed worse. This indicates that while noise injection itself may not harm performance, actively maximizing entropy during training disrupts the optimization landscape enough to reduce accuracy below standard regularization levels. These findings guide practitioners to prioritize standard deterministic training over entropy maximization for robustness tasks in subject-disjoint time-series Transformers, unless further mechanisms are introduced to stabilize the entropy objective.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor data. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may not generalize to other Transformer variants or convolutional models. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; applying it to other components might yield different results. Finally, the study focused on subject-disjoint generalization; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift) were not explicitly tested.

=== conclusion ===
This preregistered study tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These results indicate that entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this context. Practitioners should not prioritize this mechanism over standard regularization for robustness tasks without further stabilization methods.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robustness under distribution shift, yet standard variational objectives prioritize posterior fidelity over diversity. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise on a PreNormTransformerEncoder using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy with a mean paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. In a Primary cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened accuracy by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In a Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened accuracy by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts resulted in a preregistered decision of direction_refuted. These findings contradict the assumption that entropy maximization inherently enhances robustness in attention-based architectures under subject-disjoint shift, suggesting that diversity-inducing mechanisms may degrade performance when not aligned with posterior fidelity.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models deploy in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions [12]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Recent work suggests that node-based approaches perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions by inducing epistemic uncertainty through latent random variables [6]. However, it remains an open problem whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity via entropy maximization, rather than posterior fidelity via KL minimization, generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

This study addresses the gap where prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives. We test the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. Specifically, we predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098 proportion. We report results from both a Primary and a Confirmatory Replication cohort, adhering to preregistered decision rules.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems, particularly for detecting uncertain data in safety-critical systems [4]. However, the employment of BNNs is still constrained by increased computational requirements and convergence difficulties when training deep architectures [7]. Structured partial stochasticity has been proposed to simplify posterior distributions and improve approximate inference performance [18]. Regarding robustness, pretrained Transformers have been shown to improve out-of-distribution robustness compared to previous models, though larger models are not necessarily more robust [8].

In the context of covariate shift, node-based BNNs induce epistemic uncertainty by multiplying each hidden node with latent random variables [6]. Research indicates that the diversity of implicit corruptions in these models depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. Conversely, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift; specifically, Bayesian model averaging can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. Our work extends this literature by testing whether explicit entropy maximization of weight noise parameters, rather than implicit node-based noise, improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input layer, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and a final residual. The head comprised a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6).

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining domain relevance. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) and applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
We utilized the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset structure (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows) as the basis for synthetic generation. The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We executed the experiment across two cohorts. The Primary cohort used 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The Confirmatory Replication cohort used 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). We report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the Primary and Replication cohorts, respectively. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort:** Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted. The proposed condition achieved 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] accuracy, while the baseline achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912].

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort:** Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Table 2). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted. The proposed condition achieved 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] accuracy, while the baseline achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. Negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed comparably to the Baseline in both cohorts (Table 1, Table 2).

=== discussion ===
The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention significantly worsened accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the implication of prior work suggesting that increasing the entropy of latent variables enhances diversity and robustness in node-based models [6]. While [6] observed that diversity depends on entropy in the context of input corruptions, our results indicate that explicitly maximizing entropy in weight noise parameters for Transformers under subject-disjoint shift may introduce detrimental regularization rather than beneficial uncertainty.

Our findings align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Specifically, [13] noted that Bayesian model averaging can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction; our entropy-maximized weights may have exacerbated similar instability in the attention mechanisms. Furthermore, the result supports the observation that architectural modifications or uncertainty mechanisms do not guarantee robustness, consistent with findings that larger models are not necessarily more robust [8]. The negative controls (EntropyMin, FixedNoise) performing comparably to Baseline suggests that the degradation is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se, contrasting with work where weight noise injection improved noise resistance [15]. This suggests that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift without careful tuning of the entropy objective.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world subject-disjoint shift. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may not generalize to other architectures or modalities. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; whole-model entropy maximization might yield different results. Finally, while we utilized 43 seeds per cohort, the study remains limited to the specific hyperparameters and training epochs selected.

=== conclusion ===
We investigated whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Contrary to our preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both Primary and Replication cohorts. These results refute the core mechanism of prioritizing entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization without further evidence, as it may degrade performance under subject-disjoint shift.
