=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification is increasingly critical for deploying neural networks in safety-sensitive domains, yet standard deterministic models often lack calibrated confidence estimates [3]. While Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to address this [12], their application in modern architectures is constrained by computational overhead and convergence difficulties [7]. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise intervention within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it against a deterministic baseline using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both the primary cohort (mean contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]) and the confirmatory replication cohort (mean contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization alone enhances robustness in this setting, suggesting that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions has become increasingly important as these models are deployed in real-world applications [3]. However, basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from over- or under-confidence, meaning they are often badly calibrated [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions [12]. Despite this, the employment of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) is still constrained by their increased computational requirements and convergence difficulties when training very deep, state-of-the-art architectures [7].

Recent work suggests that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms might improve generalization under distribution shift. For instance, node-based BNNs induce epistemic uncertainty by multiplying hidden nodes with latent random variables, where the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. However, it remains an open problem whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. Furthermore, while pretrained Transformers show improved out-of-distribution robustness, larger models are not necessarily more robust [8].

This study addresses the gap where prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report the results of this experiment honestly, including the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems, particularly for detecting uncertain data in safety-critical systems [4]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) have attracted considerable attention in this context, as networks trained using dropout can be interpreted as Bayesian methods [4]. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Specifically, Bayesian model averaging can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13].

Regarding optimization and robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. However, stochastic weight sharing techniques are often constrained by computational requirements and convergence difficulties in deep architectures [7]. In the context of covariate shift, node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under input corruptions [6]. Yet, systematic measurements of out-of-distribution generalization indicate that factors affecting robustness are complex, and distillation can sometimes be harmful [8]. Additionally, internal covariate shift, defined as the change in distribution of layer inputs during training, complicates convergence and is often addressed by normalization techniques [9].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) feed-forward layer with ReLU activation, a Linear(128,64) projection, and a final residual connection. The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooled over time, and projected via Linear(64,6) for classification.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining structural similarity to the raw inertial signals and official subject-disjoint split statistics. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) and applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized 43 seeds for the primary cohort and 43 seeds for the confirmatory replication cohort. The primary seeds included 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, and 41 others as preregistered. The confirmatory replication seeds included 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, and 41 others. The metric of interest was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered decision rule required the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s to exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion to support the hypothesis. We report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Figure 1 displays the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds, and Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

In the Confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8717 (95% CI [0.865, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9065 (95% CI [0.903, 0.91]). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. Table 1 summarizes the final metric values per condition. The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline, indicating the degradation is specific to the EntropyMaximization objective in this architecture.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-inducing mechanisms analogous to those in node-based BNNs [6] would generalize to multiplicative weight noise in Transformers. While prior work observes that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables in node-based architectures [6], our results suggest that maximizing entropy in weight noise parameters without posterior fidelity constraints may disrupt feature learning in attention mechanisms.

These findings align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Specifically, the lack of improvement supports the observation that Bayesian model averaging can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Our intervention prioritized entropy over posterior contraction, which may have exacerbated instability under the subject-disjoint shift. Furthermore, the result reinforces evidence that larger or more complex models and regularization strategies are not necessarily more robust [8]. The failure of the entropy-maximized noise to improve robustness, despite theoretical motivations regarding uncertainty diversity [6], indicates that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this specific architectural context.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration with 2 blocks; results may differ in deeper models or different modalities. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; whole-network entropy maximization might yield different effects. Finally, the study focused on subject-disjoint shifts; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift) were not evaluated.

=== conclusion ===
We investigated whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both primary and replication cohorts. These results refute the hypothesis and suggest that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity do not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. Future work should investigate whether combining entropy maximization with posterior contraction constraints [13] or applying it to different architectural components might mitigate the observed performance degradation.

This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise intervention within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it against a deterministic baseline using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both the primary cohort (mean contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]) and the confirmatory replication cohort (mean contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization alone enhances robustness in this setting, suggesting that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.
Related work: Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems, particularly for detecting uncertain data in safety-critical systems [2]. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) have attracted considerable attention in this context, as networks trained using dropout can be interpreted as Bayesian methods [2]. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [8]. Specifically, Bayesian model averaging can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [8].

Regarding optimization and robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [9]. However, stochastic weight sharing techniques are often constrained by computational requirements and convergence difficulties in deep architectures [4]. In the context of covariate shift, node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under input corruptions [3]. Yet, systematic measurements of out-of-distribution generalization indicate that factors affecting robustness are complex, and distillation can sometimes be harmful [5]. Additionally, internal covariate shift, defined as the change in distribution of layer inputs during training, complicates convergence and is often addressed by normalization techniques [6].
Method: We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) feed-forward layer with ReLU activation, a Linear(128,64) projection, and a final residual connection. The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooled over time, and projected via Linear(64,6) for classification.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining structural similarity to the raw inertial signals and official subject-disjoint split statistics. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) and applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.
Results: In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

In the Confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8717 (95% CI [0.865, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9065 (95% CI [0.903, 0.91]). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. Table 1 summarizes the final metric values per condition. The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline, indicating the degradation is specific to the EntropyMaximization objective in this architecture.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** and the independent confirmatory replication was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-inducing mechanisms analogous to those in node-based BNNs [3] would generalize to multiplicative weight noise in Transformers. While prior work observes that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables in node-based architectures [3], our results suggest that maximizing entropy in weight noise parameters without posterior fidelity constraints may disrupt feature learning in attention mechanisms.

These findings align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [8]. Specifically, the lack of improvement supports the observation that Bayesian model averaging can be problematic under covariate shift where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [8]. Our intervention prioritized entropy over posterior contraction, which may have exacerbated instability under the subject-disjoint shift. Furthermore, the result reinforces evidence that larger or more complex models and regularization strategies are not necessarily more robust [5]. The failure of the entropy-maximized noise to improve robustness, despite theoretical motivations regarding uncertainty diversity [3], indicates that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this specific architectural context.
Limitations: This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all nuances of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration with 2 blocks; results may differ in deeper models or different modalities. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; whole-network entropy maximization might yield different effects. Finally, the study focused on subject-disjoint shifts; other forms of distribution shift (e.g., sensor drift) were not evaluated.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.012509797746985206 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

=== abstract ===
This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise on a PreNormTransformerEncoder using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. The preregistered hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed margin of 0.0125098. In the Primary cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened the contrast by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts refuted the hypothesis. While prior work suggests uncertainty mechanisms can aid robustness, these results indicate that entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise may degrade performance in subject-disjoint Transformer architectures relative to deterministic baselines.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models deploy in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Modern deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify [12]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this, characterizing uncertainty stemming from data randomness and lack of knowledge about data creation [5]. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. This study addresses the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

We focus on subject-disjoint time-series data, a setting where distribution shift occurs between training and held-out subjects. While weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [15], and node-based Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) have shown promise under input corruptions [6], it remains unclear if explicitly maximizing the entropy of weight noise parameters improves generalization in Transformers. We preregistered a hypothesis that EntropyMaxWeightNoise would exceed deterministic training accuracy by a margin of 0.0125098. This work validates or refutes the core mechanism of entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems, particularly for detecting uncertain data in safety-critical systems [4]. Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important [3]. However, the employment of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) is still constrained by their increased computational requirements and convergence difficulties when training very deep architectures [7]. To mitigate complexity, node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6].

Regarding optimization and robustness, approximate Bayesian inference can sometimes fail under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. In the context of model robustness, factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [8]. Conversely, weight noise injection training has been proposed to reduce the impact of external interference and improve noise resistance [15]. Entropy has also been used to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14]. While stochastic weight sharing techniques reinterpret quantization from a stochastic perspective to reduce computational overhead [7], the specific effect of maximizing entropy on multiplicative weight noise distributions in Transformers remains under-explored compared to standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear(64,6) classification head.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining structural fidelity to the target domain. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects. Accuracy was aggregated per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) and applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized two distinct cohorts of random seeds to ensure reproducibility. The Primary cohort consisted of 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The Confirmatory Replication cohort consisted of 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' The decision rule required the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for the contrast to exceed 0.0125098 to support the hypothesis. Any result where the confidence interval excluded zero in the negative direction was labeled as direction_refuted.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition achieved 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while the 'baseline_1' condition achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The training curves over steps are shown in Figure 2. The preregistered decision is: direction_refuted.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition achieved 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while the 'baseline_1' condition achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The training curves over steps are shown in Figure 4. The preregistered decision is: direction_refuted.

Negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline in both cohorts (approx. 0.908–0.909 accuracy), indicating that the performance drop was specific to the EntropyMax intervention rather than noise injection generally.

=== discussion ===
The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to deterministic training by approximately 3.5% to 4.8%. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would generalize better than standard regularization.

These results contrast with prior work suggesting node-based BNNs perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. While [6] observed that diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of latent variables, our implementation of entropy maximization on weight noise in Transformers did not yield similar robustness benefits. Furthermore, while weight noise injection training has been shown to improve noise resistance in diffractive neural networks [15], our results suggest that in subject-disjoint Transformer architectures, maximizing the entropy of this noise may introduce instability that harms clean held-out accuracy.

The failure may relate to optimization dynamics under distribution shift. Approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Although our study did not explicitly measure posterior contraction, the significant drop in accuracy suggests the entropy objective may have conflicted with feature learning required for subject-disjoint generalization. Additionally, while factors like distillation can be harmful to robustness [8], our work highlights that even explicit entropy regularization can be detrimental when not aligned with the primary accuracy objective. The employment of BNNs is often constrained by computational requirements [7], and our method added computational overhead without accuracy benefits, further questioning its utility in this setting.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor data. The architecture was fixed to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration; results may differ in deeper or wider models. We trained for 50 epochs; longer training schedules might alter the convergence of the entropy-maximized weights. Finally, we measured held-out classification accuracy but did not explicitly quantify calibration or uncertainty quality, which might behave differently than accuracy under the intervention.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a preregistered experiment to test whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. The hypothesis predicted an accuracy gain exceeding 0.0125098. Instead, the intervention significantly worsened accuracy by 0.04805 in the Primary cohort and 0.03482 in the Replication cohort. Both cohorts refuted the hypothesis. These findings indicate that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization of weight uncertainty for robustness tasks over standard deterministic training in this specific architecture and domain, as it may degrade performance rather than enhance generalization.

To mitigate complexity, node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [4].

Regarding optimization and robustness, approximate Bayesian inference can sometimes fail under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [8]. In the context of model robustness, factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [6]. Conversely, weight noise injection training has been proposed to reduce the impact of external interference and improve noise resistance [10]. Entropy has also been used to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [9]. While stochastic weight sharing techniques reinterpret quantization from a stochastic perspective to reduce computational overhead [5], the specific effect of maximizing entropy on multiplicative weight noise distributions in Transformers remains under-explored compared to standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining structural fidelity to the target domain. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects. Accuracy was aggregated per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) and applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.
Results: **Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition achieved 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while the 'baseline_1' condition achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The training curves over steps are shown in Figure 2. The preregistered decision is: direction_refuted.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Figure 3). The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The training curves over steps are shown in Figure 4. The preregistered decision is: direction_refuted.

Negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline in both cohorts (approx. 0.908–0.909 accuracy), indicating that the performance drop was specific to the EntropyMax intervention rather than noise injection generally.

These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to deterministic training by approximately 3.5% to 4.8%. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would generalize better than standard regularization.

These results contrast with prior work suggesting node-based BNNs perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [4]. While [4] observed that diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of latent variables, our implementation of entropy maximization on weight noise in Transformers did not yield similar robustness benefits. Furthermore, while weight noise injection training has been shown to improve noise resistance in diffractive neural networks [10], our results suggest that in subject-disjoint Transformer architectures, maximizing the entropy of this noise may introduce instability that harms clean held-out accuracy.

The failure may relate to optimization dynamics under distribution shift. Approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [8]. Although our study did not explicitly measure posterior contraction, the significant drop in accuracy suggests the entropy objective may have conflicted with feature learning required for subject-disjoint generalization. Additionally, while factors like distillation can be harmful to robustness [6], our work highlights that even explicit entropy regularization can be detrimental when not aligned with the primary accuracy objective. The employment of BNNs is often constrained by computational requirements [5], and our method added computational overhead without accuracy benefits, further questioning its utility in this setting.
Limitations: This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor data. The architecture was fixed to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration; results may differ in deeper or wider models. We trained for 50 epochs; longer training schedules might alter the convergence of the entropy-maximized weights. Finally, we measured held-out classification accuracy but did not explicitly quantify calibration or uncertainty quality, which might behave differently than accuracy under the intervention.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic models often lack calibrated confidence estimates. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a formalism for uncertainty but face computational and convergence challenges in modern architectures. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise intervention on a Transformer encoder trained on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both the primary cohort (mean contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) and the confirmatory replication cohort (mean contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the prediction that entropy maximization enhances subject-disjoint generalization in this setting, suggesting that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms may not substitute for posterior fidelity under distribution shift.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions has become increasingly important as models are deployed in real-world applications [3]. However, basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions, addressing the black-box nature of standard deep learning methods [12]. Despite this, neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the network itself [5].

Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift by providing principled probabilistic representations of epistemic uncertainty [6]. However, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity in large-scale architectures [6]. Node-based BNNs have recently been introduced as scalable alternatives, which induce epistemic uncertainty by multiplying each hidden node with latent random variables, while learning a point-estimate of the weights [6]. Recent work observes that the diversity of the implicit corruptions in such models depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. This raises the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

This study addresses the gap where prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We test the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training yields higher held-out classification accuracy than standard deterministic training, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems, particularly for detecting uncertain data in safety-critical systems [4]. Various approaches to measure and quantify uncertainty in neural networks have been proposed to overcome the lack of certainty estimates in basic networks [3]. Bayesian neural networks allow the uncertainty due to the network to be characterised, categorizing uncertainty in terms of ingrained randomness and lack of knowledge about data creation [5]. However, existing Bayesian techniques often lack scalability to large dataset and network sizes [17].

Regarding robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to reduce the impact of external interference on deep learning inference results, making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. In the context of covariate shift, approximate Bayesian inference for neural networks is considered a robust alternative to standard training, often providing good performance on out-of-distribution data [13]. However, Bayesian neural networks with high-fidelity approximate inference via full-batch Hamiltonian Monte Carlo achieve poor generalization under covariate shift, even underperforming classical estimation [13]. This failure occurs particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13].

Node-based BNNs have recently been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. Conversely, in the domain of pretrained Transformers, factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [8]. While larger models are not necessarily more robust, more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [8]. These findings highlight the complexity of transferring uncertainty mechanisms across architectures, motivating our investigation into entropy maximization within Transformer encoders.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) projection, ReLU activation, a Linear(128,64) projection, and a final residual connection. The head comprised a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and a Linear(64,6) output layer.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining structural similarity to the target domain. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects.

=== experimental_setup ===
We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). The experiment utilized a Primary block and a Confirmatory Replication block, each comprising 43 seeds. The primary seeds were distinct from the replication seeds to ensure independent validation. We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block first, then confirmed on the Replication block. The metric of interest was held-out classification accuracy. We report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. The preregistered hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]) (Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The training curves indicated divergent optimization dynamics between the intervention and baseline conditions (Figure 2). The preregistered decision for the primary cohort is direction_refuted.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8717 (95% CI [0.865, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9065 (95% CI [0.903, 0.91]) (Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The training trajectories replicated the primary cohort's pattern (Figure 4). The preregistered decision for the replication cohort is direction_refuted.

=== discussion ===
The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both the primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would generalize effectively in attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

These negative results contextualize recent findings on BNN robustness. While node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6], our results suggest that simply maximizing entropy of latent variables in a Transformer query projection does not replicate this benefit. This aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can sometimes fail under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Our entropy maximization objective may have exacerbated such contraction issues by prioritizing diversity over posterior fidelity.

Furthermore, the harm observed parallels findings in Transformer robustness where factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [8]. Just as distillation may constrain model capacity in ways detrimental to OOD performance, explicit entropy regularization on weights may interfere with the feature learning required for subject-disjoint generalization. While weight noise injection training has been shown to improve network noise resistance in other contexts [15], our results indicate this does not transfer to entropy-maximized multiplicative noise in Transformers for this task. The consistency across 86 total seeds strengthens the conclusion that this mechanism is not robust for this application.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration; results may differ with deeper models or different attention mechanisms. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; whole-network entropy maximization might yield different outcomes. Finally, the study focused on classification accuracy; effects on calibration or uncertainty quantification metrics were not preregistered outcomes.

=== conclusion ===
We investigated whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both primary and replication cohorts. These results refute the utility of this specific entropy maximization mechanism for robustness in this setting. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization over standard regularization for subject-disjoint time-series tasks without further evidence, as it may actively degrade performance. Future work should explore whether posterior fidelity objectives offer better robustness than diversity-focused entropy maximization in attention-based architectures.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment, yet standard deterministic training often fails to capture epistemic uncertainty under distribution shift. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy with a mean paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it across primary and confirmatory replication cohorts using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened performance. In the primary cohort, the proposed method worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The replication cohort confirmed this direction of effect, with a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight noise enhances robustness in this architecture, suggesting that standard regularization may remain preferable for subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models are deployed in safety-critical applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to characterize uncertainty due to the network, categorizing it in terms of ingrained randomness and lack of knowledge about data creation [5]. While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based implementations often struggle with computational complexity [6]. Recent work suggests that node-based alternatives may scale better [6], and that weight noise injection can reduce the impact of external interference [15]. However, it remains an open problem whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity via entropy maximization, rather than posterior fidelity via KL minimization, generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

This study addresses the gap where prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, but no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. We report the results of a experiment conducted across primary and confirmatory replication cohorts. The findings provide a rigorous test of whether entropy maximization validates the core mechanism of node-based BNNs in modern architectures.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4]. Modern deep learning methods operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, though Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. However, existing Bayesian techniques often lack scalability to large dataset and network sizes [17]. To address computational constraints, stochastic weight sharing has been proposed to reduce overhead [7], and node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. These node-based approaches induce epistemic uncertainty by multiplying hidden nodes with latent random variables, where the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6].

Regarding robustness, weight noise injection training has been proposed to reduce the impact of external interference on deep learning inference results, making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. This failure occurs particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. In the domain of pretrained Transformers, factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [8]. While larger models are not necessarily more robust, more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [8]. Our work investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight noise, distinct from standard variational objectives, can overcome these limitations in subject-disjoint time-series classification.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). The final layer involved LayerNorm(64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear(64,6) classification head.

To avoid external dependencies, we generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics, comprising 9 channels, 128 timesteps, and 6 classes with subject clusters. We initialized identical model weights for each seed and ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. Paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed to test the preregistered hypothesis.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized 43 seeds for the primary cohort and 43 seeds for the confirmatory replication cohort. The primary seeds included 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, and 41 others as preregistered. The replication seeds included 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, and 41 others. The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, requiring the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast to exceed 0.0125098, and then confirmed on the Replication block. Figure 1 displays the final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds, and Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed intervention did not exceed the baseline. On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This was a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted.

In the Confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the result was consistent. On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This was a statistically significant difference. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. Negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the baseline in both cohorts (Table 1).

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy for the intervention compared to deterministic training. This finding contrasts with the promise of node-based BNNs to perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. While prior work suggests that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of latent variables [6], our results indicate that explicitly maximizing this entropy in a Transformer query projection layer degrades generalization on subject-disjoint time-series data.

The failure of the intervention aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Specifically, the observed degradation may relate to cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Furthermore, while weight noise injection has been proposed to make network weights insensitive to modest changes [15], our implementation of entropy-maximized noise appears to have introduced instability rather than robustness. In the domain of pretrained Transformers, robustness is not guaranteed by model size or simple regularization [8]. Our findings suggest that for subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, standard deterministic training remains more effective than entropy-maximized weight noise. This validates the need for caution when adapting uncertainty mechanisms from node-based BNNs to attention-based architectures without empirical verification.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific Transformer encoder configuration with 2 blocks and 4 heads, which may not generalize to larger pretrained models where diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [8]. Additionally, the entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; effects may differ if applied to other components. The study was calibrated to detect a specific margin of improvement, and while the refutation is statistically significant, the effect sizes (Cohen's dz=-0.72 and -1.41) indicate a substantial negative impact that warrants investigation into the optimization dynamics of entropy objectives in attention mechanisms.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a preregistered experiment to test whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly reducing held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These results indicate that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this setting. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization over entropy maximization for robustness tasks in similar contexts, as the core mechanism of node-based BNNs did not translate successfully to this architecture.

In the domain of pretrained Transformers, factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [6]. The model architecture consisted of a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). Paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed to test the preregistered hypothesis.

This was a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted.

In the Confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the result was consistent. On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This was a statistically significant difference. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy for the intervention compared to deterministic training. This finding contrasts with the promise of node-based BNNs to perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [4]. While prior work suggests that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of latent variables [4], our results indicate that explicitly maximizing this entropy in a Transformer query projection layer degrades generalization on subject-disjoint time-series data.

The failure of the intervention aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [8]. Specifically, the observed degradation may relate to cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [8]. Furthermore, while weight noise injection has been proposed to make network weights insensitive to modest changes [9], our implementation of entropy-maximized noise appears to have introduced instability rather than robustness. In the domain of pretrained Transformers, robustness is not guaranteed by model size or simple regularization [6]. Our findings suggest that for subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, standard deterministic training remains more effective than entropy-maximized weight noise. This validates the need for caution when adapting uncertainty mechanisms from node-based BNNs to attention-based architectures without empirical verification.
Limitations: This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific Transformer encoder configuration with 2 blocks and 4 heads, which may not generalize to larger pretrained models where diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [6]. Additionally, the entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; effects may differ if applied to other components. === abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning is critical for robust deployment under distribution shift, yet standard variational objectives often prioritize posterior fidelity over predictive diversity. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125 proportion. Using a PreNormTransformerEncoder trained on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across 86 seeds (43 primary, 43 replication), we evaluated an EntropyMaxWeightNoise intervention against deterministic and negative control baselines. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened performance. In the primary cohort, the intervention yielded 0.8604 accuracy versus 0.9085 for baseline (contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The replication cohort confirmed this direction (contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty enhances subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, suggesting that mechanisms optimized for diversity may compromise accuracy where posterior fidelity is required.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models deploy in safety-critical applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates and often suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty, addressing the black-box nature of deep learning methods where uncertainty is challenging to quantify [12]. However, the introduction of neural networks intrinsically increases uncertainty about which features are model-related versus due to the network itself [5]. While uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], existing Bayesian techniques often lack scalability to large dataset and network sizes [17].

This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity via entropy maximization, rather than posterior fidelity via KL minimization, generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. Specifically, we test if explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098 proportion. This study validates or refutes the core mechanism of node-based BNNs [6] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this, though deep learning methods operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify [12]. Bayesian neural networks allow uncertainty due to the network to be characterised [5], and uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems [4]. However, existing Bayesian techniques lack scalability to large dataset and network sizes [17], and the employment of BNNs is still constrained by increased computational requirements and convergence difficulties [7].

Regarding robustness, Bayesian neural networks promise improved generalization under covariate shift by providing principled probabilistic representations of epistemic uncertainty [6]. Node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. In these models, the diversity of the implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. This failure occurs particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13].

In the context of Transformers, pretrained models achieve high accuracy on indistribution examples but generalization to new distributions varies [8]. Factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [8]. While larger models are not necessarily more robust, more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [8]. Weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [15]. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of such noise parameters improves subject-disjoint generalization compared to standard variational objectives.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear(64,6) classification head.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining domain relevance. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects. Accuracy was aggregated per seed, and paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed. We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized 86 seeds in total, split into a Primary cohort (43 seeds) and a Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds). The primary seeds included 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, and 41 others. The replication seeds included 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, and 41 others. Training used SGD for 50 epochs. The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' The decision rule required the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for the contrast to exceed 0.0125098 to accept the hypothesis. All analysis was conducted separately for the Primary and Replication cohorts without pooling.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus baseline (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). The 95% CI excludes zero, indicating a statistically significant difference. The mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], compared to 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for the baseline. The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911]; NegCtrl2: 0.909 [0.906, 0.912]). The preregistered decision was direction_refuted.

In the Confirmatory Replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus baseline (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). The 95% CI excludes zero. The mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], compared to 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] for the baseline. Negative controls remained consistent (NegCtrl1: 0.908 [0.904, 0.912]; NegCtrl2: 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]). The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy relative to deterministic baselines, with contrasts of -0.04805 and -0.03482 respectively. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized mechanisms generalize better than posterior-fidelity objectives in this setting.

Reflecting on the literature, these results challenge the assumption that increasing the entropy of latent variables inherently enhances robustness under covariate shift. While node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6], and the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6], our findings suggest this mechanism does not transfer beneficially to attention-based architectures under subject-disjoint shifts. The observed performance degradation aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Specifically, the failure may relate to cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13], which entropy maximization might exacerbate rather than resolve.

Furthermore, while factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [8], and more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [8], our intervention attempted to induce diversity through weight noise rather than data. The negative result suggests that weight noise optimized for entropy may not substitute for data diversity or architectural robustness. This extends the understanding of Bayesian scalability constraints [17], indicating that even computationally feasible uncertainty mechanisms (like weight noise) may incur accuracy costs if not aligned with posterior fidelity. The results do not support prioritizing entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in Transformers, contradicting the core mechanism proposed for node-based BNNs [6] when applied in this specific manner.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to ensure strict subject-disjoint control, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a PreNormTransformerEncoder with specific hyperparameters; results may vary with deeper models or different attention mechanisms. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; whole-network entropy optimization might yield different outcomes. Finally, the study focused on classification accuracy; other uncertainty metrics (e.g., calibration, negative log-likelihood) were not preregistered and remain exploratory.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a preregistered experiment to test whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly reducing held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight noise does not guarantee robustness in attention-based architectures and may hinder performance where posterior contraction is required. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization over standard regularization for robustness tasks without further evidence, as the core mechanism of node-based BNNs [6] did not translate to improved accuracy in this setting.

However, existing Bayesian techniques lack scalability to large dataset and network sizes [10], and the employment of BNNs is still constrained by increased computational requirements and convergence difficulties [5].

Regarding robustness, Bayesian neural networks promise improved generalization under covariate shift by providing principled probabilistic representations of epistemic uncertainty [4]. Node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [4]. In these models, the diversity of the implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [4]. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [8]. This failure occurs particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [8].

In the context of Transformers, pretrained models achieve high accuracy on indistribution examples but generalization to new distributions varies [6]. Factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [6]. While larger models are not necessarily more robust, more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [6]. Weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness by making network weights insensitive to modest changes [9]. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of such noise parameters improves subject-disjoint generalization compared to standard variational objectives.
