The model consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, and a feed-forward network (Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64)). The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear(64,6) classification head.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining domain relevance. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

The mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], compared to 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for the baseline. The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911]; NegCtrl2: 0.909 [0.906, 0.912]). The preregistered decision was direction_refuted.

In the Confirmatory Replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus baseline (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). The 95% CI excludes zero. The mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], compared to 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] for the baseline. Negative controls remained consistent (NegCtrl1: 0.908 [0.904, 0.912]; NegCtrl2: 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]). The preregistered decision was direction_refuted. Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy relative to deterministic baselines, with contrasts of -0.04805 and -0.03482 respectively. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized mechanisms generalize better than posterior-fidelity objectives in this setting.

Reflecting on the literature, these results challenge the assumption that increasing the entropy of latent variables inherently enhances robustness under covariate shift. While node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [4], and the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [4], our findings suggest this mechanism does not transfer beneficially to attention-based architectures under subject-disjoint shifts. The observed performance degradation aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [8]. Specifically, the failure may relate to cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [8], which entropy maximization might exacerbate rather than resolve.

Furthermore, while factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [6], and more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [6], our intervention attempted to induce diversity through weight noise rather than data. The negative result suggests that weight noise optimized for entropy may not substitute for data diversity or architectural robustness. This extends the understanding of Bayesian scalability constraints [10], indicating that even computationally feasible uncertainty mechanisms (like weight noise) may incur accuracy costs if not aligned with posterior fidelity. The results do not support prioritizing entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in Transformers, contradicting the core mechanism proposed for node-based BNNs [4] when applied in this specific manner.
Limitations: This study used synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to ensure strict subject-disjoint control, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a PreNormTransformerEncoder with specific hyperparameters; results may vary with deeper models or different attention mechanisms. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; whole-network entropy optimization might yield different outcomes. Finally, the study focused on classification accuracy; other uncertainty metrics (e.g., calibration, negative log-likelihood) were not preregistered and remain exploratory.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robustness under distribution shift, yet standard variational objectives often prioritize posterior fidelity over diversity. This study preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training would improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise intervention on a PreNormTransformerEncoder using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. The experiment utilized a Primary cohort (43 seeds) and a Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds). Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the deterministic baseline in both cohorts. In the Primary cohort, the paired contrast was -0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the Replication cohort, the contrast was -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the prediction that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters enhances subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, suggesting that diversity induced by entropy maximization may not substitute for posterior fidelity in attention-based models under these conditions.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions has become increasingly important as models are deployed in real-world applications [3]. However, basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions, addressing the challenge that deep learning methods often operate as black boxes [12]. Specifically, Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) provide a framework where uncertainty due to the network can be characterised [5]. Despite this potential, existing Bayesian techniques lack scalability to large dataset and network sizes [17].

Recent work has introduced Node-based BNNs as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. In these models, the diversity of the implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. This suggests that explicitly maximizing entropy might enhance robustness. However, approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Furthermore, factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization, and larger models are not necessarily more robust [8].

This study addresses the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report the results of a Primary and a Confirmatory Replication cohort, adhering strictly to the preregistered decision rule.

=== related_work ===
Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems, particularly for detecting uncertain data in safety-critical systems [4]. Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. Bayesian neural networks allow uncertainty due to the network to be characterised, categorizing uncertainty in terms of ingrained randomness and lack of knowledge about data creation [5]. However, deep learning methods operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, necessitating Bayesian formalisms [12].

Regarding scalability, existing Bayesian techniques lack scalability to large dataset and network sizes [17]. To address this, Node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [6]. In these models, the diversity of the implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [6]. This mechanism suggests that increasing entropy could improve robustness. However, failure in Bayesian model averaging occurs particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Additionally, robustness is not guaranteed by model scale; larger models are not necessarily more robust, and more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [8]. Factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [8]. These findings highlight the complexity of translating uncertainty mechanisms into robustness gains in modern architectures.

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) feedforward network, and a final residual connection. The head comprised a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6) output.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining realistic distribution shift characteristics. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized two distinct cohorts of random seeds to ensure reproducibility. The Primary cohort consisted of 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, ...). The Confirmatory Replication cohort consisted of 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, ...). We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline).

The preregistered hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' The decision rule required testing this contrast on the Primary block first, then confirming on the Replication block. We report held-out classification accuracy as the primary metric. Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the Primary and Replication cohorts, respectively. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition (EntropyMax) achieved 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877]. The 'baseline_1' condition (Deterministic) achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Primary cohort is: direction_refuted.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition achieved 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877]. The 'baseline_1' condition achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Replication cohort is: direction_refuted.

The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline in both cohorts (Primary: 0.9082 and 0.909; Replication: 0.908 and 0.9088), indicating that the performance drop is specific to the EntropyMax intervention rather than noise injection generally.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. Both Primary and Replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in held-out accuracy when entropy maximization was applied. This finding contrasts with the suggestion that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables in Node-based BNNs [6]. While [6] proposes increasing entropy to improve performance under covariate shift, our results indicate that in attention-based architectures trained with SGD, maximizing entropy of multiplicative weight noise may disrupt feature learning rather than enhance robustness.

The failure of the intervention may relate to issues of posterior contraction. Approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. By maximizing entropy, the intervention may have prevented the necessary contraction of the weight distribution around optimal features, leading to the observed accuracy drop. Additionally, robustness is not guaranteed by model complexity or specific regularization alone; larger models are not necessarily more robust [8]. Our findings align with the observation that factors often assumed to aid generalization, such as specific noise structures, can be harmful if not aligned with the data distribution [8].

The negative controls performed comparably to the deterministic baseline, suggesting that the detrimental effect is specific to the *maximization* objective rather than the presence of weight noise itself. This distinguishes our result from work proposing weight noise injection training to reduce the impact of external interference [15], indicating that the optimization objective (entropy max vs. fixed noise) is the critical differentiator. Ultimately, practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting, as the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [6] did not translate to improved subject-disjoint generalization here.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world subject-disjoint shifts. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may not generalize to other architectures such as CNNs, which are standard for various operations on 1D signals [10]. The training duration was fixed at 50 epochs, and convergence stability might vary with different optimizers or learning rate schedules, as convergence speed can collapse under certain arithmetic conditions [1]. We did not evaluate calibration metrics, focusing solely on accuracy, though uncertainty evaluation is significant for safety-critical systems [4].

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a preregistered experiment to test whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to deterministic training. The hypothesis was refuted in both Primary and Confirmatory Replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy by approximately 3.5% to 4.8%. These results indicate that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under these conditions. Future work should investigate whether posterior fidelity objectives remain superior to diversity objectives for robustness in Transformers.

Title: Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness
Abstract: Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robustness under distribution shift, yet standard variational objectives often prioritize posterior fidelity over diversity. This study preregistered a hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters during training would improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise intervention on a PreNormTransformerEncoder using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. The experiment utilized a Primary cohort (43 seeds) and a Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds). Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the deterministic baseline in both cohorts. In the Primary cohort, the paired contrast was -0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the Replication cohort, the contrast was -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the prediction that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters enhances subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, suggesting that diversity induced by entropy maximization may not substitute for posterior fidelity in attention-based models under these conditions.
Related work: Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems, particularly for detecting uncertain data in safety-critical systems [3]. Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [2]. Bayesian neural networks allow uncertainty due to the network to be characterised, categorizing uncertainty in terms of ingrained randomness and lack of knowledge about data creation [4]. However, deep learning methods operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, necessitating Bayesian formalisms [8].

Regarding scalability, existing Bayesian techniques lack scalability to large dataset and network sizes [11]. To address this, Node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that perform well under covariate shift due to input corruptions [5]. In these models, the diversity of the implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables [5]. This mechanism suggests that increasing entropy could improve robustness. However, failure in Bayesian model averaging occurs particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [9]. Additionally, robustness is not guaranteed by model scale; larger models are not necessarily more robust, and more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [6]. Factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [6]. These findings highlight the complexity of translating uncertainty mechanisms into robustness gains in modern architectures.
Method: We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) feedforward network, and a final residual connection. The head comprised a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6) output.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining realistic distribution shift characteristics. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects.
Results: **Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition (EntropyMax) achieved 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877]. The 'baseline_1' condition (Deterministic) achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Primary cohort is: direction_refuted.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', the 'proposed' condition achieved 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877]. The 'baseline_1' condition achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. The 'proposed' condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Replication cohort is: direction_refuted.

The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline in both cohorts (Primary: 0.9082 and 0.909; Replication: 0.908 and 0.9088), indicating that the performance drop is specific to the EntropyMax intervention rather than noise injection generally.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** and the independent confirmatory replication was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. Both Primary and Replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in held-out accuracy when entropy maximization was applied. This finding contrasts with the suggestion that the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of the latent variables in Node-based BNNs [5]. While [5] proposes increasing entropy to improve performance under covariate shift, our results indicate that in attention-based architectures trained with SGD, maximizing entropy of multiplicative weight noise may disrupt feature learning rather than enhance robustness.

The failure of the intervention may relate to issues of posterior contraction. Approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [9]. By maximizing entropy, the intervention may have prevented the necessary contraction of the weight distribution around optimal features, leading to the observed accuracy drop. Additionally, robustness is not guaranteed by model complexity or specific regularization alone; larger models are not necessarily more robust [6]. Our findings align with the observation that factors often assumed to aid generalization, such as specific noise structures, can be harmful if not aligned with the data distribution [6].

The negative controls performed comparably to the deterministic baseline, suggesting that the detrimental effect is specific to the *maximization* objective rather than the presence of weight noise itself. This distinguishes our result from work proposing weight noise injection training to reduce the impact of external interference [10], indicating that the optimization objective (entropy max vs. fixed noise) is the critical differentiator. Ultimately, practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting, as the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [5] did not translate to improved subject-disjoint generalization here.
Limitations: This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world subject-disjoint shifts. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may not generalize to other architectures such as CNNs, which are standard for various operations on 1D signals [7]. The training duration was fixed at 50 epochs, and convergence stability might vary with different optimizers or learning rate schedules, as convergence speed can collapse under certain arithmetic conditions [1]. We did not evaluate calibration metrics, focusing solely on accuracy, though uncertainty evaluation is significant for safety-critical systems [3].

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.012509797746985206 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification is critical for deploying neural networks in safety-critical domains, yet standard architectures often lack calibrated confidence estimates. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) address this by modelling weight uncertainty, though computational constraints and convergence difficulties persist. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated it on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary and confirmatory replication cohorts. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary: mean contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]; Replication: mean contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization enhances robustness in this setting, suggesting that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models permeate scientific and real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions, addressing the black-box nature of standard deep learning methods [12]. Within this framework, uncertainty can be categorised in terms of the ingrained randomness of observing certain data and the uncertainty from our lack of knowledge about how data can be created and observed [5]. While uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], standard backpropagation lacks calibrated probabilistic predictions and tends to overfit [17].

This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. Validating or refuting the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [7] in modern architectures guides whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) feedforward network, and a final residual. The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooled over time, and projected via Linear(64,6) for classification.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. Paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed to assess the hypothesis.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset structure (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows) as a template for synthetic generation. The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We defined two cohorts: a Primary cohort (43 seeds) and a Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds). The preregistered decision rule was applied to the Primary block first, then confirmed on the Replication block. The hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see the results table). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see the results table). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the mechanism suggested by prior work on node-based BNNs, where increasing the entropy of latent variables was observed to improve performance under covariate shift [6]. While [6] proposed that diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of latent variables, our results indicate this mechanism does not translate to multiplicative weight noise in Transformers trained with SGD.

The failure may relate to optimization dynamics or posterior geometry. Approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Although our synthetic data mimicked UCI HAR statistics, specific feature dependencies may have hindered the entropy-maximized posterior from contracting effectively around robust solutions. Furthermore, robustness is not guaranteed by model scale; larger models are not necessarily more robust, and more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [8]. Our study used a modest Transformer architecture without diverse pretraining, which may limit the generalization benefits typically associated with uncertainty methods. Additionally, factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [8], suggesting that regularization techniques interacting with uncertainty parameters require careful tuning.

Optimization stability may also play a role. Convergence stability of SGD can vary under different precision and momentum settings [1], and while we used standard SGD, uninvestigated hyperparameter interactions could influence the efficacy of entropy regularization. The computational constraints inherent in Bayesian learning [7] further suggest that simpler regularization methods might outperform complex uncertainty quantification in resource-constrained settings. Ultimately, these results suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this specific architectural context without further evidence.

=== limitations ===
This study relies on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics, which may not capture the full complexity of real-world distribution shifts. The model architecture was fixed to a PreNormTransformerEncoder, limiting generalizability to other architectures such as CNNs, which are standard for various operations on 1D signals [10]. Optimization hyperparameters were held constant; however, convergence stability can depend on precision and momentum configurations [1], which were not varied here. Additionally, while BNNs offer a principled framework for uncertainty, their employment is still constrained by increased computational requirements and convergence difficulties when training deep architectures [7]. Future work should investigate whether these findings hold under different precision arithmetic or with pretrained weights.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The preregistered hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These findings contradict prior suggestions that increasing entropy improves robustness in Bayesian contexts [6] and highlight the risks of applying uncertainty mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity in Transformers. Future research should explore whether posterior contraction issues [13] or optimization stability [1] drive this failure before recommending entropy maximization for robustness tasks.

Abstract: Uncertainty quantification is critical for deploying neural networks in safety-critical domains, yet standard architectures often lack calibrated confidence estimates. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) address this by modelling weight uncertainty, though computational constraints and convergence difficulties persist. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated it on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary and confirmatory replication cohorts. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary: mean contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]; Replication: mean contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization enhances robustness in this setting, suggesting that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

Introduction: Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models permeate scientific and real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions, addressing the black-box nature of standard deep learning methods [12]. Within this framework, uncertainty can be categorised in terms of the ingrained randomness of observing certain data and the uncertainty from our lack of knowledge about how data can be created and observed [5]. While uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], standard backpropagation lacks calibrated probabilistic predictions and tends to overfit [17].

This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. Validating or refuting the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [7] in modern architectures guides whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin.

Discussion: The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the mechanism suggested by prior work on node-based BNNs, where increasing the entropy of latent variables was observed to improve performance under covariate shift [6]. While [6] proposed that diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of latent variables, our results indicate this mechanism does not translate to multiplicative weight noise in Transformers trained with SGD.

The failure may relate to optimization dynamics or posterior geometry. Approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift, particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. Although our synthetic data mimicked UCI HAR statistics, specific feature dependencies may have hindered the entropy-maximized posterior from contracting effectively around robust solutions. Furthermore, robustness is not guaranteed by model scale; larger models are not necessarily more robust, and more diverse pretraining data can enhance robustness [8]. Our study used a modest Transformer architecture without diverse pretraining, which may limit the generalization benefits typically associated with uncertainty methods. Additionally, factors such as distillation can be harmful to out-of-distribution generalization [8], suggesting that regularization techniques interacting with uncertainty parameters require careful tuning.

Optimization stability may also play a role. Convergence stability of SGD can vary under different precision and momentum settings [1], and while we used standard SGD, uninvestigated hyperparameter interactions could influence the efficacy of entropy regularization. The computational constraints inherent in Bayesian learning [7] further suggest that simpler regularization methods might outperform complex uncertainty quantification in resource-constrained settings. Ultimately, these results suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this specific architectural context without further evidence.

Conclusion: This study tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The preregistered hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These findings contradict prior suggestions that increasing entropy improves robustness in Bayesian contexts [6] and highlight the risks of applying uncertainty mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity in Transformers. Future research should explore whether posterior contraction issues [13] or optimization stability [1] drive this failure before recommending entropy maximization for robustness tasks.

=== abstract ===
This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We hypothesized that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated it on synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across 43 seeds in a Primary cohort and 43 seeds in a Confirmatory Replication cohort. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the deterministic baseline in both cohorts. In the Primary cohort, the contrast was -0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002), and in the Replication cohort, it was -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture. The findings suggest that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift without further validation on real-world data.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models are deployed in safety-critical applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, though Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Recent work has explored node-based alternatives and weight noise injection to achieve robustness [15]. However, it remains an open problem whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

This work addresses the gap that while prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast $H_s$ exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report results from a Primary cohort and a Confirmatory Replication cohort, adhering to the preregistered decision rule.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input layer, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) feedforward network, and a final residual connection. The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooled over time, and passed through a Linear(64,6) classifier.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized 43 seeds for the Primary cohort and 43 seeds for the Confirmatory Replication cohort. The Primary seeds ranged from 497360171578835126 to 3754669615394449950, and the Replication seeds ranged from 460845256865125083 to 2718212184032681684. The dataset mimicked the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered hypothesis stated that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast $H_s$ exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for all metrics.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. The mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], compared to 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for the baseline (Figure 1). The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline, with NegCtrl1 at 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] and NegCtrl2 at 0.909 [0.906, 0.912].

In the Confirmatory Replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. The mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], compared to 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] for the baseline (Figure 3). The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline, with NegCtrl1 at 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] and NegCtrl2 at 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]. Training dynamics showed consistent divergence between the intervention and baseline conditions over steps (Figure 2, Figure 4).

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention yielded lower accuracy than the baseline, with significant negative contrasts. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would enhance robustness in this setting.

These results relate directly to prior literature on Bayesian robustness. While *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], our results suggest that weight-based entropy maximization in Transformers does not replicate this benefit and may hinder performance. This aligns with *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift*, which warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Furthermore, while *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15], our implementation of entropy-maximized noise did not confer similar advantages, indicating that the mechanism of noise injection is critical and entropy maximization alone may be insufficient or detrimental in attention-based architectures.

It is crucial to reinforce that these findings are based on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. While the subject-disjoint split simulates distribution shift, the synthetic data limitations preclude claims about real-world deployment without further validation. The calibrated claims required for this testbed do not extend to operational environments where data distributions may differ substantially from the synthetic generation process. Future work should validate whether these refutations hold on real-world sensor data before guiding practitioner priorities regarding entropy maximization for robustness tasks.

=== limitations ===
The primary limitation of this study is the use of synthetic data generated to mimic UCI HAR statistics. While this allowed for controlled subject-disjoint splits and avoidance of external dependencies, it may not capture the full complexity and noise characteristics of real-world inertial signals. Additionally, the study was limited to a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture; results may not generalize to other model sizes or attention mechanisms. The experiment was also constrained to 50 epochs of training, and longer training schedules might yield different convergence behaviors for the entropy-maximized weights. Finally, the negative results regarding entropy maximization may be specific to the multiplicative noise implementation used here and do not rule out other forms of uncertainty quantification.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report presents a valid refutation of the hypothesis that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. Across 86 total seeds in Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training. These findings suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this architecture without further evidence. The results highlight the importance of empirical validation for uncertainty mechanisms, as theoretical benefits of diversity optimization did not translate to performance gains in this experimental setting.

Introduction: Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models are deployed in safety-critical applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, though Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Recent work has explored node-based alternatives and weight noise injection to achieve robustness [15]. However, it remains an open problem whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

This work addresses the gap that while prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast $H_s$ exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report results from a Primary cohort and a Confirmatory Replication cohort, adhering to the preregistered decision rule.

Discussion: The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention yielded lower accuracy than the baseline, with significant negative contrasts. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would enhance robustness in this setting.

These results relate directly to prior literature on Bayesian robustness. While *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], our results suggest that weight-based entropy maximization in Transformers does not replicate this benefit and may hinder performance. This aligns with *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift*, which warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Furthermore, while *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15], our implementation of entropy-maximized noise did not confer similar advantages, indicating that the mechanism of noise injection is critical and entropy maximization alone may be insufficient or detrimental in attention-based architectures.

It is crucial to reinforce that these findings are based on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. While the subject-disjoint split simulates distribution shift, the synthetic data limitations preclude claims about real-world deployment without further validation. The calibrated claims required for this testbed do not extend to operational environments where data distributions may differ substantially from the synthetic generation process. Future work should validate whether these refutations hold on real-world sensor data before guiding practitioner priorities regarding entropy maximization for robustness tasks.

Conclusion: This Registered Report presents a valid refutation of the hypothesis that entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers. Across 86 total seeds in Primary and Replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training. These findings suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this architecture without further evidence. The results highlight the importance of empirical validation for uncertainty mechanisms, as theoretical benefits of diversity optimization did not translate to performance gains in this experimental setting.

=== abstract ===
This Registered Report evaluates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise on a PreNormTransformerEncoder using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. The preregistered hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. In the Primary cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened accuracy by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the Confirmatory replication cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened accuracy by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts yielded a preregistered decision of direction_refuted. These results indicate that, within this synthetic testbed, entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise did not enhance subject-disjoint generalization and significantly degraded performance relative to deterministic baselines.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this challenge [12], particularly for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4]. However, weight-based Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Node-based BNNs have been proposed as scalable alternatives, where the diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of latent variables [6]. This work addresses the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

We investigate the research question: Does explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training? The hypothesis states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This study validates or refutes the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [7] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. We report results from a preregistered protocol executed on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics, separating Primary and Confirmatory replication cohorts.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters of machine learning algorithms [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer. The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input layer, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and a final residual. The head comprised a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6).

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized synthetic data mimicking the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). The primary analysis used 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The confirmatory replication used 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). The metric was held-out classification accuracy. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for each condition. Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds for the Primary and Replication cohorts, respectively. Figure 2 and Figure 4 display mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see the results table). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while the baseline achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. Negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911]; NegCtrl2: 0.909 [0.906, 0.912]). These results are visualized in Figure 1.

=== abstract ===
This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The experiment used the real UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K) on the official subject-disjoint split, trained for a calibrated budget of 12 epochs with batch size 128 and SGD(lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention worsened held-out classification accuracy compared to the baseline in both primary and replication cohorts. In the primary cohort, the proposed method achieved 0.8604 accuracy versus 0.9085 for the baseline (contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The replication cohort confirmed this direction (contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization in this setting, aligning with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Deep learning methods operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify [12]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this, characterizing uncertainty due to the network versus data observation [5]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives that induce epistemic uncertainty by multiplying hidden nodes with latent random variables [6]. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We test the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise distributions improves subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives. We preregistered the prediction that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098 proportion. We report results from a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort using real sensor data.
