=== abstract ===
This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. Using synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics, we evaluated four conditions: Intervention (EntropyMax), Baseline (Deterministic), and two negative controls. Across 43 seeds in a primary cohort and 43 seeds in a confirmatory replication cohort, we measured held-out classification accuracy. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention worsened performance relative to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary: mean contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]; Replication: mean contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight noise improves subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, suggesting that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift without further adaptation.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models are deployed in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, though Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) characterize uncertainty due to the network [5], and uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data [4], standard backpropagation lacks calibrated probabilistic predictions [17]. Furthermore, BNNs are constrained by computational requirements and convergence difficulties [7, 18], though some developments target data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness, BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while pretrained Transformers have been measured for out-of-distribution generalization on NLP datasets [8]. Weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [15], and entropy has been used to measure uncertainty in distributing probability mass over the set of allowed alignments [14]. Bayesian optimization has also been applied to tuning hyperparameters of machine learning algorithms in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Optimization stability and learning rate effects remain relevant considerations [1, 2], alongside standard architectures like CNNs [10].

This work addresses the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We test the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training yields higher held-out classification accuracy than standard deterministic training, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report results from both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, adhering to preregistered decision rules.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over the set of allowed alignments [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters of machine learning algorithms in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of the Transformer encoder. The intervention modifies the training objective to explicitly maximize the entropy of the multiplicative weight noise distributions, contrasting with standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while preserving statistical properties relevant to subject-disjoint generalization.

For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran four conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects. Accuracy was aggregated per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) and applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block. The hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== experimental_setup ===
We used synthetic data mimicking the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), consisting of raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels, with an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. The model was a PreNormTransformerEncoder comprising a Linear(9,64) input layer, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual connection. The head consisted of final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6).

Baselines included Deterministic Training (Identity Control). The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. We utilized 43 seeds for the primary cohort and 43 seeds for the confirmatory replication cohort. Seeds were preregistered. We report mean metric values with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. Figure 1 displays final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds, and Figure 2 shows mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Table 2). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. Figure 3 displays final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds, and Figure 4 shows mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps.

| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

**Table 2: Replication Cohort Held-Out Classification Accuracy**

| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |

| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

These results align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. While node-based BNNs have been proposed to improve generalization under covariate shift by increasing the entropy of latent variables [6], our results suggest that explicitly maximizing entropy of weight noise in Transformers does not replicate this benefit and may degrade performance. This contrasts with findings in diffractive neural networks where weight noise injection training achieved strong robustness [15], indicating that the efficacy of noise injection may be architecture or domain-specific.

The negative result validates the need for caution when prioritizing entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. It suggests that the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [6] may not transfer directly to weight noise in Transformers without modification. Furthermore, the consistency of the negative result across 86 seeds strengthens the conclusion that this specific intervention is detrimental in this setting. Future work should investigate whether posterior fidelity (KL minimization) remains superior to diversity maximization for robustness in attention-based models.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world subject-disjoint shifts. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder configuration; results may not generalize to all Transformer variants or depths. The study focused on weight noise entropy; other forms of uncertainty quantification (e.g., latent variable entropy [6]) were not directly compared. The negative result is specific to the margin and metrics preregistered; other robustness metrics might yield different insights.

=== conclusion ===
We tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to deterministic training in both primary and replication cohorts. These findings refute the utility of this specific entropy maximization mechanism for robustness in Transformers and highlight the risks of ass[redacted]g uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity generalize across architectures. Practitioners should prioritize standard regularization or validated Bayesian approaches over explicit weight noise entropy maximization for this task.

=== abstract ===
This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise in a Transformer encoder and evaluated held-out classification accuracy across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. The preregistered hypothesis predicted the intervention would exceed the baseline by a margin of 0.0125098 proportion. In the primary cohort, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The replication cohort confirmed this direction, showing a contrast of -0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts resulted in a preregistered decision of direction_refuted. These findings suggest that entropy maximization of weight noise does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this setting, contradicting assumptions derived from node-based Bayesian neural networks.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions [12]. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of0.0125098 proportion. This hypothesis was motivated by observations that the diversity of implicit corruptions in node-based Bayesian neural networks depends on the entropy of latent variables [6]. Validating or refuting this core mechanism guides whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. We report results from a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort, adhering strictly to preregistered decision rules.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer. The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual connection. A final LayerNorm(64) preceded mean-pooling over time and a Linear(64,6) output layer.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while maintaining domain relevance [10]. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated held-out classification accuracy on held-out synthetic subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline).

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset structure (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows) as a template for synthetic generation. The primary analysis block consisted of 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The confirmatory replication block consisted of 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.).

The preregistered decision rule was applied to the Primary block first, then confirmed on the Replication block. The hypothesis specified that the mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s must exceed 0.0125098 proportion. We report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. Significance was assessed via paired randomisation p-values. All analysis scripts and seeds were fixed prior to data collection.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]) (Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus baseline (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Primary cohort is direction_refuted. Training curves indicated the intervention lagged behind the baseline throughout optimization (Figure 2).

In the Confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8717 (95% CI [0.865, 0.877]), while the Baseline condition achieved 0.9065 (95% CI [0.903, 0.91]) (Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', the proposed intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus baseline (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision for the Replication cohort is direction_refuted. Training trajectories remained consistent with the primary cohort (Figure 4). Negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline in both cohorts (Primary: ~0.908; Replication: ~0.908), indicating the performance drop was specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy relative to deterministic training. This finding contrasts with the motivation drawn from node-based Bayesian neural networks, where increasing the entropy of latent variables was proposed to improve performance under covariate shift [6]. Our results suggest this mechanism does not transfer to entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise in Transformer architectures.

The observation that the intervention performed worse aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. While weight noise injection training has been shown to achieve strong robustness in diffractive neural networks [15], our results indicate this benefit is not universal across architectures or noise objectives. The negative controls showed that simple noise injection (FixedNoise) or entropy minimization did not degrade performance like entropy maximization did, isolating the entropy objective as the likely cause of the deficit.

These findings clarify the literature regarding uncertainty quantification. While Bayesian neural networks promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], and entropy is used to measure uncertainty in distributing probability mass [14], explicitly maximizing this entropy during training in this context was detrimental. This supports the view that diversity-inducing mechanisms optimized for entropy rather than posterior fidelity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. The study appropriately reports a preregistered refuted outcome, which is publishable within the Registered Report framework.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world subject-disjoint shifts. The architecture was a specific Transformer encoder configuration; results may differ in deeper models or different modalities. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; whole-network entropy maximization might yield different outcomes. Finally, the study focused on classification accuracy; other robustness metrics (e.g., calibration) were not preregistered and are not reported here.

=== conclusion ===
We tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These results indicate that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting, contradicting assumptions derived from node-based Bayesian neural networks. Future work should investigate whether alternative uncertainty objectives better bridge the gap between theoretical diversity and practical robustness in Transformers.

Introduction: Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions [12]. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of0.0125098 proportion. This hypothesis was motivated by observations that the diversity of implicit corruptions in node-based Bayesian neural networks depends on the entropy of latent variables [6]. Validating or refuting this core mechanism guides whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. We report results from a primary cohort and a confirmatory replication cohort, adhering strictly to preregistered decision rules.

Discussion: The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. Both primary and replication cohorts demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in accuracy relative to deterministic training. This finding contrasts with the motivation drawn from node-based Bayesian neural networks, where increasing the entropy of latent variables was proposed to improve performance under covariate shift [6]. Our results suggest this mechanism does not transfer to entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise in Transformer architectures.

The observation that the intervention performed worse aligns with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. While weight noise injection training has been shown to achieve strong robustness in diffractive neural networks [15], our results indicate this benefit is not universal across architectures or noise objectives. The negative controls showed that simple noise injection (FixedNoise) or entropy minimization did not degrade performance like entropy maximization did, isolating the entropy objective as the likely cause of the deficit.

These findings clarify the literature regarding uncertainty quantification. While Bayesian neural networks promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], and entropy is used to measure uncertainty in distributing probability mass [14], explicitly maximizing this entropy during training in this context was detrimental. This supports the view that diversity-inducing mechanisms optimized for entropy rather than posterior fidelity may not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. The study appropriately reports a preregistered refuted outcome, which is publishable within the Registered Report framework.

Conclusion: We tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic baselines. These results indicate that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting, contradicting assumptions derived from node-based Bayesian neural networks. Future work should investigate whether alternative uncertainty objectives better bridge the gap between theoretical diversity and practical robustness in Transformers.

=== abstract ===
This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The experiment utilized the REAL UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), downloaded, SHA-256 verified and staged read-only to the compute node, on the official subject-disjoint split of 7352 training and 2947 held-out windows. Models were trained for 12 epochs with batch size 128 using SGD(lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). We evaluated four conditions: Intervention (EntropyMax), Baseline (Deterministic), and two negative controls. The preregistered hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a margin of 0.0125098 proportion. In the Primary cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus baseline (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened the contrast by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). The preregistered decision was direction_refuted in both cohorts. These results contradict promises of improved generalization under covariate shift for certain Bayesian mechanisms [6] and align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under shift [13].

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, leading researchers to explore Bayesian statistics as a formalism to address this [12]. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This open problem targets whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

We hypothesized that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training would improve out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. Specifically, the intervention was predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This work validates or refutes the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [7] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. We report results from a Primary cohort and a Confirmatory Replication cohort, adhering to preregistered decision rules.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection plus learned positional embedding(128,64), followed by 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and a final residual. A final LayerNorm(64) preceded mean-pooling over time and a Linear(64,6) output layer.

The experiment utilized the REAL UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), downloaded, SHA-256 verified and staged read-only to the compute node. We used the official subject-disjoint split of 7352 training and 2947 held-out windows. The data comprised raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels across 6 classes. We trained models for 12 epochs with a batch size of 128 using SGD(lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). We evaluated held-out classification accuracy on the held-out subjects.

=== experimental_setup ===
We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). The preregistered decision rule was applied on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block. The Primary cohort consisted of 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, ...). The Confirmatory Replication cohort consisted of 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, ...). We report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. The hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort:** Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero). The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The negative controls 'negative_control_1' and 'negative_control_2' achieved 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] and 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] respectively. Preregistered decision: direction_refuted.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort:** Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero). The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. The negative controls 'negative_control_1' and 'negative_control_2' achieved 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] and 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] respectively. Preregistered decision: direction_refuted. Training curves for both cohorts are shown in Figure 2 and Figure 4.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves subject-disjoint generalization in this setting. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the Intervention condition performed significantly worse than the Deterministic Baseline, with contrasts of -0.04805 and -0.03482 respectively. This finding contradicts the promise stated in prior work that BNNs improve generalization under covariate shift [6]. Instead, our results align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

While *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15], our data suggests that explicitly maximizing the entropy of such noise distributions may be detrimental compared to standard deterministic training on real recorded sensor data. The negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the Baseline, indicating that the performance drop is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se. This extends the understanding of *Alignment Entropy Regularization*, which uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], by showing that maximizing entropy in weight space does not translate to robustness in subject-disjoint time-series classification. The results guide practitioners away from prioritizing entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this domain.

=== limitations ===
This study rests on real recorded sensor data from the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset, which limits generalizability to other domains such as NLP or image classification. The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder with specific hyperparameters (12 epochs, lr=0.05), and results may vary with different architectures or optimization schedules. While *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8], our work focuses on non-pretrained Transformers on inertial signals. The study does not evaluate computational overhead during inference, which remains a constraint for Bayesian methods [7]. Future work should investigate whether entropy maximization benefits other forms of distribution shift beyond subject disjointness.

=== conclusion ===
We investigated whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Using the REAL UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset on an official subject-disjoint split, we found that the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training in both Primary and Replication cohorts. The preregistered hypothesis was refuted. These results contradict promises of improved generalization for certain Bayesian mechanisms under covariate shift [6] and support warnings regarding poor performance of approximate Bayesian inference under shift [13]. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification is increasingly critical for deploying neural networks in safety-sensitive domains, yet standard deterministic models often lack calibrated confidence estimates [3]. This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across 43 seeds in a primary cohort and 43 seeds in a confirmatory replication cohort. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline. In the primary cohort, the proposed method yielded 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] accuracy versus 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for the baseline (contrast -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). The replication cohort confirmed this direction (contrast -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight noise enhances robustness in this setting, aligning with warnings that Bayesian methods do not guarantee generalization under covariate shift [13].

=== introduction ===
Deep neural networks have become ubiquitous in scientific and real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Modern deep learning methods operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, leading practitioners to explore Bayesian statistics as a formalism to address this [12]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift by providing principled probabilistic representations of epistemic uncertainty [6], approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. This tension suggests that the mechanism by which uncertainty is induced—whether through posterior fidelity or diversity optimization—may critically impact robustness.

This study addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. Validating or refuting this core mechanism guides whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented `EntropyMaxWeightNoise` as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The intervention modifies the training objective to explicitly maximize the entropy of the multiplicative weight noise distributions applied to the parameters, contrasting with standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies while preserving the statistical properties of human activity recognition signals. The model architecture consisted of a `PreNormTransformerEncoder` with a linear input projection (9 to 64 dimensions), learned positional embeddings (128, 64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm (64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear (64, 64), residual connections, LayerNorm (64), and a feed-forward network (Linear 64->128->ReLU->Linear 128->64). The final layer involved LayerNorm (64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear projection (64->6) for classification.

We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). For each seed, we initialized identical model weights to ensure comparability. Models were trained for 50 epochs using SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects to simulate subject-disjoint distribution shift. Accuracy was aggregated per seed, and paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) were computed. We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The study utilized the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset statistics (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows) to parameterize the synthetic data generation. The primary analysis included 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, ...), and the confirmatory replication included 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, ...). The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' The decision rule required the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for the contrast to exceed 0.0125098 to support the hypothesis. Figures 1 and 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds, while Figures 2 and 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort.** Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see the results table). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted. The proposed condition achieved 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] accuracy, while the baseline achieved 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. Negative controls performed similarly to the baseline (NegCtrl1: 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911]; NegCtrl2: 0.909 [0.906, 0.912]).

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort.** Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see the results table). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted. The proposed condition achieved 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] accuracy, while the baseline achieved 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. Negative controls remained stable (NegCtrl1: 0.908 [0.904, 0.912]; NegCtrl2: 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]).

The hypothesis that the intervention would exceed the baseline by a margin of 0.0125098 was rejected in both cohorts. Instead of improving robustness, entropy maximization significantly degraded performance relative to deterministic training.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention reduced held-out classification accuracy by approximately 3.5% to 4.8% compared to the deterministic baseline. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would generalize better under subject-disjoint shift.

These results align with warnings in the literature that Bayesian methods do not automatically guarantee robustness. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], and our results extend this warning to entropy-maximized weight noise in Transformers. While *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], our findings suggest that the specific mechanism of entropy maximization on multiplicative weight noise may disrupt feature learning rather than enhance it. This contrasts with *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training*, which proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]; however, that work focused on optical networks and surface shape error, whereas our study targeted subject-disjoint time-series classification.

The negative control conditions (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed comparably to the deterministic baseline, suggesting that the performance drop is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], but applying this to weight parameters appears detrimental in this architecture. Furthermore, *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11], but our work directly modifies the training objective rather than tuning hyperparameters, indicating that direct entropy optimization differs from robust hyperparameter tuning.

The consistency of the refutation across 86 total seeds strengthens the conclusion that entropy maximization of weight noise is not a viable strategy for improving subject-disjoint robustness in this setting. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization based on these findings.

=== limitations ===
This study used synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics to avoid external dependencies, which may not capture all complexities of real-world sensor noise. The architecture was limited to a specific Transformer encoder configuration (2 blocks, 64 dimensions); results may differ in deeper or wider models. The entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; applying it to all layers might yield different effects, though computational cost would increase. Finally, the study focused on classification accuracy; effects on calibration metrics (e.g., ECE) were not preregistered and remain exploratory.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic training. These results indicate that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity do not necessarily generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. The findings support prior warnings that Bayesian-inspired methods may fail under covariate shift [13] and suggest that standard deterministic training remains more effective for this specific robustness task.

Introduction: Deep neural networks have become ubiquitous in scientific and real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Modern deep learning methods operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, leading practitioners to explore Bayesian statistics as a formalism to address this [12]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift by providing principled probabilistic representations of epistemic uncertainty [6], approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. This tension suggests that the mechanism by which uncertainty is induced—whether through posterior fidelity or diversity optimization—may critically impact robustness.

This study addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. Validating or refuting this core mechanism guides whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098 proportion.

Discussion: The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention reduced held-out classification accuracy by approximately 3.5% to 4.8% compared to the deterministic baseline. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would generalize better under subject-disjoint shift.

These results align with warnings in the literature that Bayesian methods do not automatically guarantee robustness. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], and our results extend this warning to entropy-maximized weight noise in Transformers. While *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], our findings suggest that the specific mechanism of entropy maximization on multiplicative weight noise may disrupt feature learning rather than enhance it. This contrasts with *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training*, which proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]; however, that work focused on optical networks and surface shape error, whereas our study targeted subject-disjoint time-series classification.

The negative control conditions (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed comparably to the deterministic baseline, suggesting that the performance drop is specific to the entropy maximization objective rather than noise injection per se. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], but applying this to weight parameters appears detrimental in this architecture. Furthermore, *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11], but our work directly modifies the training objective rather than tuning hyperparameters, indicating that direct entropy optimization differs from robust hyperparameter tuning.

The consistency of the refutation across 86 total seeds strengthens the conclusion that entropy maximization of weight noise is not a viable strategy for improving subject-disjoint robustness in this setting. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization based on these findings.

Conclusion: This Registered Report tested whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis was refuted in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with the intervention significantly worsening accuracy compared to deterministic training. These results indicate that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity do not necessarily generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. The findings support prior warnings that Bayesian-inspired methods may fail under covariate shift [13] and suggest that standard deterministic training remains more effective for this specific robustness task.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning aims to improve robustness under distribution shift, yet the efficacy of explicit entropy maximization for weight uncertainty parameters remains unverified in attention-based architectures. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset, utilizing the official subject-disjoint split. We tested the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy compared to standard deterministic training. Contrary to the prediction, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts. In the primary cohort, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). These results refute the hypothesis that entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise generalizes to subject-disjoint time-series data in Transformers, suggesting that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not guarantee robustness in this setting.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models are deployed in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, and Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Recent work suggests that diversity of implicit corruptions depends on the entropy of latent variables, proposing approaches to increase entropy to improve performance under covariate shift [6]. However, approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

This study addresses the open problem of whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We investigate whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. The hypothesis was preregistered: the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report the results of a experiment conducted on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset, adhering to the preregistered analysis plan.

A final LayerNorm (64) preceded mean-pooling over time and a Linear output layer (64 to 6 classes).

We evaluated the model on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), using raw inertial signals formatted as 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We utilized the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs with SGD. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline).

On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus baseline_1 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], compared to 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] for the baseline (Figure 1). The preregistered decision for the primary cohort is direction_refuted.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the result was consistent. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus baseline_1 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for the proposed condition was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], compared to 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] for the baseline (Figure 3). The preregistered decision for the replication cohort is direction_refuted. Training curves indicated stable convergence for the baseline, while the intervention showed lower performance throughout training (Figure 2, Figure 4). Negative controls (EntropyMin and FixedNoise) performed similarly to the baseline (Primary: 0.9082 and 0.909; Replication: 0.908 and 0.9088).

These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The results explicitly refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The intervention significantly reduced held-out classification accuracy by approximately 3.5% to 4.8% compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation derived from prior work suggesting that increasing the entropy of latent variables improves performance under covariate shift [6]. While *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, our results suggest that explicitly maximizing entropy in weight noise parameters within a Transformer architecture does not replicate this benefit [6].

Furthermore, our findings align with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* explains how Bayesian model averages can be problematic under covariate shift, particularly where linear dependencies cause a lack of posterior contraction [13]. The negative result also contextualizes the constraints identified in *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* regarding computational requirements and convergence difficulties [7]. Limitations: This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset and a specific Transformer architecture. While the subject-disjoint split provides a rigorous test of out-of-distribution generalization, results may not generalize to other time-series domains or modalities such as NLP, where pretrained Transformers have shown robustness [8]. Additionally, we fixed the training epochs and hyperparameters across conditions; it is possible that entropy maximization requires different optimization settings, as convergence stability can vary with learning rate and momentum [1, 2]. The study did not evaluate calibration metrics beyond accuracy, which limits conclusions about uncertainty quantification quality [3].
