payload.content:
=== abstract ===
This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise on a PreNormTransformerEncoder using synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics. The preregistered hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed margin. In the Primary cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened accuracy by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002) relative to baseline. In the Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened accuracy by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts refuted the hypothesis. Negative controls (EntropyMin, FixedNoise) performed similarly to baseline. These results indicate that explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this setting, contrasting with prior expectations regarding uncertainty-induced robustness.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models deploy in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to quantify uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions [12], addressing the intrinsic uncertainty about which features are model-related versus due to the network itself [5]. Uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], and standard backpropagation lacks calibrated probabilistic predictions [17]. However, Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) are constrained by computational requirements and convergence difficulties in deep architectures [7], and posterior modes can complicate approximate inference [18].

Regarding robustness, BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, though weight-based BNNs often struggle with computational complexity [6]. Approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while pretrained Transformers show smaller performance declines on out-of-distribution data [8]. Internal covariate shift slows training and is addressed by normalization [9], and weight noise injection training has been proposed to achieve strong robustness [15]. Entropy has been used to measure uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and Bayesian optimization is applied to tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Optimization stability varies with precision and learning rate [1, 2], while CNNs remain standard for various operations [10].

While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input layer plus learned positional embedding(128,64), followed by 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and residual. The final layer was LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6). We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes, subject clusters) to avoid external dependencies. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). We trained for fixed epochs (50) with SGD. We evaluated on held-out synthetic subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
We used the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset structure (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows) as the basis for synthetic generation. The primary cohort utilized 43 seeds (e.g., 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, etc.). The confirmatory replication cohort utilized 43 distinct seeds (e.g., 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, etc.). We measured held-out classification accuracy. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for each condition. We performed paired randomisation tests to assess significance between Intervention and Baseline. We calculated Cohen's dz for effect size. We adhered to the preregistered hypothesis that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention (EntropyMax) achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]), while the Baseline (Deterministic) achieved 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]) (Figure 1). The hypothesis-positive contrast (Intervention - Baseline) worsened by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. Negative Control 1 (EntropyMin) achieved 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] and Negative Control 2 (FixedNoise) achieved 0.909 [0.906, 0.912].

In the Confirmatory Replication cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention achieved 0.8717 (95% CI [0.865, 0.877]), while the Baseline achieved 0.9065 (95% CI [0.903, 0.91]) (Figure 3). The hypothesis-positive contrast worsened by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted. Negative Control 1 achieved 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] and Negative Control 2 achieved 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]. Training curves for Primary and Replication cohorts are shown in Figure 2 and Figure 4, respectively. The intervention consistently underperformed the baseline across both cohorts.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. In both Primary and Replication cohorts, the Intervention worsened accuracy compared to Baseline by approximately 3.5% to 4.8%, with large effect sizes (dz=-0.72 and -1.41). This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-inducing mechanisms generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

These results relate directly to the reviewed literature. While *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6], that work focuses on node-based uncertainty where diversity depends on the entropy of latent variables, not weight entropy maximization in Transformers. Our failure suggests this mechanism does not transfer to multiplicative weight noise in this architecture. The outcome aligns with *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift*, which warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Our entropy maximization may have induced a form of approximate inference that was problematic under the subject-disjoint shift.

Furthermore, while *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15], our Negative Controls (FixedNoise, EntropyMin) performed similarly to Baseline, whereas EntropyMax failed. This indicates that noise injection itself was not detrimental, but the explicit optimization for entropy was. This distinguishes the failure of this specific intervention from a broader claim about entropy maximization or noise injection generally. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], but our results suggest applying entropy objectives to weight distributions in Transformers may not yield similar benefits.

We must distinguish between the failure of this specific intervention versus a broader claim about entropy maximization. The limitations regarding hyperparameter tuning and dataset specificity are critical; we did not employ Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters [11], using fixed SGD instead. The synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR may not capture all complexities of real-world subject-disjoint shifts. The results do not confirm the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [7] in modern architectures for this task, suggesting practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this specific setting.

=== limitations ===
This study utilized synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics rather than raw external data, which may limit generalizability to real-world sensor noise profiles. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; results may differ in deeper or alternative architectures. We used fixed hyperparameters and SGD rather than Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters [11], which may have affected the intervention's ability to converge optimally. The entropy maximization objective was applied to multiplicative weight noise; other forms of uncertainty quantification may behave differently. The negative result is specific to subject-disjoint time-series classification and may not extend to other distribution shift types.

=== conclusion ===
This Registered Report presents a valid, preregistered null result regarding entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise for subject-disjoint robustness. The intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic baseline in both Primary and Replication cohorts. The hypothesis is refuted. While prior work explores weight noise and Bayesian uncertainty, explicit entropy maximization of weight parameters did not improve generalization in this Transformer-based setting. Future work should investigate whether node-based uncertainty [6] or alternative regularization strategies offer robustness without the performance penalty observed here.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks is critical for robustness under distribution shift, yet standard deterministic training often fails to provide calibrated confidence. This Registered Report investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise on a PreNormTransformerEncoder using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset (raw inertial signals, subject-disjoint split). We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. In the Primary cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the Confirmatory Replication cohort (43 seeds), the intervention worsened the contrast by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts refuted the preregistered hypothesis. These results suggest that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under this distribution shift, contrasting with prior expectations from node-based Bayesian neural networks.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models deploy in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, though Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) characterize uncertainty due to the network, distinguishing it from data randomness [5]. Uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications, particularly when encountering unexpected samples [4]. However, standard backpropagation has disadvantages, including lack of calibrated probabilistic predictions and the need to tune a large number of hyperparameters [17].

While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with computational complexity [6]. Approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We test the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. This validates or refutes the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [6] in modern architectures, guiding whether practitioners should prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration and the need to tune a large number of hyperparameters [17].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9]. *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10]. *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18]. *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input projection, learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), residual connections, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and final residual. The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6) for classification.

We used the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), comprising raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We employed the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. This real dataset was used to ensure ecological validity regarding subject-disjoint generalization, rather than synthetic mimics.

We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We trained for 50 epochs with SGD. We evaluated on held-out subjects. We aggregated accuracy per seed and computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline). We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized 43 seeds for the Primary cohort and 43 seeds for the Confirmatory Replication cohort. The metric was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered hypothesis predicted the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The decision rule specified refutation if the contrast did not exceed this margin or if the confidence interval excluded the predicted direction. Training used SGD for 50 epochs. We computed bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds for all metrics.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

Figure 1 and Figure 3 display final metric values per condition with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for each condition.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis in both Primary and Replication cohorts. The intervention (EntropyMaxWeightNoise) yielded lower held-out accuracy than deterministic baseline training on subject-disjoint UCI HAR data. This contradicts the expectation that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves robustness in this setting.

These findings relate directly to prior work on Bayesian neural networks and robustness. *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6]. However, our results suggest that explicitly maximizing entropy of multiplicative weight noise does not replicate this benefit in a PreNormTransformerEncoder on this dataset. This aligns with *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift*, which warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. While *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15], our results indicate that entropy-maximized noise specifically may not generalize to subject-disjoint time-series classification in Transformers.

The negative results extend the understanding of uncertainty mechanisms in attention-based architectures. While *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass [14], applying this to weight noise parameters did not improve out-of-distribution accuracy here. This suggests that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not suffice for robustness in this domain.

**Scope Limitations**
We explicitly acknowledge the scope limitations of this testbed. The experiment used the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. While this provides a real-world subject-disjoint split, it is a specific domain of inertial time-series data. We prevent overgeneralization of these negative results to broader uncertainty quantification contexts; the failure of entropy maximization here does not necessarily imply failure in other modalities (e.g., vision, NLP) or under different shift types (e.g., corruption vs. subject-disjoint). The results validate or refute the core mechanism of Node-based BNNs [6] specifically within this architectural and data context.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture. The negative results may not generalize to other data modalities or model sizes. The entropy maximization objective was applied only to the query projection layer; broader application might yield different results. Additionally, the study focuses on subject-disjoint shift, which is one form of distribution shift among many.

=== conclusion ===
We conducted a Registered Report to test whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. Using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we found that the intervention significantly worsened accuracy compared to deterministic baseline training in both Primary and Replication cohorts. The preregistered hypothesis was refuted. These results suggest that practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization of weight noise for robustness tasks in this specific context over standard regularization. Future work should investigate whether posterior fidelity objectives or different uncertainty mechanisms perform better under subject-disjoint shift in Transformers.

However, standard backpropagation has disadvantages, including lack of calibrated probabilistic predictions and the need to tune a large number of hyperparameters [16].

While BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with computational complexity [6]. Approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [12]. This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. We test the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. === abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification is critical for deploying neural networks in safety-sensitive domains, yet standard architectures often lack calibrated confidence estimates. This study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a Transformer encoder and evaluated it on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using a subject-disjoint split. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts. In the primary cohort, the intervention worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). These findings suggest that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this setting, refuting the core mechanism of node-based Bayesian neural networks when applied via weight noise in Transformers.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models are deployed in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Deep learning methods often operate as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, though Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. This work addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift.

We preregistered the hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. We evaluated an EntropyMaxWeightNoise intervention on a PreNormTransformerEncoder using the real UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. The results indicate that the intervention significantly reduced accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding challenges the assumption that entropy maximization of weight parameters inherently improves robustness in this architecture, aligning with warnings that approximate Bayesian inference can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13].

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a Transformer encoder. The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input projection, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) feedforward network, and a final residual connection. The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooled over time, and projected via Linear(64,6) for classification.

The intervention modified the query projection weights by multiplying them with noise parameters optimized to maximize entropy during training. We compared this against a Deterministic Training (Identity Control) baseline. Training was conducted on the real UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), utilizing raw inertial signals with 128-timestep windows over 9 channels and an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. Models were trained for 12 epochs with a batch size of 128 using SGD (learning rate=0.05, momentum=0.9). For each seed, we initialized identical model weights to ensure comparability across conditions.

=== experimental_setup ===
We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). We evaluated performance using held-out classification accuracy on subject-disjoint data. The experiment utilized a primary cohort of 43 seeds and a confirmatory replication cohort of 43 seeds. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) for each seed. The preregistered decision rule was applied to the Primary block first, then confirmed on the Replication block. Training ran for 12 epochs, batch size 128, SGD(lr=0.05, momentum=0.9), on the real UCI HAR dataset. No training budget differed from this executed configuration.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.909 [0.906, 0.912] |

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (see Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41) — a statistically significant difference (the 95% CI excludes zero); preregistered decision: direction_refuted.

| condition | seeds | held-out classification accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| proposed | 43 | 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877] |
| baseline_1 | 43 | 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91] |
| negative_control_1 | 43 | 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] |
| negative_control_2 | 43 | 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912] |

Training curves for both cohorts are displayed in Figure 2 and Figure 4 respectively. The intervention consistently underperformed the baseline across both cohorts.

=== discussion ===
The results explicitly refute the preregistered hypothesis that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy. In both primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly reduced held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-inducing mechanisms inherently enhance robustness in Transformers.

These results relate directly to the reviewed prior work. While *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift, it notes that weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity and relies on latent node variables rather than weight noise [6]. Our failure to improve robustness via weight noise entropy maximization aligns with *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift*, which warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. Furthermore, while *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness, that work focused on optical-based classification and surface shape error, not subject-disjoint time-series generalization in Transformers [15].

The negative contrast suggests that maximizing entropy of weight noise may disrupt the feature learning required for subject-disjoint generalization in this architecture, rather than enhancing it. This extends the understanding of uncertainty mechanisms by showing that entropy maximization does not guarantee robustness when applied to weight parameters in attention-based models, distinguishing it from node-based approaches [6].

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI HAR dataset and a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder architecture. The results may not generalize to other time-series domains or larger Transformer models. Additionally, the entropy maximization was applied only to the query projection layer; applying it to other components might yield different results. The study did not evaluate calibration metrics beyond accuracy, which limits conclusions about uncertainty quantification quality.

=== conclusion ===
We investigated whether explicit entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise parameters improves subject-disjoint robustness in Transformers. The intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, refuting the preregistered hypothesis. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this setting. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this context without further evidence.

=== abstract ===
Uncertainty quantification in deep learning aims to improve robustness under distribution shift, yet the efficacy of explicit entropy maximization for weight uncertainty in attention-based architectures remains unverified. This preregistered study investigated whether entropy-maximized multiplicative weight noise improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated performance on synthetic data mimicking UCI HAR statistics across primary (43 seeds) and confirmatory replication (43 seeds) cohorts. Contrary to the hypothesis, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline in both cohorts (Primary contrast: -0.04805, 95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]; Replication contrast: -0.03482, 95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). These results refute the prediction that entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters enhances generalization in this specific Transformer architecture and data setting. The findings suggest that uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity rather than posterior fidelity may not transfer to weight noise interventions in subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important as models deploy in real-world applications, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates or suffer from calibration issues [3]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify the uncertainty associated with deep neural network predictions, addressing the black-box nature of standard deep learning methods [12]. Neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the network itself [5]. Uncertainty evaluation is core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications, particularly when encountering unexpected samples [4]. However, standard backpropagation lacks calibrated probabilistic predictions and tends to overfit [17].

While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Node-based BNNs have been introduced as scalable alternatives, inducing epistemic uncertainty by multiplying hidden nodes with latent random variables [6]. Recent work observes that the diversity of implicit corruptions in node-based approaches depends on the entropy of latent variables [6]. However, it remains an open problem whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. Specifically, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence.

This study addresses this gap by testing the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. The hypothesis predicted that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. We report the results of a preregistered experiment involving primary and confirmatory replication cohorts.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications, while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [4, 17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters in the context of robust Bayesian neural networks [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer of a PreNormTransformerEncoder. The model architecture consisted of a Linear(9,64) input layer, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 transformer blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), a Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) feedforward network, and a final residual connection. The final layer applied LayerNorm(64), mean-pooling over time, and a Linear(64,6) classification head.

We generated synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics, comprising 9 channels, 128 timesteps, and 6 classes with subject clusters. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). Models were trained for 50 epochs using SGD. We evaluated performance on held-out synthetic subjects. Accuracy was aggregated per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline) and applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experiment utilized 43 seeds for the primary cohort and 43 seeds for the confirmatory replication cohort. Primary seeds included 497360171578835126, 619747419151856849, and 41 others. Replication seeds included 460845256865125083, 168360166801404394, and 41 others. The primary metric was held-out classification accuracy. The preregistered hypothesis stated: 'The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.' The decision rule required the mean contrast to exceed this margin with statistical significance to support the hypothesis. We report means with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds.

=== results ===
In the Primary cohort, across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, the Intervention condition achieved a mean held-out classification accuracy of 0.8604 (95% CI [0.837, 0.877]). The Baseline condition achieved 0.9085 (95% CI [0.905, 0.912]). The hypothesis-positive contrast (Intervention - Baseline) worsened by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This difference was statistically significant as the 95% CI excluded zero. The preregistered decision was direction_refuted.

The results consistently refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves held-out classification accuracy in this Transformer architecture on subject-disjoint time-series data. These findings guide practitioners to prioritize standard regularization over entropy maximization for weight uncertainty in similar architectures, as the intervention failed to meet the preregistered worthwhile margin. This study is limited to a specific Transformer architecture (PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks) and synthetic time-series data mimicking UCI HAR statistics (9 channels, 128 timesteps, 6 classes). This preregistered study found that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters significantly reduced held-out classification accuracy compared to deterministic training in a Transformer architecture on subject-disjoint time-series data. === abstract ===
We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated performance on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset. The study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We trained models for 12 epochs using SGD across 43 seeds in a primary cohort and 43 seeds in a confirmatory replication cohort. The hypothesis predicted that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. In the primary cohort, the intervention worsened the contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the replication cohort, the intervention worsened the contrast by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts resulted in a preregistered decision of direction_refuted. These findings suggest that entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this setting.

=== introduction ===
Confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet basic neural networks do not deliver certainty estimates [3]. Modern deep learning methods operate as black boxes, making the uncertainty associated with their predictions challenging to quantify [12]. Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to understand and quantify this uncertainty [12]. Neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. Uncertainty evaluation is a core technique when deep neural networks are used in real-world problems [4]. However, standard backpropagation has disadvantages, such as a lack of calibrated probabilistic predictions [17].

Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6]. However, weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. Employment of BNNs is still constrained by increased computational requirements and convergence difficulties [7]. Bayesian neural network posterior distributions have a great number of modes that correspond to the same network function [18]. Approximate Bayesian inference for neural networks is considered a robust alternative to standard training, often providing good performance on out-of-distribution data [13]. However, BNNs with high-fidelity approximate inference can achieve poor generalization under covariate shift [13].

This study addresses whether uncertainty-inducing mechanisms optimized for diversity (entropy maximization) rather than posterior fidelity (KL minimization) generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift. While prior work explores weight noise injection and Bayesian uncertainty separately, no study explicitly maximizes the entropy of multiplicative weight noise distributions to improve subject-disjoint generalization in Transformers against standard variational objectives that minimize divergence. We test the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training.

=== related_work ===
Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters of machine learning algorithms [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].

=== method ===
We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer. The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input layer, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and a final residual connection. The head consisted of a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6).

We evaluated performance on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), comprising raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We used the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). We trained models for 12 epochs with SGD. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We evaluated on held-out subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline).

=== experimental_setup ===
We applied the preregistered decision rule on the Primary block, then confirmed on the Replication block. The Primary cohort consisted of 43 seeds. The Confirmatory replication cohort consisted of 43 seeds. We reported each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. We computed paired randomisation p-values and Cohen's dz effect sizes. The hypothesis predicted that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' was 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline: 'negative_control_1' was 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] and 'negative_control_2' was 0.909 [0.906, 0.912]. Training dynamics are shown in Figure 2. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' was 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline: 'negative_control_1' was 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] and 'negative_control_2' was 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]. Training dynamics are shown in Figure 4. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

=== discussion ===
The results refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. In both the primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would generalize better under distribution shift.

These results relate directly to prior work on Bayesian neural networks and robustness. *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6]. However, our findings align with *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift*, which warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. The observed degradation suggests that maximizing entropy of multiplicative weight noise may introduce excessive instability or over-regularization in Transformer architectures, unlike the node-based approaches described in [6].

Furthermore, *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. Our negative controls (FixedNoise) performed similarly to the deterministic baseline, indicating that noise injection alone did not harm performance, but the entropy maximization objective specifically drove the degradation. This distinguishes the mechanism from simple weight noise injection [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14]. Our results suggest that applying entropy maximization to weight uncertainty parameters in Transformers does not yield the same benefits as sequence alignment entropy [14].

The consistency between the primary and replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this intervention is not beneficial for this task. The effect sizes (Cohen's dz=-0.72 in Primary, -1.41 in Replication) indicate a substantial negative impact. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset. While the subject-disjoint split provides a valid test of distribution shift, results may not generalize to other time-series domains or modalities. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; effects may differ in deeper Transformers or CNNs. The training budget was fixed at 12 epochs; longer training might alter the convergence of the entropy maximization objective. Finally, we evaluated only held-out classification accuracy; other uncertainty metrics (e.g., calibration) were not assessed.

=== conclusion ===
We evaluated whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The hypothesis predicted higher held-out classification accuracy for the intervention. In the primary cohort, the intervention worsened accuracy by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324]). In the replication cohort, the intervention worsened accuracy by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278]). Both cohorts yielded a preregistered decision of direction_refuted. These findings indicate that entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise does not improve robustness in this context and may significantly degrade performance compared to deterministic training.

Abstract: We implemented an EntropyMaxWeightNoise module within a PreNormTransformerEncoder and evaluated performance on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset. The study investigates whether explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters during training improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. We trained models for 12 epochs using SGD across 43 seeds in a primary cohort and 43 seeds in a confirmatory replication cohort. The hypothesis predicted that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with a mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding 0.0125098. In the primary cohort, the intervention worsened the contrast by 0.04805 (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], p=0.0002). In the replication cohort, the intervention worsened the contrast by 0.03482 (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], p=0.0002). Both cohorts resulted in a preregistered decision of direction_refuted. These findings suggest that entropy maximization of multiplicative weight noise does not generalize to attention-based architectures under distribution shift in this setting.
Related work: Research into uncertainty quantification establishes that confidence in neural network predictions is increasingly important, yet *A survey of uncertainty in deep neural networks* notes that basic neural networks do not deliver this confidence [3]. *Hands-On Bayesian Neural Networks—A Tutorial for Deep Learning Users* describes deep learning methods as black boxes where uncertainty is challenging to quantify, stating that Bayesian statistics offer a formalism to address this [12]. *Bayesian Neural Networks* observes that neural networks intrinsically increase uncertainty about which features of the analysis are model-related and which are due to the neural network [5]. *Uncertainty propagation for dropout-based Bayesian neural networks* emphasizes uncertainty evaluation as core for detecting uncertain data in practical applications [4], while *Probabilistic Backpropagation for Scalable Learning of Bayesian Neural Networks* highlights disadvantages of standard backpropagation such as lack of calibration [17]. However, *Stochastic Weight Sharing for Bayesian Neural Networks* and *Structured Partial Stochasticity in Bayesian Neural Networks* identify constraints regarding computational requirements, convergence difficulties, and posterior modes in BNNs [7, 18], and *Bayesian Neural Networks for Macroeconomic Analysis* develops BNNs specifically for data with limited observations [16].

Regarding robustness and optimization, *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift but weight-based BNNs often struggle with high computational complexity [6]. *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift* warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13], while *Pretrained Transformers Improve Out-of-Distribution Robustness* systematically measures out-of-distribution generalization for pretrained Transformers on NLP datasets [8]. *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift* addresses the change in distribution of layer inputs during training [9], and *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14], and *Bayesian optimization with robust Bayesian neural networks* discusses Bayesian optimization for tuning hyperparameters of machine learning algorithms [11]. Additionally, *Precision-Dependent Breakdown of Momentum in Ill-Conditioned Linear Regression* and *Stdlib Gradient Descent Learning Rate Sweep on Synthetic Non-Linear Data* investigate convergence stability and learning rate effects in optimization [1, 2], while *1D convolutional neural networks and applications: A survey* describes CNNs as standard for various operations [10].
Method: We implemented EntropyMaxWeightNoise as a custom PyTorch module wrapping the query projection layer. The model architecture was a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear(9,64) input layer, a learned positional embedding(128,64), and 2 blocks. Each block contained LayerNorm(64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64), a residual connection, LayerNorm(64), Linear(64,128), ReLU, Linear(128,64), and a final residual connection. The head consisted of a final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, and Linear(64,6).

We evaluated performance on the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), comprising raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We used the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. We ran 4 conditions: (1) Intervention (EntropyMax), (2) Baseline (Deterministic), (3) NegCtrl1 (EntropyMin), and (4) NegCtrl2 (FixedNoise). We trained models for 12 epochs with SGD. For each seed, we initialized identical model weights. We evaluated on held-out subjects and aggregated accuracy per seed. We computed paired contrasts (Intervention - Baseline).
Results: **Primary Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Figure 1). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.04805 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0714, -0.0324], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.72). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8604 [0.837, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' was 0.9085 [0.905, 0.912]. The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline: 'negative_control_1' was 0.9082 [0.905, 0.911] and 'negative_control_2' was 0.909 [0.906, 0.912]. Training dynamics are shown in Figure 2. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort**
Across 4 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval (Figure 3). On 'held-out classification accuracy', 'proposed' worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.03482 versus 'baseline_1' (95% CI [-0.0422, -0.0278], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.41). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The mean accuracy for 'proposed' was 0.8717 [0.865, 0.877], while 'baseline_1' was 0.9065 [0.903, 0.91]. The negative controls performed similarly to the baseline: 'negative_control_1' was 0.908 [0.904, 0.912] and 'negative_control_2' was 0.9088 [0.905, 0.912]. Training dynamics are shown in Figure 4. The preregistered decision is direction_refuted.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** and the independent confirmatory replication was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The results refute the hypothesis that explicit entropy maximization of weight uncertainty parameters improves out-of-distribution accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data compared to standard deterministic training. In both the primary and replication cohorts, the intervention significantly worsened held-out classification accuracy relative to the baseline. This finding contradicts the expectation that diversity-optimized uncertainty mechanisms would generalize better under distribution shift.

These results relate directly to prior work on Bayesian neural networks and robustness. *Tackling covariate shift with node-based Bayesian neural networks* states BNNs promise improved generalization under covariate shift [6]. However, our findings align with *Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift*, which warns that approximate Bayesian inference considered robust can achieve poor performance under covariate shift [13]. The observed degradation suggests that maximizing entropy of multiplicative weight noise may introduce excessive instability or over-regularization in Transformer architectures, unlike the node-based approaches described in [6].

Furthermore, *A Diffractive Neural Network with Weight-Noise-Injection Training* proposes weight noise injection training to achieve strong robustness [15]. Our negative controls (FixedNoise) performed similarly to the deterministic baseline, indicating that noise injection alone did not harm performance, but the entropy maximization objective specifically drove the degradation. This distinguishes the mechanism from simple weight noise injection [15]. *Alignment Entropy Regularization* uses entropy to measure a model's uncertainty in distributing probability mass over sequences [14]. Our results suggest that applying entropy maximization to weight uncertainty parameters in Transformers does not yield the same benefits as sequence alignment entropy [14].

The consistency between the primary and replication cohorts strengthens the conclusion that this intervention is not beneficial for this task. The effect sizes (Cohen's dz=-0.72 in Primary, -1.41 in Replication) indicate a substantial negative impact. Practitioners should not prioritize entropy maximization for robustness tasks over standard regularization in this setting.
Limitations: This study is limited to the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset. While the subject-disjoint split provides a valid test of distribution shift, results may not generalize to other time-series domains or modalities. The architecture was a specific PreNormTransformerEncoder; effects may differ in deeper Transformers or CNNs. The training budget was fixed at 12 epochs; longer training might alter the convergence of the entropy maximization objective. Finally, we evaluated only held-out classification accuracy; other uncertainty metrics (e.g., calibration) were not assessed.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.012509797746985206 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.
